stories.Headline: Oracle abandons $7 billion Tencent AI deal under Trump pressure, FT reports
stories.Summary:
Oracle has reportedly cancelled a contract worth about $7 billion to lease artificial intelligence chips to the Chinese technology company Tencent, according to a report from the Financial Times that was picked up by several financial news sites on November 4, 2026. The reports say Oracle dropped the agreement after U.S. officials raised questions about it, and one outlet described the move as coming under pressure from the Trump administration. The deal had been revealed in September and was described as Tencent's largest foreign chip leasing arrangement. Oracle's stock slipped in overnight trading after the news emerged.

Under the terms that were reported, the five-year contract would have given Tencent access to about 100,000 high-end AI processors through Oracle data centers in Southeast Asia. One of the articles said the chips involved were made by Nvidia and would have been used for Chinese AI workloads. The contract was said to include an upfront payment of roughly 30% of its estimated value. The articles did not say whether Oracle would keep any advance payments, or how the cancellation would affect its financial forecast.

The responsible parties are Oracle and the U.S. officials who questioned the arrangement, though the articles do not name any individual officials or quote anyone from Oracle, Tencent or the government. The reports attribute the decision to concerns in Washington about Chinese access to sophisticated computer technologies. One analysis said the cancellation shows that U.S. export scrutiny is shaping which AI contracts Oracle can actually turn into revenue. That same analysis said it reinforces an existing risk for the company rather than creating a new one.

The cancellation highlights the regulatory uncertainty facing cloud providers that use offshore facilities to serve Chinese technology firms, and it raises the question of whether other overseas customers could face similar limits. It also arrives as Oracle is investing heavily in more AI computing capacity, so losing a large contract could remove a significant source of expected income. Separately, Deloitte announced a unified Oracle business group that combines its Oracle consulting, implementation and managed services into one unit. Looking ahead, the articles say investors should watch whether Oracle discloses the financial effect of the cancellation and whether it can replace the lost capacity with commitments from other customers.

stories.Headline: AI platform reproduced Michigan music publishers' copyrighted works without authorization, lawsuit says
stories.Summary:
A Michigan-based music publisher tied to rapper Eminem has sued the artificial intelligence company Suno, alleging that its platform reproduced copyrighted works without permission. The lawsuit was filed on a Friday in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, and it says Suno used 269 musical compositions by Eminem that the publisher, Eight Mile Style, owns or controls. The publisher says those works were used to train Suno's AI model so that users could generate sound recordings from text prompts. Suno, which has an office in San Francisco, is accused of direct copyright infringement, circumvention of protection measures, and removal or alteration of copyright management information.

Suno's AI music generator lets users create a song with vocals and lyrics by describing it in words and clicking a button. According to the court document, the company made illicit copies of millions of copyrighted musical works, including Eight Mile Style's, and built a paid platform on those copies. The lawsuit, citing the digital media company 404 Media, also alleges that Suno scraped millions of songs and lyrics from YouTube Music, Deezer and Genius. As an example, the court document describes a case where Suno generated a track called "Lose Yourself" for a user, which reproduces the lyrics of Eminem's hit song word for word.

Eight Mile Style asks the federal court to find that Suno willfully infringed its copyrights and to order the impoundment or destruction of all unauthorized copies of its works. The publisher is also seeking damages that could exceed $40 million. In a written statement to CBS News, Suno said it exists to help people create original music and does not allow unauthorized use of an artist's work. The company said it blocks prompts naming specific artists and songs, works with third-party providers to screen uploaded audio and lyrics, and plans to add further safeguards.

stories.Headline: Tessl launches software factory platform for AI coding agents
stories.Summary:
Tessl, an AI-native software development firm based in New York, has launched an open standards platform for building software factories. The launch was reported on November 6 and November 8, 2026. The platform is meant to move teams from using coding assistants one developer at a time toward systems where AI agents carry out a larger share of the software development lifecycle. Tessl says that worries about low-quality "AI slop" output, the security risks of giving agents more access, and unpredictable costs have slowed how quickly teams hand work to agents.

Its platform is designed to work with any agent and any model, linking ticket implementation, code review, and vulnerability remediation. Teams on the platform can write reusable skills that describe how an agent should handle a particular task. These skills can be chained into repeatable workflows called loops, with verification and feedback steps that check the output. Over time, Tessl says the loops will improve themselves using those checks and feedback.

The company says it uses the platform internally, and that 80 per cent of one week's pull requests needed no human hand-editing. It also reports that the cost per pull request fell from $75 to $13 across implementation, review, security fixes, and other steps. Ready-made workflows include Ticket to PR, Code Review, and Vulnerability Remediation, which uses scanners such as Snyk to propose fixes and then rescan. Tessl was founded in 2024 by Guy Podjarny, the founder of Snyk, and has raised more than $120 million to date.

Podjarny said that teams are not struggling to assign work to agents, and that the harder problem is getting agents to understand the limits of their work and when to stop. He also said that verification has to accompany greater agent autonomy, and that Tessl Factory supports a gradual approach set by the pace of each team. To encourage first-time users, Tessl is offering $200 in usage credits valid for 30 days from activation, available until November 30. The articles describe this as part of a broader shift toward software factories in which people define and oversee outcomes while agents do most of the execution.

stories.Headline: Democrat shaping AI policy bought chip stocks despite backing congressional trading ban
stories.Summary:
Rep. Josh Gottheimer, a New Jersey Democrat who helps write his party's artificial intelligence agenda, has disclosed new purchases of AI-linked stocks, CNBC reported on Nov. 7. A filing received by the House Clerk on Nov. 4 shows a purchase of Benchmark Electronics stock on Oct. 12 and Applied Materials stock on Oct. 26, each worth between $1,001 and $15,000. Both were made in a jointly owned Morgan Stanley account, which had earlier bought three lots of Advanced Micro Devices shares. The same filing lists a sale of PT Telekomunikasi Indonesia stock. The purchases came just months after he voted to bar lawmakers and their families from buying individual stocks.

The Stop Insider Trading Act, which would prohibit members and their families from buying most individual stocks, passed the House on July 22, but it has not become law. Gottheimer was one of only 13 Democrats to vote for it, while some Democrats objected to a voter-ID provision attached to it. Four years earlier, he backed legislation requiring lawmakers to use blind trusts and pledged to set one up himself. The five AI-linked trades CNBC counted were worth between $5,005 and $75,000 in total, which is small beside the household's disclosed assets of $15.1 million to $59 million, including up to $44.5 million in stocks.

Filings show the AMD buys were made in April and May, before the vote, and that an Applied Materials position was bought in August and sold in September before the October repurchase. Gottheimer's spokesman, Haraden Bottomley, said the congressman handed control of his investments to a third party with full investment discretion before taking office in 2017. He added that Gottheimer is awaiting congressional approval of a blind trust and has meanwhile set up an independent trust. Gottheimer, a former Microsoft executive, sits on the House Financial Services subcommittee that oversees AI in finance, has introduced AI regulation legislation, and co-chairs a commission developing Democrats' broader AI agenda.

CNBC noted there is no evidence of wrongdoing. His household has reported more than 1,100 securities transactions over three years. The disclosures draw fresh attention because Democrats are set to take control of Congress in January, which will give them new power to investigate and regulate the AI industry. Reps.

Maxine Waters and Greg Casar have introduced a resolution opposing taxpayer bailouts for AI companies, referred in part to Gottheimer's committee, and Casar has called for AI executives to testify under oath. The purchases came shortly before a sharp selloff, in which the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.5% on Thursday, with Nvidia down more than 9% and AMD down about 17%. Benchmark fell nearly 17% over Wednesday and Thursday to close at $59.34, roughly 25% below its price on the day of Gottheimer's purchase, before recovering somewhat on Friday. Applied Materials was Benchmark's largest disclosed customer in 2025, making up 14% of its revenue.

stories.Headline: OCC Sets New Expectations for Banks' Use of AI
stories.Summary:
The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency released a supervisory framework on November 4, 2026, laying out how its examiners will assess banks' use of artificial intelligence, with a particular focus on generative AI and increasingly autonomous AI agents. It came with OCC Bulletin 2026-54. The agency said it used AI to help draft the guidance, but that a human reviewed, edited and approved the final version. Baker Donelson noted that federal agencies must now call AI "super intelligence" under President Trump's September 29 Executive Order 14434.

The framework creates four illustrative risk tiers. At the bottom, Tier 4 covers low-risk internal productivity tools, while Tier 1 covers critical uses such as autonomous payment agents, real-time credit decisioning and the release of fraud holds. Risk is judged by what an AI system is allowed to do rather than by how sophisticated it is, so a simple agent that can move money can rank above an advanced model used only for internal drafting. As the stakes rise, examiners may look for stronger testing, tighter limits on autonomy, more meaningful human oversight and greater operational safeguards.

The OCC says the framework imposes no new regulatory requirements and is a resource for examiners, not a self-assessment tool for banks. Much of it is written in permissive terms such as "may" and "could," and it is meant to support examiners' risk-based judgment. It explains how AI can introduce or amplify risks banks already manage, including operational, cybersecurity, privacy, credit and compliance risks. Baker Donelson's analysis says banks need not reinvent their risk programs, but must be able to show those programs address how AI is actually used in their organizations.

The framework fills a gap, because the revised interagency model risk management guidance issued in April, OCC Bulletin 2026-13, expressly excludes generative and agentic AI. That makes the new document the main supervisory reference for those systems. Although it applies to OCC-supervised institutions, Baker Donelson expects the Federal Reserve and the FDIC to take note, so state-chartered banks should be paying attention. Elsewhere, on November 2, the compliance technology firm iCOMPASS introduced a product called KY-AI at Hong Kong FinTech Week, pointing to the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's ART Framework, introduced on October 15, which stresses accountability, resilience and trust as AI becomes more autonomous.

stories.Headline: AI Deepfakes of CEOs and Lawyers Stole $129 Million, Prosecutors Say
stories.Summary:
Three men are charged in a federal indictment unsealed November 5 in Manhattan with using artificial intelligence to impersonate corporate chief executives and attorneys at large law firms. Prosecutors say the group persuaded employees at hospitals, a bank and other companies to wire more than $129 million into accounts it controlled between 2024 and early 2026. The defendants are Jacob Soall, 41, of Marbella, Spain, Sharon Hazan, 54, of Israel, and Guy Sheetrit, 42, of Israel and the United Arab Emirates. Spanish police arrested Soall in June and Hazan in August, Britain's National Crime Agency detained Sheetrit in September, and U.S. extradition requests for all three are pending.

The scheme typically began with an email that appeared to come from a company's chief executive, asking for help with a confidential deal. Employees then received calls in which the group allegedly used AI to copy the executive's voice and, in some cases, face, before handing them to a fake lawyer who borrowed the name of a real attorney at a major firm. The indictment says a handwritten script titled "Lawyer Call" was used to discourage employees from discussing the transaction with colleagues. Victims named by their losses include a British financial technology company, which lost about $11.6 million, a Florida pet food maker, a Massachusetts mutual fund company, a Missouri hospital system and a Rhode Island bank. The money moved through accounts in several countries before being converted into cryptocurrency and divided among the conspirators.

Each defendant faces seven counts, including wire fraud, aggravated identity theft and money laundering, with a combined maximum of 104 years in prison. U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald urged businesses to consider how to guard against what he called the emerging threat of AI-enabled crime. Prosecutors say Hazan, who was convicted of bank fraud conspiracy in the same court in 2008, boasted of laundering more than $400 million in three years. These are allegations, and none of the three has been convicted. The FBI has asked anyone who believes they were targeted to contact the bureau through its online tips page.

The case is a reminder of how much the scheme depended on trust in a familiar voice rather than on hacking. The losses are roughly five times the $25.6 million that British engineering firm Arup lost in 2024 after an employee joined a video call with a deepfake of its finance chief. The indictment also reports that one attempted transfer of about $2.85 million from a major New York investment bank was stopped by the bank's back office before it left. Prosecutors have not said how much of the money has been recovered, and the extradition process for all three defendants is still pending.

stories.Headline: Older Nvidia Chips Just Cost Oracle Its Microsoft AI Deal
stories.Summary:
Microsoft is winding down a multi-year contract to rent AI computing capacity from Oracle, and reports on November 6, 2026 said Oracle's stock fell to a new 52-week low of $109.21 as a result. People familiar with the matter said Microsoft declined to renew the agreement, which dates to 2023 and originally supplied servers for the AI version of Bing, and has been switching the capacity off in recent months. Those sources said the hardware relied on older Nvidia chips that no longer met Microsoft's specifications, though the chip generation was never named and Microsoft declined to comment. Oracle closed that day at $116.01, up 0.74%, for a market value of $361.69 billion, after falling about 5.2% intraday from the prior close of $115.16.

The contract's size and value were never disclosed, so its financial weight is unclear, though one report describes it as a small line item for a company worth $3.94 trillion. Oracle says demand for its AI infrastructure remains strong and that GPUs coming up for renewal were renewed or rented to new customers at a 20% premium in September, with most of them four years old or older. Oracle's utilization was reported at 97.9% that quarter, and its cloud business brought in $18 billion in the year ended May 2026. Microsoft, meanwhile, spent $45.2 billion on capital expenditures in its September quarter, has committed more than $80 billion to renting capacity from third parties such as CoreWeave and Nebius, and plans to narrow that list to a few key suppliers. One source notes that CoreWeave rose 6.14% and Nebius rose 7.58% on November 6.

Microsoft has not explained the decision beyond the reported technical reasons, while Oracle has argued that even its older GPUs still command premium rental prices. Oracle's stock had already fallen sharply, down more than half from its June 1 high of $248.15, and it fell 6.93% on November 5 when the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped 12%. Oracle's free cash flow was -$5.396 billion last quarter, which makes lost renewals more costly. Upcoming checkpoints include CoreWeave's report on November 10, Nvidia's on November 17, and Oracle's next report, expected around December 9, though the company has not confirmed that date. One analysis says falling usage, a vanishing renewal premium, or a close below $109.21 would undercut the view that the stock already reflects much of the downside.

stories.Headline: Tesla unveils AI accelerator roadmap, adopts new 'SI' branding in 'Super Intelligence' push — SI6 to bring 80X more compute performance, Dojo 3 headed to space
stories.Summary:
Tesla has published a revised roadmap for its AI accelerator chips, outlining a new sixth-generation inference chip called the SI6 and a third-generation Dojo training accelerator. The company is now renaming its chip family from the "AI" prefix to "SI," a shift that follows President Trump's call to replace artificial intelligence with super intelligence. Tesla's chips previously used the AI4, AI5 and AI6 labels, and the presentation switched them to SI4, SI5 and SI6. The disclosure came in early November 2026. The SI6 is expected to deliver 80 times the compute of the fourth-generation SI4, which is in volume production and used in vehicles.

Based on the SI4's estimated 216 to 576 TOPS, that works out to roughly 17.28 to 46.08 POPS, and the chip will carry about nine times the SI4's memory. Tesla did not say which data formats the SI6 supports, so those figures are estimates. The chip is slated for launch around 2029 to 2030 and is expected to be made by Samsung on a 2nm-class process. The third-generation Dojo, called D3, will use a chiplet design with 2.5D and 3D packaging and stacked HBM instead of the wafer-scale approach of the first generation.

Tesla has not said whether it has fully given up wafer-scale integration, but the reasons for moving to HBM are clear from the roadmap. Modern AI models need large amounts of memory for parameters, activations and intermediate data, which makes the limited SRAM of the earlier design a poor fit for capacity. Tesla describes D3 as optimized for space, training and scaling, which suggests at least some versions will be built for extraterrestrial use and need radiation hardening. Compute figures, memory capacity, the manufacturing process and the development schedule for D3 have not been released.

The roadmap also reflects Elon Musk's earlier decisions, including the August 2025 cancellation of the wafer-level Dojo project and an August 2026 statement that SpaceX and xAI would rely exclusively on Nvidia hardware. The reported specifications come from Tesla's presentation materials and from estimates built on the SI4, so the final numbers may change before the chips reach production. Tesla has also been criticized for labeling one process node as 5nm-class when the SI4 is generally understood to use a 7nm-class process. Further details on the SI6 and D3 are expected as development progresses, and the company's next disclosures will show whether the targets hold.

stories.Headline: How to get started with AI agents, which are best for specific tasks
stories.Summary:
Agentic artificial intelligence is spreading well beyond tech circles, as Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic and other companies compete for consumer buyers of AI agents designed to act on a user's behalf. Those agents handle tasks ranging from buying groceries to managing to-do lists, and their popularity surged this year even though the leading AI labs have offered agent-like tools for years. Newcomers can find it hard to tell the offerings apart or to know which agent suits which job. The articles also note that agents work better the more they know about a person, which forces users to decide how much personal information they are willing to share.

Many people in the tech world use several agents from different labs rather than relying on one. Jose Artigas, a business consultant working on AI strategy, said no single agent can yet do everything, so he and others use a "stack" of tools. The consumer agents differ in cost: some are free, some need a monthly subscription, and others are still in testing or unavailable in many countries outside the U.S. Clara Gigling, founder of Oudae Labs, described setting one agent to do the work while another critiques it, which she said helps catch mistakes. Experts advise against depending on a single agent if the goal is higher output and productivity.

The companies market their agents with different emphases. Anthropic said it built Claude Duet for professionals and small business owners, while Meta said Muse can help with saving money, health, shopping and relationships. Claude Duet, OpenAI's Dots and xAI's Grok Bot have been described as colleague-like, and Muse and Instinct from Spear Street Technology as personal assistants. Artigas suggested Claude Duet for side hustles or new businesses, Dots for specialized technical work, Instinct for tedious emails and travel bookings, and Muse as a starting point for beginners because it is user-friendly. Experts also recommend testing agents to see which fit your preferences and the quality of their work.

To begin, Gigling suggested listing tasks you repeat often and delegating some of them, while being specific about goals, context and tools. Artigas recommended starting with one annoying, repeated online task, such as a long email or a delayed flight booking. Agents can work with inboxes, calendars, identification, credit card numbers and bank accounts, which has raised privacy concerns. Gigling advised curiosity but caution about what you share, and noted that many companies have published privacy policies describing how agents run on dedicated cloud computers and how users can control memory retention.

stories.Headline: Investigation reveals $11 AI voice cloning scam
stories.Summary:
Researchers at KMBC 9 tested how easily an AI tool could copy a person's voice and fool someone who knows them. Cybersecurity expert Aaron Weissenfluh of Tenfold Security collected 32 minutes of audio of KMBC 9 reporter Byra Berry from videos already posted publicly on YouTube and Facebook. He then used voice-cloning software that cost $11 to build a digital copy of her voice, and some comparable programs are free. Berry never had to record in a studio or read a script, because the audio was already online for anyone to hear. The test showed how little is needed to create a convincing imitation.

In the test, Berry's cousin received a phone call from the AI-generated voice and believed she was speaking with Berry. The cousin only noticed pauses in the conversation, and the voice was otherwise convincing enough to pass as the real person. The investigation raised the question of how persuasive the call would have been without those pauses. Scammers can use the same technology to impersonate a loved one, and a familiar voice can create immediate trust, especially when the caller claims an emergency or asks for money. The article notes that AI-generated deepfakes are improving faster than the laws meant to control them.

The article offers practical advice for protecting yourself. If an unexpected caller claiming to be a family member asks for money, do not rely on the voice alone, and be wary of anyone who pressures you to act right away or asks you to keep the call secret. Hang up and phone the person back using a number you already know. Families can also agree on a code word to verify identity during an emergency.

The article further advises caution about posting videos of yourself online, since scammers may need little more than publicly available recordings to work with. The article's central takeaway is that hearing a familiar voice no longer proves you are speaking with the person you think you are. The report comes from the KMBC 9 investigation, which was shared with other Hearst Television stations and published on those stations' websites on November 6, 2026. The articles do not describe any specific further steps by regulators or companies.

stories.Headline: Tencent Cloud Enterprise Unveils Full-Stack Intelligent Private Cloud for Sovereign Agentic AI
stories.Summary:
Tencent Cloud Enterprise, or TCE, used the AI-Powered Private Cloud for Global Markets session of the 2026 Tencent Global Digital Ecosystem Summit in Shenzhen, China, on November 6, 2026, to show how highly regulated industries can run production-grade agentic AI inside their own boundaries. The company launched two major solutions, the Full-Stack Intelligent AI Suite and Lite Deployment, and presented joint research reports it prepared with Gartner and Omdia. The theme of the session was full-stack intelligence and sovereign AI. Kaibo Sha, Vice President at Tencent Cloud, argued that once an agent touches core business data and critical systems, the key questions are where the data is processed, who operates the system, and what foundation the agent runs on. The Full-Stack Intelligent AI Suite is described as the company's flagship release of the year and marks a shift from a full-stack cloud to a full-stack intelligent cloud.

It has four selectable layers: a converged compute, storage and networking foundation, a model service layer built on TokenHub, an agent runtime layer with a cloud-native sandbox, egress control and identity credentials, and an agent application layer. TokenHub is a private platform for LLM services that offers metered, callable inference on an industry-standard API with multi-tenant isolation. The suite is said to deliver more than 250,000 TPM of measured single-accelerator throughput, cache hit rates above 90%, and up to 220% throughput gains on alternative silicon, and it has been validated at 10,000-GPU scale. Its resilience target is a recovery time objective of two minutes or less and a recovery point objective of zero, and the company says data, model weights and inference traffic stay inside the customer's sovereignty boundary. Lite Deployment targets organizations that want to start small before committing larger budgets.

According to the release, it delivers a complete full-stack cloud from eight servers, made up of three master nodes, three block storage nodes and two network function nodes, without reducing core infrastructure capability. An AI-only entry point can begin with three servers and include private model services. The same architecture can grow from a single availability zone to metro dual-AZ active-active and then to cross-region disaster recovery. It is delivered as software on existing hardware, requires no capital-heavy refresh and carries no minimum spend.

One large futures brokerage used this route to run core trading systems across heterogeneous chip architectures, starting AI on three servers and expanding as volumes grew. Tencent Cloud Enterprise and Gartner also released A Practical Guide to Building Sovereign AI Cloud Platforms, which treats sovereignty as a spectrum resting on data, operations and technology and sets out adoption paths for financial services, healthcare, public service cloud and telecommunications. The guide cites Gartner research projecting that by 2028, strict data sovereignty and privacy rules will push over 25% of enterprises in regulated industries to move their primary GenAI workloads back on-premises, and that through 2029, dependence on proprietary foundation models will lock more than 50% of GenAI adopters into one public cloud provider's ecosystem. The article is cut off before it lists the remaining findings, so the rest of the research and any further next steps are not described here.

stories.Headline: Christopher Nolan Previews DGA’s Next Phase of AI Protections: ‘It’s Down to the Studios’
stories.Summary:
Christopher Nolan, who has been president of the Directors Guild of America since fall 2025, spoke on the Hollywood Insiders podcast on Saturday, November 7, 2026, about the guild's fight against artificial intelligence in film and television. He praised the DGA and the Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers for negotiating what he called excellent language and guardrails on AI in production. He also said the next challenge, protecting copyrighted work from AI, rests mainly with the studios. His remarks were reported by TheWrap and Deadline in articles published on November 7 and 8, 2026.

Nolan said the guild is focused on holding studios accountable for protecting their copyrights, but that the DGA cannot do this itself because, with very few exceptions, its members do not hold the copyrights to the films they work on. He argued that "AI" is too broad a term, one that companies use to avoid responsibility by portraying the technology as an uncontrollable force. He said existing laws already protect creators and that companies hiding behind fair use arguments will not hold up in court in the long run, pointing to some significant judgments already issued against that defense. He also said he was pleased that the closing credits of his film The Odyssey, from Universal, include for the first time a notice stating the film cannot be ingested or used as AI training data.

Nolan compared this principle to the long-settled rules on sampling music, saying that taking another's work, feeding it into a machine, and selling the output even in disguised form should not count as fair use. He acknowledged the matter will have to be settled through courts and legislation, and that it will take a long time. Deadline reported that Nolan had earlier said the guild needs a voice in how AI tools are used and in shaping the legal framework, because members' residuals depend on how their work is monetized. He described the effort as an ongoing fight rather than one with a fixed endpoint.

stories.Headline: Securing AI Agents: Lessons From Real-World Deployment
stories.Summary:
Uber published an engineering article on November 6, 2026, by Sean Tout, Director of Engineering & Science, describing how it secures AI agents in production. The article, first posted on uber.com in the early hours of that day, explains that agentic AI differs from conventional software because agents reason over content from users, webpages, documents, tools, and other agents, and can turn that reasoning into real-world actions. That shifts part of the attack surface into the semantic layer, where risks such as prompt injection, tool and memory poisoning, goal hijacking, behavioral drift, and hallucination-driven actions appear. Uber says the question for these systems goes beyond whether an agent is authorized, asking whether a proposed action fits the user's request, the agent's persona and intents, the user's role, and the full session history.

The company built a defense-in-depth framework called Uber Secure AI that covers the agent lifecycle in three layers: provisioning-time validation, runtime enforcement, and continuous assurance. The framework includes an agent registry, personas and explicit intents, constraints, tool and MCP validation, context-aware guardrails, continuous red teaming, and end-to-end observability and replay. Uber also describes prompt provenance and evidence chaining, which link privileged actions back to what the user actually requested. Runtime evaluation has to stay within strict latency budgets, so the article says Uber favors small, specialized models that run locally over large general-purpose language models. The article also notes that stronger enforcement can produce false blocks, so Uber calibrates thresholds per agent rather than applying one uniform setting, and it automates onboarding so the secure path is the easiest one for developers.

The articles name Sean Tout as the author, and a second version of the page lists Max Zhurovich, Senior Staff Software Engineer, and Adi Raghavendra, Senior Engineering Manager, as co-authors. Uber presents the work as a set of shared practices meant to help engineering teams build these protections into agentic systems from the start. The authors state that security, accuracy, latency, cost, agent autonomy, and developer experience cannot be optimized independently, and they describe effective agent guardrails as both a security problem and a distributed systems engineering problem. The excerpts available do not describe any specific incident or deployment outcome beyond the framework itself.

stories.Headline: Seattle Public Schools tightens student access to YouTube, Minecraft, and AI
stories.Summary:
Seattle Public Schools announced new limits on student access to YouTube, Minecraft, and AI tools at a special School Board meeting on Wednesday, November 4, 2026. Starting the following Monday, November 9, YouTube will be blocked on district devices for students in kindergarten through fifth grade, and Minecraft will be blocked for all grades except classes where teachers use it for instruction. The district also closed a route that let students reach Google's Gemini chatbot through AI summary results in Google search, after students discovered the workaround. Earlier, Gemini had been banned only for kindergarten through second grade, and it is now blocked districtwide.

Beginning in January, third through fifth graders will no longer receive individual school laptops and will instead share devices from carts or labs, a change the district had already made for kindergarten through second grade in September. Those students will also face a 60-minute daily screen-time cap, following the 30-minute cap set for the younger grades. Assistant Superintendent of Academics Mike Starosky described these limits as guidance rather than policy, calling the 60-minute figure "more of a trial run" that could be lowered. The district has not banned generative AI outright, and it continues to offer tools such as MagicSchool AI, Canva's Magic Write, and Adobe Firefly, while Microsoft Copilot remains available to staff only. An AI literacy plan lays out a grade-by-grade approach in which students start learning about AI in third grade and use it more directly in high school.

Superintendent Ben Shuldiner, who arrived in February, said he wanted to remove YouTube as soon as he started, though the district first consulted teachers who use it in lessons, and some limited educational use may continue. Assistant Superintendent of Technology Carlos Del Valle explained that the district already blocked chatbots such as Claude and Grok, and an update from its web-filtering vendor closed the Gemini route. Shuldiner framed the moves as a reassessment of pandemic-era technology policies, while Starosky said the guidance rests on child-development research from groups including the American Academy of Pediatrics and Common Sense Media. Critics, including parent advocates and board members, questioned that research because several of those groups receive tech-industry funding, and some argued the district has not shown that its AI tools improve learning.

Parents and advocates gathered outside the district headquarters before the meeting, with roughly 40 to 50 people attending a rally hosted by Seattle Families for Intentional Tech. Emily Cherkin, a Seattle parent and longtime critic of classroom technology, said the district seemed to recognize it could no longer ignore them, and rally speaker Danica Noble, a former Federal Trade Commission attorney who appears to have won a state House seat, said she plans to push statewide legislation in January. Board Director Liza Rankin said she had long asked for the YouTube block, and Board Vice President Evan Briggs said claims about AI's benefits felt "very based on vibes." Shuldiner argued that students need to learn about technology rather than be shielded from it, a position Cherkin called inexcusable. The broader debate over how schools should handle AI remains active, with advocates seeking a full pause on student-facing generative AI until independent research proves it safe.

stories.Headline: "By 2027 we could witness a Chernobyl of artificial intelligence": the warning of Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton
stories.Summary:
Geoffrey Hinton, a Nobel Prize winner and one of the founders of artificial intelligence, has warned that AI could cause a large-scale accident within the next year or so. In an interview with the Guardian, published in early November 2026, the British computer scientist said such an event might hit financial systems or electricity grids. He compared it to the Chernobyl disaster, though he did not predict a nuclear accident. Hinton, who is 78, said that humanity might have been better off never developing the technology. Coverage from thevermilion.com and ukrmedia.news reported his remarks in the same period.

Hinton said that within a decade, if not sooner, society will learn whether it can manage the risks of AI. He warned of a widening gap between rich and poor, serious cultural problems, mass unemployment and, ultimately, the breakdown of social order. He also said that AI could have a positive future if its dangers are handled well. The articles present these as his own assessments rather than established facts. Ukrmedia.news noted that he had repeatedly raised similar concerns since leaving Google in 2023.

Hinton criticized the leaders of major AI companies, naming Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk and Sam Altman. He said he believed they understood the risks but were more concerned with money than with safety. Ukrmedia.news described this as his personal view about their motives, not a proven fact. Hinton also pointed to recent cybersecurity incidents triggered autonomously by AI agents as a warning sign. He likened them to the 1979 Three Mile Island partial meltdown, while the articles treat the Chernobyl comparison as a metaphor for a large event.

The articles say Hinton wants independent testing of powerful AI models before they are released, similar to the approval process for medicines. He argued that voluntary commitments by companies are insufficient and called for common standards and international cooperation. He also said he does not think losing control of AI is inevitable if more resources go into safety research. The articles note that the feared disaster has not yet happened, so his warning remains a judgment about potential risks.

stories.Headline: Inside Inner Mongolia, China's fastest-growing AI data center region, where construction is accelerating with low building cost and no public backlash (SemiAnalysis)
stories.Summary:
Envision Group, a renewable systems integrator, has opened a wind-powered AI data center campus in Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia, which SemiAnalysis visited in September 2026. The campus, called Galaxy, is planned for up to 800MW of IT capacity, roughly the size of the core Stargate Abilene campus in Texas. Its first 120MW phase was delivered within a year, at about a fifth of US costs, and the full campus is expected by the end of 2027. The article describes the region as China's fastest-growing AI data center area, with construction accelerating and little public backlash.

Envision designed and integrated much of the campus itself, which the article describes as one of the most vertically integrated setups the authors have seen. The company builds its own wind farms and a dedicated power line to supply the site, and its blade factory sits across the road. Inside the campus, Envision designed the low-voltage power modules and an 800V system, made the battery storage that smooths the load, and co-designed the prefabricated substation. In one 5MW hall, solid-state transformers convert 10kV AC from the grid directly to 800V DC for the racks, removing several conversion stages. The cooling design shares one water loop between liquid- and air-cooled servers and uses no central chiller plant.

The power model, which China calls source-grid-load-storage, pairs a project's own wind or solar farm and batteries with its datacenter through a dedicated line rather than the public grid. Galaxy's two wind farms have a combined 420MW of capacity, about 1.75 times the 240MW datacenter load, and Envision aims to supply over 60% of the first two phases' power from them. The authors say siting, oversizing and a 4-hour battery make this possible, and they note that the wind farms sit about two hours' drive from the campus. The article also explains that Inner Mongolia holds about 57% of China's usable wind resources, a region with more wind than its existing industry and population can use. Envision's datacenter plans in the region total 3GW, and Galaxy is the first.

The authors frame Galaxy as part of a wider pattern in which Chinese industrial groups with strengths in energy, construction or electrical equipment are moving into AI infrastructure, often because returns on the projects themselves are thin. They say Galaxy's scale and its use of wind rather than gas turbines set it apart from Abilene, which Crusoe built and leased to Oracle for OpenAI. The article says a further expansion could take Galaxy to about 1GW if a nearby wind turbine factory is converted. The authors plan a later report on the constraints on Inner Mongolia's datacenter growth, including power, land and water.

stories.Headline: 3 Cash Rich AI Stocks Investors Are Watching As Debt Costs Rise
stories.Summary:
Investors who follow AI stocks are watching three cash rich tech companies as rising debt costs and regulatory concerns push balance sheets back into focus. The article, published by Simply Wall St on Yahoo Finance Singapore on 8 November 2026, names NetApp, Rambus and Keysight Technologies as examples of low leverage firms tied to the AI news cycle. The three companies are described as a sample from a wider screen that surfaced 50 more similar companies, which the article does not cover. The piece says AI hype is colliding with politics and credit markets, and that this is separating cash rich giants from more stretched borrowers. NetApp is described as a provider of enterprise data management software, storage systems and cloud services used for AI and analytics workloads.

The article reports that it generates about US$6.7 billion from its hybrid cloud segment and US$733 million from public cloud. It cites around 350 AI and data lake deals in the first quarter of fiscal 2027 as projects move into production. Rambus, which makes high speed memory interface chips and security silicon, is said to have posted record quarterly revenue of US$207.4 million, with guidance for further sequential growth in the third quarter of 2026. Keysight Technologies, which supplies test and design tools for AI data center and networking buildouts, is reported to generate about US$4.7 billion from its communications business and roughly US$1.9 billion from its electronic industrial business. The article presents these companies as relatively low risk because they sell infrastructure and tools rather than relying on heavy borrowing to build AI capacity.

It describes NetApp's focus on cash generation and balance sheet discipline, Rambus's asset light fabless model, and Keysight's emphasis on test gear and software over giant server farms. Each company profile also points to a margin or earnings question that readers would need to examine further. The article is labeled as general in nature, produced with AI automation, and not financial advice, and it states that Simply Wall St has no position in the stocks mentioned. The article itself offers no forecast beyond the company guidance it cites, and it directs readers to full narratives and a screener for their own research. It does not say how the debt cost pressures will affect these specific companies over time.

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence Raises Growing Concerns Over Human C
stories.Summary:
Ocient, a Chicago-based data analytics company, has raised $100 million in a Series C round to expand its agentic artificial intelligence analytics business. The round was co-led by Boka Capital and OCA Ventures, with participation from earlier investors including Greycroft Partners, In-Q-Tel, Blue Bear Capital, Buoyant Ventures, PSP Partners and Pritzker Group Venture Capital. The new financing brings the company's total funding to $260 million. Its growth is being driven by demand from national security organizations and telecommunications providers that want to analyze massive datasets without sampling.

The funding will accelerate delivery of OcientAIQ Solutions, which let AI agents and human analysts query datasets measured in petabytes. The company says its revenue is expected to more than triple in its current fiscal year, which ends in January, after doubling the year before. Chief Executive John Morris said customers in cybersecurity and telecommunications have long been forced to sample network data because they lack systems that can ingest it quickly and store tens of petabytes affordably. The platform combines ingestion, analytics, governance and agent orchestration, and its architecture avoids constant data movement and replication. Morris also noted that software agents, rather than human analysts alone, are now querying the system, which has increased usage and demand for fuller datasets.

Morris presented the company as a data infrastructure provider rather than a cybersecurity tool, saying Ocient does not build detection algorithms. Government and defense customers make up a substantial part of the business, and the company recently set up a dedicated national security subsidiary to serve them. Morris said the funding should be enough to help the company reach breakeven, though he gave no timetable. Much of the investment will go toward hiring sales and customer delivery staff while engineering development continues. He also said most new opportunities now involve on-premises deployments, as customers seek lower costs or stronger data sovereignty and protection.

Ocient competes with Snowflake, Databricks and open-source analytics platforms, although Morris said its technology often complements those products. Looking ahead, the company plans to expand into Europe, Asia-Pacific and Latin America while pursuing more cybersecurity customers. The article does not provide details on specific contract values or the timing of expansion. Its reporting is based on the company's announcement and statements from Morris.

stories.Headline: Seoul stocks sharply down late Fri. morning on AI rout
stories.Summary:
On Friday morning, November 6, 2026, Seoul stocks fell sharply as investors worried that the Democratic Party's sweeping victory in the U.S. midterm election could slow data center construction. By 11:20 a.m., the benchmark KOSPI had dropped 240.41 points, or 4.47 percent, to 5,143.39. Shortly after the opening bell, the Korea Exchange briefly halted trading in KOSPI stocks for 20 minutes once the index had fallen more than 8 percent. The sell-off followed a rout on Wall Street overnight, where investors dumped major artificial intelligence and data center stocks after the election results.

The S&P 500 lost more than 4 percent, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq shed over 5 percent. The decline spread across the Seoul market, with shares falling almost everywhere. Chip giants Samsung Electronics and SK hynix dropped more than 3 percent and 6 percent, respectively. Carmaker Hyundai Motor fell 4.6 percent, defense group Hanwha Aerospace slipped 4.41 percent, and battery maker LG Energy Solution eased 0.14 percent.

The Korean won traded at 1,356.2 won to the U.S. dollar at 11:20 a.m., weaker by 0.7 won from the previous close. The articles do not describe any new policy or rule taking effect, only the market reaction to the election outcome. The articles attribute the worry to the Democratic Party's midterm victory, which investors feared could restrict data center building. Han Ji-young, an analyst at Kiwoom Securities, said that because Texas accounts for about 27 percent of all U.S. data center construction, limits in such areas could have negative ripple effects.

The articles do not name a specific official or company responsible for the sell-off, and they do not give further comment from the government or exchange beyond the trading suspension. The episode shows how closely Seoul's major stocks now track the outlook for artificial intelligence and data center demand in the United States. The articles do not say how long the sell-off would last or whether trading would resume at a higher level. They report only the midday figures, leaving the rest of the trading session and any later recovery outside their scope.

stories.Headline: AI Chip Stocks Bounce After Global Rout—But Is the Bubble Starting to Burst?
stories.Summary:
On Thursday, AI chip stocks sold off sharply across Wall Street and Asia, then bounced on Friday, November 6, 2026. Nvidia fell 9.3% on Thursday before rising 2.78% to $186.64, while AMD dropped 17.3% a day earlier and recovered to $449.04. Both remain well below their October peaks. Taiwan's benchmark fell more than 8% over the week, its worst in months, and South Korea's KOSPI lost 6% on Friday.

Investors are now asking whether this is a normal correction or the start of a bubble bursting. A correction means a market has fallen at least 10% from a recent peak, which does not necessarily signal that the underlying business is shrinking. A bubble bursting is more serious and occurs when expectations prove unrealistic and the money supporting the boom disappears. One article describes how a stock trading at high multiples can lose a large share of its value even if profits do not fall. The distinction matters for judging what happens next.

Several pressures contributed to the selloff. In 40 of 41 local ballot contests on November 3, voters favored limiting data center development, and Ballotpedia found the results sent a clear political message. Data centers are the largest growth driver for chipmakers, so restrictions could delay orders or push construction elsewhere. Doubts also predated the election, as AI companies were spending heavily before returns were clear and borrowing costs were rising. Reuters quoted strategist Steve Sosnick warning that heavily owned stocks were already priced to perfection.

The articles draw a comparison to the dot-com crash, when the Nasdaq lost roughly 77% between March 2000 and October 2002. Analysts warn that AI could face a similar gap between long-term promise and near-term profit, especially for smaller AI-cloud providers that borrow heavily to expand. One article reported that the cost of insuring against a default by CoreWeave had climbed above 1,000 basis points, a sign of rising concern about repayment. Still, broader bond markets were operating relatively normally, and the articles say large profitable firms such as Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta are better positioned to absorb setbacks. Results from CoreWeave, Applied Materials and Cisco next week, along with inflation data, are expected to show whether customers are still ordering capacity and equipment.

stories.Headline: AI can be delegated authority, but not responsibility: Türkiye's technology minister
stories.Summary:
Turkish Industry and Technology Minister Mehmet Fatih Kacir said on Saturday that artificial intelligence should not operate without clear accountability, speaking at the TRT World Forum panel "Navigating Responsibility in the Age of AI." He warned that increasingly autonomous AI systems raise serious questions about transparency, safety and accountability. Kacir said that authority could be handed to AI but responsibility could not. He pointed to risks including algorithmic discrimination, cybersecurity threats, deepfakes and the concentration of computing power among a small number of technology companies.

Kacir noted that more than 90 percent of the world's notable frontier AI models in 2025 were developed by industry. He said just five companies controlled an estimated 70 percent of global AI computing power. He called for a human-centred, risk-based regulatory approach, arguing that AI applications with significant consequences for individuals should face stronger safeguards and meaningful human oversight. The minister's remarks framed these safeguards as central to technological progress.

Outlining Türkiye's ambitions, Kacir said the country's 2026-2030 Artificial Intelligence Action Plan aims to place Türkiye among the leading countries in AI technologies. The plan targets AI literacy training for 5 million citizens, the development of 10,000 advanced AI experts and 100,000 AI professionals, and the opening of at least 2,000 public datasets to researchers and entrepreneurs. It also aims to expand data centre capacity to at least one gigawatt by 2030 and attract at least $10 billion in private-sector-led investment in data centres, cloud computing and AI infrastructure. Kacir added that the country's Turkish large language model, BILGE, would strengthen technological independence, with its first version soon to be made available to developers.

Kacir also announced plans to establish regulatory sandboxes in priority sectors and an AI Ethics Board to address privacy, discrimination and children's safety. He said Türkiye was committed to contributing to global AI governance through the G20, OECD, UNESCO, the Organisation of Turkic States and the United Nations. The articles do not say when the ethics board or sandboxes will be set up. The remarks were reported by TRT World, citing the Anadolu Agency.

stories.Headline: AI infrastructure grows in Texas with new facilities in Dallas, College Station - NBC 5 Dallas-Fort Worth
stories.Summary:
In Bryan, a 73-megawatt data center is being developed on 25 acres of Texas A&M's RELLIS Campus by Austin-based ThisWay Global, which calls its project the Research and AI Compute Center, or RACC. The facility is focused on sovereign artificial intelligence, a model that lets organizations keep tighter control over their data and the output of AI systems. The center plans an eight-week course for eligible students and community members, extending training beyond Texas A&M's own students. The company expects to begin computing at the Bryan site by June 2027. Students and researchers say that a nearby facility would make it easier to keep their work on campus instead of seeking outside partners for large computing systems.

In Dallas, technology integrator GDT has opened what it calls an "AI factory," a supercomputer lab where businesses can build and test AI applications before investing in their own systems. The lab runs on NVIDIA GPUs, NetApp storage and Cisco networking, and companies can use it to judge whether a given AI use case makes sense for their operations. GDT executives say large enterprises now need to deploy AI at scale, which is far more complex than casual use of a public chatbot. GDT's vice president of advisory and transformation, Chris Kapusta, said the lab is meant to speed companies from exploring AI to confirming real value. He added that the facility gives North Texas businesses local access to the technology and draws national attention to the region.

GDT's CEO, Shawn O'Grady, compared AI to a hammer, arguing that the tool itself is not the problem and that its effect depends on how people use it. Kapusta said bad actors are already using AI to search for security weaknesses, while companies can use the same technology to find and fix vulnerabilities first. ThisWay Global's CEO, Stefan Fable, said AI will become part of everyday systems, including payment systems and points of sale. He also stressed that users keep control over both inputs and outputs in a sovereign setup, which he called important for research, regulated industries and defense. Together, the two projects reflect a push to put computing power within reach of more people as AI spreads through business, research and daily life.

stories.Headline: Camerimage Opens With a Robot, an AI Reckoning and a Minute of Silence for Kraków
stories.Summary:
The Camerimage Film Festival opened on Saturday in Toruń, Poland, with artificial intelligence as its central theme. In place of festival director Marek Żydowicz, a humanoid robot called Edward Warchocki gave the opening address and then took part in a long conversation with Żydowicz about AI's role in cinema. The festival also began with a minute of silence for the victims of a mass shooting in Kraków earlier that day. Local politicians acknowledged the attack before the program started.

The opening ceremony at the Jordanki Culture Centre lasted three hours and included video messages on AI in entertainment from Francis Ford Coppola, Gal Gadot, Christopher Nolan, Maggie Gyllenhaal, Steven Spielberg and Ben Affleck. Darren Aronofsky received the festival's honorary Award for Director, and he is a strong supporter of generative AI since launching his studio Primordial Soup last year. He said it was his third visit to the festival and praised it for honoring everyone who makes films possible. Karolina Gruszka and Janusz Kamiński also received awards during the evening.

The opening film, Luca Guadagnino's Artificial, continued the AI theme. Guadagnino and cinematographer Malik Hassan Sayeed discussed the film on stage, and Sayeed described AI as just a tool, like any other. Guadagnino, who shot the film on 35 mm, said its real subject is the economic and political power that tech leaders have gained over people's lives. Neon will release Artificial in the United States on December 25.

The festival was overshadowed by the Kraków shooting. According to reports, at least six people were killed and more than a dozen injured when a gunman suspected of far-right ties drove into the city's historic Main Market Square and opened fire. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said three more bodies were later found at the suspect's home, making it Poland's deadliest shooting in decades. Camerimage runs through November 14.

stories.Headline: Meta preparing to launch Muse AI assistant in UK
stories.Summary:
Meta has introduced Spaces, a new feature within its Muse app that lets users build customised interactive experiences using artificial intelligence. The feature was announced around November 7, 2026, and is available in all markets where Muse is offered. Users describe what they want, such as a personal planner, a shopping tracker, a game or a project dashboard, and Muse builds it. The tool can be refined over time by adding features, changing the design or adjusting how it works. Spaces is the second major Muse feature Meta has announced in a week.

Users can place their spaces in the sidebar or main navigation tabs, hide ones they are not using, and schedule when specific spaces appear. For example, someone could show a weekly work planner on weekdays and switch to a weekend planning space on Saturdays. Spaces also supports connections with third-party applications, which allows it to refresh information in the background, such as concert announcements, price movements and savings progress. Users can add notes, edit information and mark tasks as complete directly within a space. Meta is also exploring ways to let people share their spaces and collaborate with others.

Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg highlighted the feature in a post on X, saying he had been experimenting with Spaces and had built a barbecue game, an event tracker and a home control dashboard. The launch expands Meta's Muse AI agents, which were introduced in September. During the company's October earnings call, Zuckerberg said the agents had reached 10 million users across the United States and Canada, less than two months after their debut. Meta recently also introduced Muse Voice, which lets US users interact with their AI avatars through video calls and spoken instructions.

The Times reported that Meta is preparing to launch Muse in the United Kingdom, and that Zuckerberg is targeting billions of users for the AI agent, which can shop, fill in forms and book appointments online. The Spaces update shows the company widening what Muse can do beyond answering questions. The articles do not say when Muse will arrive in the UK, nor do they give details of how Spaces would be offered there. stories.Headline: AI Era Business Strategy: Tencent's WorkBuddy-Centric Layout, Alibaba's Qwen AI, ByteDance's Doubao AI – Leading Competitive Enterprise AI Development
stories.Summary:
Tencent used its 2026 Global Digital Ecosystem Conference to launch a set of AI office products centered on WorkBuddy, according to a 36Kr report dated November 5. Dowson Tong, Senior Executive Vice President of Tencent Group and CEO of its Cloud and Smart Industries Group, introduced Buddy One, an office suite that ties Tencent Docs, Tencent Meeting and Tencent Cloud Drive together under unified accounts, a unified points pool and a unified data pool. Tencent also rolled out a new Tencent Cloud Drive, described as a memory space for the Agent era that keeps the context, records and rules AI agents build up while working. A day earlier, on November 4, Tencent released its flagship Hy4 model, which adds visual understanding for the first time and powers an update to WorkBuddy, according to the South China Morning Post.

On pricing, the Buddy One VIP individual membership costs 700 yuan on a continuous monthly subscription, the same as the earlier WorkBuddy Individual Flagship Edition. It bundles Tencent Meeting Professional Edition and Tencent Docs Super Member Plus, along with 50,000 general AI points and 1TB of shared storage each month. Buddy One is aimed mainly at individual users, even though it supports multi-person collaboration, while a WorkBuddy Enterprise Edition builds on it with an open platform and stronger enterprise security. Tencent said Hy4 can process images, analyse complex charts and carry out visual mathematical reasoning. It called the model one of the strongest open-weight models available, while admitting it still trails leading closed-source systems on tough internal benchmarks such as research-level mathematics, long-horizon coding, model self-improvement and advanced visual question answering.

Liu Yi, a Vice President of Tencent Cloud who heads the CodeBuddy and WorkBuddy effort, said Tencent has never worried about holding a leading position. He noted that the market is at a very early stage, with about 90 percent of enterprises yet to adopt Agents at scale, and said future competition will turn on service quality, model collaboration and implementation teams. Dowson Tong said that if users eventually stop using the standalone Tencent Meeting client in favor of doing that work inside WorkBuddy, Tencent might reconsider whether to keep a separate client. He added that habits formed over a short time are hard to change and that Tencent will not force anyone to switch products.

The 36Kr article places Tencent's moves alongside similar integration by rivals, noting that Alibaba's Qwen has linked products such as Fliggy and Amap and that ByteDance connects Doubao with Feishu. Separately, Xinhua reported on October 31 that Alibaba announced a partnership with Apple to bring Qwen into Apple Intelligence through Siri, Writing Tools and Visual Intelligence. Testing begins in the iOS developer beta on November 4, with a rollout to Chinese users in the official iOS 27.3 release in December. Users can choose whether to enable it, and Alibaba said it will not use their requests or responses for model training. Alibaba CEO Eddie Wu said Qwen will work with Apple to deliver new AI-powered service experiences, and the feature is open to those who buy an Apple Intelligence-capable iPhone in China.

stories.Headline: Kookmin University research team develops AI model to predict properties of mixtures
stories.Summary:
A research team at Kookmin University, led by chemistry professor Joung Joon-young, has built an artificial intelligence model that predicts the properties of chemical mixtures from the identities and proportions of their components. The university announced the work on Thursday, and the findings were published in the Chemical Engineering Journal under the title "Encoding composition-dependent intermolecular interactions into learned molecular representations." The team also included Kim Ji-hwan, a student in the university's integrated master's and doctoral program, and undergraduate Kim Chan-joong. The model, called MEMo, was announced as a new tool for a field the articles describe as central to everyday products.

Most chemical products people use are mixtures, including industrial solvents, battery electrolytes, automotive fuels, and cosmetic and pharmaceutical formulations. Their properties depend on which substances are combined and in what proportions, and those changes do not follow the mixing ratios in a simple, direct way. Earlier AI approaches learned each molecule's properties separately and then averaged them by mixing ratio, which missed how molecules interact and how those interactions shift with composition. MEMo accounts for both molecular identity and mixing proportions from the start, first learning each molecule's traits and then letting molecules exchange information so the model can learn their interactions. The team tested it against more than 860,000 experimental measurements from the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology across five properties: density, speed of sound, vapor pressure, refractive index and surface tension.

According to the articles, MEMo predicted four of the five properties better than conventional methods. The gains were largest for mixtures with strong intermolecular interactions, such as ionic liquids and aqueous salt solutions, and for mixtures containing molecules the model had not seen during training. Joung said the key was building a model that understands molecular behavior on the same principle that governs mixtures, and he expects it to shorten and cheapen materials development by predicting properties for different compositions without physical experiments. He named battery electrolyte design, eco-friendly solvents and carbon dioxide capture materials as possible applications. The articles do not say when or how the model will be made available for these uses.

stories.Headline: Why Do We Still Need AI When It Has Snatched Up All Graphics Cards and Memory?
stories.Summary:
The first article, published by 36Kr on November 4, 2026, reports that graphics cards and memory have become scarce for gamers because manufacturers have shifted production toward AI and professional cards. It says the RTX 5090 is nearly impossible to buy, the RTX 5080 has roughly doubled in price, AMD is preparing another price increase, and Intel's Arc B580 may be discontinued. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman drew anger when he said ordinary consumers' memory is used only about 5 percent of the time and that this allocation is unreasonable, suggesting the hardware belongs in data centers running around the clock. Elon Musk joined the online backlash, and the article argues that Altman's view is illogical, because data center cards may sit idle in warehouses, and because the purpose of AI should be to give people more leisure rather than take away their entertainment.

The article cites a whistleblower channel, Moore's Law Is Dead, which claims AI card makers pressured customers into advance contracts, while the customers' facilities were not ready, leaving many cards stacked and unused. It also says some purchased cards may exist only as delivery vouchers, and that companies may use unreceived hardware as collateral for loans. The author notes that investor Michael Burry is reportedly buying put options on AI companies expiring as early as 2027. Using a British financial blogger's estimate, the article compares the cost of 200 hours of the upcoming GTA 6 at about $2 per day with roughly $5,000 for the same stretch spent on nights out, and it concludes that for many ordinary consumers games are the only affordable high-quality entertainment, so taking them away would likely push people toward free short videos rather than a more refined life.

The second article, published by GameGPU on November 7, 2026, covers the release of gputaskman, an open-source utility under the MIT license, with version 0.3.3 published in its repository. The tool monitors GPU load, video memory use, and per-process resource consumption, along with temperature, power, and frequencies, and it runs in the terminal with real-time graphs. It supports Windows with NVIDIA and AMD cards, Linux, WSL, and Apple Silicon on macOS, and it can detect local AI runtimes such as llama.cpp, Ollama, and LM Studio. For compatible models it estimates how memory is split among weights, the KV cache, and compute buffers, though the developer says these figures are approximations from model metadata and logs rather than direct readings of video memory. Results can be saved as JSON, Windows builds need no Python installation, and the developer calls the project experimental, with some features still limited.

stories.Headline: Anthropic AI models accelerate research pace, alarming researchers
stories.Summary:
Anthropic's AI models are now improving roughly twice as fast as they were a year ago, according to a new report from the AI safety research organization METR. The findings come from an 11-week investigation inside Anthropic and offer some of the clearest evidence so far that AI is speeding up its own development. METR concluded that most of this acceleration, as of October, comes from AI rather than from simply adding computing power. Employees using the company's most capable internal model reported being about 12 times as productive with AI help, roughly double what staff had reported a few months earlier using Mythos 5.

The report also identified three newer Anthropic models, called Model 2, Model 3, and Model 4, which finished training between July and October but have not been released. METR said these unreleased internal models contribute heavily to the productivity gains, and it found no clear signs of diminishing returns that might slow the pace. For now, the acceleration appears to come mostly from AI assisting human researchers, though METR warned that fully autonomous contributions may play a larger role soon. Researchers said the findings suggest that AI systems building more powerful successors on their own may be closer than previously thought.

A central complaint is that Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence METR considered most informative from the public version of its roughly 100-page report. METR said that much of the withheld material could support several interpretations, which makes it hard for outsiders to check the conclusions. Anthropic cofounder Sam McCandlish acknowledged the redactions in a public post, saying the company judged that revealing what drives the speedup was commercially sensitive and could give rivals a roadmap to move faster. He said Anthropic made the right call despite the trade-off, and that the company plans to publish its own report on the pace of AI progress in the coming weeks.

The report has drawn sharp criticism from AI safety researchers, who point to an apparent contradiction in Anthropic's position. The company has been among the most vocal advocates for safety and for slowing AI development, yet the findings suggest it is helping accelerate the technology while withholding key details. Some researchers said the results indicate that even aggressive predictions about AI progress may be too conservative, and Apollo Research's CEO said the pace appeared broadly in line with expectations, perhaps a little faster. The report covers only Anthropic, but OpenAI has said it is working toward an AI researcher capable of advancing deep learning and alignment by March 2028.

The report says Ternus held a closed-door meeting with Federighi in the weeks before publication, urging him to move past incremental Siri changes. The goal described is a more autonomous, agentic Siri that can manage tasks on a user's behalf, possibly as early as next year. Ternus succeeded Tim Cook as chief executive in September 2026, and the reporting places this push within that management transition. Apple has not publicly confirmed the meeting or any change to Federighi's role.

The reporting also describes changes to how Apple builds its software. Engineers are reportedly getting more time to explore and build new features before those features are locked in, affecting iOS 28, iPadOS 28 and macOS 28. Bloomberg's coverage adds that Apple lacks a computer-use capability comparable to agents from OpenAI and Anthropic, which can operate software and click buttons for a user. Separately, one report says Siri AI will not gain more control over Apple apps until spring 2027. These accounts suggest a timeline in which the schedule itself is being reworked to make room for faster AI development.

Responsibility for the software organization rests with Federighi, who oversees software engineering across the iPhone, iPad and Mac. According to the Bloomberg reporting, his hands-on management style and his preference for competing ideas and shorter-term planning have sometimes complicated development. Bloomberg also reports that Mike Rockwell, the executive who helped rescue Siri AI, is seriously considering leaving his role as Siri chief, or Apple altogether, next year. The articles do not say that Federighi is leaving or being replaced. They describe Ternus as wanting the company to respond more quickly to rivals, which reports say have been expanding their AI products.

The context is that Apple faces concern about falling behind competitors, and some commentators argue that its large store of on-device data and privacy stance could give it an edge in personal AI. Several outlets report that Siri AI leadership may be changing and that more departures are rumored, though those points remain unconfirmed by Apple. The reports point toward iOS 28 and the next Siri features as the next milestones to watch. Whether the faster schedule produces the agentic capabilities described has not yet been shown.

stories.Headline: Jesse Eisenberg "experiments" with AI to make sure it's still bad at writing
stories.Summary:
Jesse Eisenberg, the writer, director and actor, told Variety in a new interview that he sometimes tests AI to see whether it can write well yet. He said he remains paranoid about the technology, but he checks it regularly and finds it still writes badly, which relieves him for now. The interview was conducted alongside his co-star Julianne Moore, who is in his new A24 film The Debut, and both were asked how they feel about AI shaping Hollywood. Eisenberg said that when he asks AI to write a scene, the results remain poor.

The articles frame his concern as a question of how far the technology is from producing good work. Eisenberg described a scenario in which a child could put on a headset and watch a made-to-order movie, and he said that possibility worries him. One article notes that AI has already entered the entertainment industry, citing Netflix's use of some form of AI on 300 titles and its recently launched AI Discover feature. It also mentions an AI bot that used actress Mia Goth's name and likeness in viral posts, and efforts to promote the AI actor Tilly Norwood. Eisenberg's remarks sit within a broader Hollywood debate in which some creatives strongly oppose AI, others are skeptical, and some embrace it.

Eisenberg responded to the threat by pointing to the staying power of human creativity. He said the creative spirit will keep finding ways to entertain people and to speak about things in a way that computers may not. He also cited the Greek plays written about 2,500 years ago, which are still performed in much the same way, as evidence that lasting art endures. He said people still want to gather in the same room to watch and hear stories, a habit he compared to cave dwellers around a campfire. He added, however, that his real worry is whether artists will still be able to earn a living from their work, and he said he is not fully sure about that.

The articles place these comments within a wider pattern of entertainers speaking out about AI. Masako Nozawa, the voice of Goku in Dragon Ball, criticized people who used AI to imitate her voice, and Nicolas Cage said he would probably not work with Amazon again after declining to sign its AI waiver. Mario creator Shigeru Miyamoto said Nintendo would prefer to take a different direction on the subject. Eisenberg's next film, The Debut, is set to arrive on December 11, 2026.
