stories.Headline: Woori, MSCI Chiefs Discuss Climate, AI Finance
stories.Summary:
Woori Financial Group Chairman Yim Jong-ryong met Henry Fernandez, chairman and CEO of the global investment information provider MSCI, at Woori's headquarters in Jung-gu, Seoul, on November 5, 2026. The two men discussed how climate change and artificial intelligence are affecting the financial industry and what responses might be needed. The meeting was arranged to reaffirm the role of financial companies in supporting corporate low-carbon transition and technological innovation during a fast-changing global environment. Reports on the meeting appeared in the Korea Herald and BusinessKorea on November 6.

Yim described the founding philosophy of Daehan Cheonil Bank, the predecessor of Woori Financial, and said its goal of supplying funds for the national economy and industrial development has carried forward into productive, inclusive and ESG finance. He said the group would significantly strengthen financial support for green industries, using its corporate finance capabilities in line with the government's Korean-style Green Great Transformation, or K-GX, strategy. Woori has set a target of providing 100 trillion won, about $72.5 billion, in ESG finance by 2030, and it had reached a cumulative 67 trillion won by the end of 2025. The group's stated aim is to do more than supply money and to help companies make a soft landing into a low-carbon economic structure. The Korea Herald gave the target as $73.7 billion, a different conversion of the same figure.

Woori is also bringing AI into its operations to make financial work more efficient. It runs a "K-Taxonomy Expert Consultation AI Service" that supports reviews of whether corporate activities meet the Korean Green Taxonomy, which defines environmentally sustainable economic activities. With this support, Woori Bank had provided green loans meeting those standards worth 180 billion won, about $130.5 million, by the end of September 2026. The Korea Herald put that figure at 1.8 trillion won, so the two outlets disagree on the scale of these loans. Yim said the meeting gave both sides a chance to exchange views on global financial issues, and that the group will keep supporting companies' low-carbon transition while pursuing companywide innovation and productivity gains through AI.

stories.Headline: What it takes to avoid ‘cognitive surrender’ to AI
stories.Summary:
A Boston Globe opinion piece by Zachary Clifton, a Yale student, examines how students are increasingly leaning on AI when they struggle with coursework, a habit that MIT's Ad Hoc Committee on AI Use in Teaching, Learning, and Research Training calls "cognitive surrender." The MIT committee's report found that current AI tools can produce credible solutions to nearly any undergraduate written assignment, including essays, proofs, science and math problems, and coding work. It also found students skipping office hours and abandoning study groups, and it called for a response everywhere, especially at MIT. Clifton frames the problem as one that can still be addressed by giving students incentives to do work that can be credibly assessed.

Clifton describes a Yale class, Advanced Nonfiction Writing, taught by writer-in-residence Anne Fadiman, who has taught at Yale since 2005. Students must submit two writing samples and a letter to gain admission, then meet with Fadiman one-on-one at least five times each semester for hour-long editing sessions. Fadiman's clear rule is "Don't use it to write your essays," and she explains that classmates reading the essays will notice AI use. Clifton says this policy rests on three ideas: students should not use AI, learning comes through reading, writing, and discussion, and peers should be able to see one another's work. He notes that the small, intensive format is hard to copy at other universities, but that the policy itself could be applied elsewhere.

Clifton proposes several measures beyond Fadiman's policy. Professors should require students to prove they wrote their essays, including showing research and revision, and they could review version histories in Google Docs when grading, so a student who spends 20 hours and writes four drafts is credited for that effort. He also suggests banning laptops, tablets, and phones from classes except where the work is digital, pointing to the University of Chicago Law School, which barred them from its first-year courses this fall. Smaller classes and longer meetings, such as a 12-person seminar meeting three hours a week, would let professors know students personally, which Clifton believes may discourage lying about AI use. He acknowledges these steps could amount to surveillance and reduce student privacy and autonomy.

A separate Techgig article from November 6, 2026, reports that Addy Osmani, an engineer on Anthropic's Claude Code team, has warned that relying on AI agents can lead to cognitive surrender. Osmani says his own daily work increasingly runs through AI agents, which reduces the critical thinking it demands. He describes three forms of diminished thinking: cognitive offloading, which he endorses for low-stakes tasks while keeping ownership; deferral, where AI output becomes new input; and cognitive surrender, a term from Wharton School researchers for complete trust in AI outputs, which he calls lazy. Osmani warns that frequent surrender builds "cognitive debt," and he advises engineers to ask whether they formed a hypothesis before querying an AI, to verify AI-generated code as a habit, and to recognize that unexercised skills will degrade.

stories.Headline: Military spouse uses AI to help veterans navigate VA benefits
stories.Summary:
Tracy Contrino, a Calvert County military spouse, has launched TheClusterFix, an independent nonprofit that uses an AI assistant called Frank to help veterans find and understand benefits information from the Department of Veterans Affairs and other federal sources. The idea grew out of her own frustration while trying to help her husband, who served 18 years in the Army and National Guard and is rated 100% P&T disabled, navigate the VA system. Contrino says the tool is meant to show veterans where to start and what steps may come next, not to replace the VA or give legal or medical advice. The organization stresses that it is not affiliated with or part of the VA.

Frank is built to draw on publicly available VA and federal information and to answer questions quickly, without appointments or waiting. Contrino says many of the questions it receives so far concern general and education benefits, and the group has begun working with higher education institutions. Hope Bald, the board president, says Frank surfaced information for her own claim that a service officer had not mentioned, and the team is now expanding its guidance on VA education benefits. The nonprofit is free for veterans, relies on grants and community donations, and hopes to add partnerships, a broader resource center and more data collection that does not identify individuals.

Contrino describes getting a disability rating as a tedious process that can take months or even years, and she says denials can leave veterans confused about their next move. She says many veterans feel alone in the process and give up, even though some available benefits can be significant for them and their families. Her stated goal is to save veterans time, possibly days, weeks or months, spent searching websites or waiting on hold, and not to compete with the VA. Bald says she and Contrino want veterans to receive clear answers rather than confusion.

A separate opinion piece on RealClearDefense, written by Rob Schroder, founder and CEO of SteerBridge and a Marine Corps veteran, makes a related argument about federal benefits. It refers to a presidential executive order directing the Department of War and the VA to modernize record sharing, build digital tools and improve transition assistance. Schroder argues that AI should speed up processing by organizing records, summarizing evidence and automating administrative tasks, but that qualified VA personnel, not AI, should decide whether a veteran is entitled to a benefit. He says SteerBridge has helped agencies cut processing times, such as handling education benefits in seconds rather than weeks and screening disability evidence in hours rather than months, and he urges judging modernization by measurable results for veterans.

stories.Headline: Hundreds of Artex AI hacking tools found exposed online
stories.Summary:
Security researchers found hundreds of copies of Artex, a Chinese-made open source AI hacking tool, publicly exposed on the internet where anyone could reach them. The tool, which automatically probes computer systems for weaknesses, has been linked to cyberattacks since its public release in July. Cybersecurity firm Censys identified more than 800 distinct Artex deployments accessible from the web without a password. Those findings were reported in early November 2026.

Because Artex is free to download and run, it has become a popular option for people who cannot use the most advanced cybersecurity AI models from Anthropic or OpenAI. Microsoft has described it as a system of AI agents able to carry out attacks from reconnaissance through data theft with little human involvement. The software does not require its servers to be reachable from the internet, so the exposure is a misconfiguration. Some of the exposed systems also contain hidden malicious software used to keep access to a victim's network.

Censys said that not every Artex instance is run maliciously, since many are used by authorized testers, but it could not explain why so many are exposed. Silas Cutler, a principal security researcher at Censys, wrote the blog post detailing the findings. CrowdStrike attributed an attack on the Korean finance industry in September to a Chinese-speaking hacker who used an Artex instance and left an open directory. Microsoft reported that hackers using Artex broke into customers' cloud environments during an attack on IT support giant ConnectWise in October, and that the speed left defenders little time to respond.

Many of the attacks linked to Artex exploited simple weaknesses, such as guessing weak or known passwords and the absence of multi-factor authentication. Artex's developers have announced it will go closed-source, which limits further releases to paying customers. Dozens of copies of its code remain on code-sharing sites, where they can still be used in active attacks. The episode shows that even powerful hacking tools can expose both attackers and their targets when basic security is missing.

stories.Headline: CoreWeave's bond yield tops 16% as AI credit stress spreads wider - Quartz
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave's borrowing costs jumped again this week. The yield on its 9.625% bond due in 2032 climbed above 16%, according to CNBC, as investors asked for more protection against default across AI-linked borrowers. On Thursday, its five-year credit default swaps rose beyond 1,289 basis points, a level higher than their October peak, before easing 8% on Friday to around 1,155. The bonds had already slid on Wednesday after Democratic candidates who want to curb data center construction won governorships, Texas among them, according to Bloomberg. That day the 2031 unsecured bonds hit a low of 79.5 cents per dollar of face value, the 2030 and 2032 notes also fell with yields topping 15%, and the stock dropped 9.9% to close at $48.42, its weakest finish since May 2025.

The political risk centers on possible limits on data center building. Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa has pressed for a moratorium, and Democrats Amy Acton in Ohio and Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia have also advocated slowing construction, according to Bloomberg. CNBC, citing Goldman Sachs, reported that moratoriums could touch 45% of the data center capacity in the nationwide pipeline, with Texas holding a big share. The stress has spread beyond CoreWeave, as default protection on Nvidia debt rose 76% over the past month, Broadcom's rose 49% and Amazon's rose 44%. Those contracts remain low in absolute terms, with Nvidia's near 139 basis points and Oracle's around 298, compared with about 1,155 for CoreWeave.

A CoreWeave spokesperson said the company does not currently expect any impact to its existing customer commitments or associated backlog from shifts in the political landscape, according to Bloomberg. Financing for AI projects has not stopped, and Goldman Sachs counts five AI-linked bond sales worth a combined $67 billion since Oct. 29, according to CNBC. National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett told CNBC on Friday that he expects data centers to keep expanding at the projected pace. Separately, Motley Fool columnist Leo Sun, writing on Yahoo Finance, warned that CoreWeave's high yields are a red flag for AI debt.

The company's costs were already climbing before this week. In October its 2032 bond carried a yield to maturity of 14.8% and its stock fell 16% in one day. Net interest expense was $640 million in the second quarter, more than double the $267 million a year earlier, and in that quarter it raised more than $10 billion in unsecured debt and convertible bonds plus a $3.1 billion term loan. Sun noted that CoreWeave ended that quarter with $72 billion in total liabilities and a debt-to-equity ratio of 14.3, and that its senior bonds begin maturing in 2030. He added that rivals Nebius and IREN carry far lower leverage, with debt-to-equity ratios of 1.7 and 2.8, though tighter credit could make financing harder for them too.

stories.Headline: China's 'potato capital' cultivates new crop of data centres as AI boom takes root - CNA
stories.Summary:
Ulanqab, a city in China's Inner Mongolia region known as the country's "potato capital," is rapidly turning its farmland into sites for AI data centres. Reporting by CNA visited the city, where the boom is changing local livelihoods and raising questions about water use in a drought-prone area. Farmer Zhang Zhiyong, 64, said developers began approaching residents of his village, Shengjiaying, about two years ago to buy land for data centres. He received more than 200,000 yuan (US$30,000) for about 0.7 hectares of his roughly 1.3 hectares, and now grows potatoes on just one mu, about 670 square metres.

Ulanqab has long been a major agricultural producer, with annual potato output approaching 4 million tonnes, nearly 5 per cent of China's total, according to People's Daily in 2023. Now a different industry is taking hold, as Xinhua reported in October that the city has signed 109 computing-centre projects. As of August, AI-focused computing made up more than 90 per cent of the city's total computing capacity. The city is part of China's "East Data, West Computing" strategy, which moves computing work from the more developed east to western areas with more land and energy.

President Xi Jinping visited the Chahar High-Tech Development Zone on October 16, a data-centre hub housing facilities run by Huawei, Alibaba and Apple. According to state media, Xi was briefed on green computing infrastructure and called for closer coordination between computing, electricity and water resources. Local officials and developers are responsible for the expansion, and the articles say the central leadership is paying close attention to it. Water sustainability in the drought-prone region remains a concern raised by the reporting.

The construction boom has also changed local business, with food vendors serving workers at the sites. Food hawker Gao Lina, 46, said she sells about 100 portions of pork rib rice a day at the Bayin data-centre cluster, and about 30 roadside eateries were seen operating nearby. Her stall moved there about a year ago, and she hopes to stay for another two to three years as more facilities are planned. At Yiwutang, a vendor said his customers have shifted from construction workers to engineers as building gives way to equipment installation.

stories.Headline: [PRNewswire] Agoda and OpenAI Bring AI Learning to Life
stories.Summary:
Agoda, the digital travel platform, hosted the 12th edition of its Agoda Tech Camp Day on November 5 and 6, 2026, in Bangkok, welcoming more than 420 students from four Thai universities. This edition was run with OpenAI and brings the program's total reach to over 4,100 students since 2023. Workshops introduced students to basic AI concepts and to practical uses of ChatGPT for their studies and future careers, drawing on examples from Agoda's own work. The program was framed around the finding from Agoda's AI Developer Report 2026 that junior developers were nearly three times as likely as senior developers to name a lack of skills as a barrier to wider AI agent adoption.

During the workshops, students compared Chat mode with Work mode in ChatGPT and used personal instructions, tools and skills to guide an agent through multi-step tasks. Among the projects, they turned spreadsheet data into a presentation and an interactive web app, and they built and published their own applications. They also learned to package workflow instructions into reusable skills so an agent could repeat a set of steps from one prompt. Participating students will receive two months of ChatGPT Plus access to keep practicing after the event. The students came from first to fourth year at Sripatum University, Rajamangala University of Technology Phra Nakhon, Rajamangala University of Technology Thanyaburi and Suan Sunandha Rajabhat University.

Agoda's Chief Technology Officer, Idan Zalzberg, said that AI is most useful when people understand its abilities and limits and can apply it to a problem they care about. He said the event shares Agoda's practical experience with future tech talent and, through OpenAI, adds expertise in building AI, helping students use it responsibly. Sandy Kunvatanagarn, OpenAI's Head of Policy for ASEAN, said Thai students are already curious about AI and that the goal is to build their confidence and judgment, including checking sources and questioning output. Dr. Preesan Rakwatin of the Digital Economy Promotion Agency attended the opening ceremony and said that building AI skills is essential for Thailand's young people and its digital economy. Government support also came alongside the Ministry of Higher Education, Science, Research and Innovation and the Bangkok Metropolitan Administration.

The companies present the event against a backdrop of strong AI use in Thailand, which ranks among the top 20 countries for weekly active ChatGPT users. According to OpenAI's internal data, creative media, writing and communication, and education and learning are the three most common ChatGPT uses among 18- to 24-year-olds there. Agoda says the program fits Thailand's push for AI adoption, which it links to productivity, growth and new jobs, and it points to the company's engineering teams in Thailand as part of that effort. Since launching, Agoda Tech Camp Day has also covered UX/UI design and web development for high school and university students, with workshops led by Agoda engineers. The post, labeled as breaking news, said Anthropic would be "tokenized on day one" and launched "on IPO day." It gave no date, price or token terms, and it did not say Anthropic was involved. The post had drawn 74,231 views when the outlet checked on November 7.

Ondo's product page describes Ondo Stocks as giving eligible investors outside the United States onchain economic exposure to publicly traded securities. According to that page, the tokens are fully backed by underlying shares and are secured by U.S. stocks, ETFs and cash held with U.S. broker-dealers, with an independent Verification Agent reviewing the backing daily. Anthropic also says it does not currently intend to list its Class A common stock on any exchange in those international jurisdictions. A separate Anthropic notice warns that any sale or transfer of its stock not approved by its board is void, and that third parties offering tokenized securities may be offering an investment with no value. stories.Headline: European Social Good Projects Reveal Crucial Machine Learning and Statistics Balance
stories.Summary:
Researchers Theo Berger and Hannes Scheffter examined European Data Science for Good initiatives, which are non-profit networks that match volunteers with charities and public bodies to build data applications. Their study, published in EPJ Data Science, reviewed 335 projects from 23 organisations across ten European countries, carried out between 2011 and 2024. From that pool they identified a core sample of 99 projects with full documentation, source code and validation records, and catalogued 146 distinct analytical methods within them. The authors classified each method as statistical or machine learning using a five-rule framework, and an independent second coding produced strong agreement, with observed agreement of 89.6 percent.

The results show that machine learning dominated the civic projects overall, though not uniformly. Of the 99 core projects, 55 relied only on machine learning, 33 only on statistical approaches, and 11 used both, so machine learning appeared in 66.6 percent of projects against 44.4 percent for statistics. Natural language processing was the single most common technique, making up 19.9 percent of all methods. The choice of method tracked the type of target variable: machine learning covered 86 percent of nominal targets and 94.1 percent of ordinal targets, but for continuous metric targets statistical methods held 74.5 percent of applications, with exploratory and descriptive analysis the largest single category. The authors also found that combining both paradigms in one project was rare, and that 91 percent of projects had operational lifespans of six months or less, which they linked to volunteer turnover and inconsistent documentation.

The authors draw implications for university training, arguing that programmes should move beyond generic computing modules toward a "T-shaped" profile, with deep technical skill in one area and broad competence in statistics, data hygiene, spatial reasoning and communication with non-technical partners. They also argue that graduates should learn to judge whether a problem calls for predictive algorithms or simpler interpretable statistical methods. The study further recommends service-learning capstones, project-based coursework and transparent documentation standards to address the short life and weak record-keeping of volunteer projects. The articles provided do not describe any specific follow-up steps or policy changes beyond these recommendations.

stories.Headline: JPMorgan and Mastercard back Seattle startup Firmly’s bet on AI shopping agents
stories.Summary:
Seattle-area startup Firmly, which helps online retailers sell through AI shopping assistants, has raised a $15 million Series A round led by Squarepoint Capital. J.P. Morgan Payments, Mastercard, Samsung Next and several other investors also took part, and the company announced the round in early November 2026. The round brings Firmly's total funding to roughly $20 million. Firmly was founded in 2019 and had previously raised $5.2 million before partnering with Perplexity on shopping features in its AI search app in March 2025.

The company's software connects a retailer's existing online store to AI assistants, marketplaces and other shopping channels, so customers can buy products inside those third-party services without visiting the retailer's website. Retailers keep their own payment providers and customer relationships, and they choose which products to offer. Firmly links to retailers' systems only with their explicit permission, and it does so without having software click through web pages, which distinguishes it from browser-based shopping agents. The company also launched Ask Agent, an AI shopping assistant for retailers' own websites, which lets shoppers describe what they want and check out without leaving the chat. Mastercard is also a commercial partner, since Firmly handles the merchant side of Mastercard Agent Connect, a service launched in September that links merchants, AI agents and payment providers through one integration.

Firmly's co-founder and CEO, Kumar Senthil, said in a blog post that every new AI assistant or marketplace is another place to sell, but that connecting to each one can require serious engineering. He told Axios Pro that merchants are in the business of selling products rather than managing protocols, and that Mastercard is recruiting merchants for its service, which gives Firmly a route to new customers. Senthil has said that connecting a merchant took four to six weeks in 2024 but now takes a day or less, including testing. Firmly charges merchants $2,000 to $15,000 a month, depending on the total value of the merchandise they sell. Its listed retail customers include Best Buy, Furniture.com and Backcountry, and RetailMeNot and an AI shopping app called Wizard also use its technology.

The funding comes as AI shopping agents move into the mainstream, with Meta's Muse assistant able to browse retail sites and buy items with a user's approval. Amazon has blocked Muse from its site and is suing Perplexity over a shopping agent in the startup's Comet browser. Other investors in the round include Alumni Ventures, ARK Invest, Benhamou Global Ventures, Granada Funds, Hike Ventures, The Mercantile Companies and Versus Ventures. The articles do not say what Firmly plans to do with the new capital.

stories.Headline: LA City Council Orders Report on AI Rent-Setting Software
stories.Summary:
The Los Angeles City Council voted unanimously this week to order a full study of how artificial intelligence tools are used to set rents across the city. The vote stops short of creating any new rule, but it opens the door to future regulation. Council members instructed housing staff to report back with policy recommendations on algorithmic rent-setting and other AI technologies used by housing providers. The council itself did not adopt any regulation with this action.

The vote formalizes a motion introduced on Oct. 13 by Councilwoman Eunisses Hernandez, who called for regulatory safeguards, transparency requirements, registration programs and dedicated funding. Hernandez said corporate landlords are increasingly using these tools to set prices and manage vacancies, and that the city has no way to track their effect on the rental market. Council members Marqueece Harris-Dawson, Monica Rodriguez and Imelda Padilla seconded the motion. Hernandez also credited Councilwoman Heather Hutt, who had introduced a similar motion the previous year.

The report will be prepared by the housing department, the chief legislative analyst, the city administrative officer and city attorneys. Their assignment covers a registration and disclosure program for multifamily housing providers using such software, and tenant notice requirements when AI influences rent, renewals or occupancy. Officials must also examine the city's legal authority to restrict technology that relies on nonpublic competitor information, plus annual fees and whether a special fund could pay for eviction prevention and tenant services. The council further asked for a review of practices in Berkeley and West Hollywood, along with updates on a federal antitrust lawsuit joined by California in August 2024 and a September 2025 Nevada settlement with RealPage.

Other California cities have already acted. West Hollywood adopted Ordinance No. 26-08 on May 4, 2026, which bars landlords from using covered algorithmic devices to set rents or occupancy levels, with civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation. San Francisco passed a similar ban in 2024, yet asking rents there still rose 14% from March to July 2026, according to ApartmentList data cited by the San Francisco Standard. Research on the software has drawn scrutiny as well, with a UC Berkeley School of Information study in spring 2025 finding an association between RealPage use and higher rents. For now, Los Angeles is gathering information, and the shape of any future policy will depend on the report it has ordered.

stories.Headline: Media executive calls for greater cooperation, human oversight in AI-driven journalism--China Economic Net
stories.Summary:
Sumeyra Teymur, CEO of Turkish news platform Haberler.com, said that artificial intelligence is opening new possibilities for journalism but that media organizations must work together more closely so that technological progress goes hand in hand with reliable reporting. She made these remarks in Istanbul on November 7, 2026, in an interview published by Xinhua ahead of the 7th World Media Summit in Beijing. The summit is hosted by Xinhua News Agency and the Beijing Municipal People's Government, and it runs from November 5 to 9 under the theme "Media in the Intelligent Age: From Consensus to Action." Teymur said that she had been impressed by China's efforts to bring advanced technology into its media industry. She recalled seeing AI anchors present news during an earlier visit to the country.

Teymur described how her own platform uses AI in daily work. Haberler.com receives more than 2,000 news articles from various sources each day, and its system organizes that content, generates headlines, and adds relevant photos and videos to articles. These tools allow her editorial team to handle a larger volume of news than it could otherwise manage. She also said she was interested in using humanoid robots to cover dangerous situations such as earthquakes and armed conflicts, where sending human reporters could put them at risk. The article presents these examples as signs of how the technology might expand what newsrooms can do.

Teymur stressed, however, that people must remain in the loop. She warned that AI can make mistakes and can be used to create fabricated news, images, and videos, as well as to manipulate voices and identities. She said that whenever her organization uses AI, a human checks the content, and she emphasized that media outlets have a responsibility to verify information before publishing it. Her position is that these checks are a core duty of the media organizations themselves rather than an optional safeguard.

Teymur also called for stronger international cooperation among media organizations in sharing information, technological expertise, and cultural stories. She noted that no single organization can stop the rapid spread of misinformation across borders on its own. She said she looked forward to exchanging experiences with Chinese journalists and strengthening ties with Chinese media organizations during the summit. stories.Headline: The AI Trade Unwind Crushed The S&P 500 This Week
stories.Summary:
Markets slid sharply in the first week of November 2026 as a sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks spread across the United States and Asia. According to the Mott Capital Management analysis, the SMH semiconductor fund fell more than 11% over the week, the Nasdaq nearly 5%, the S&P 500 nearly 3%, and the IWM about 2%. The market had rallied on Wednesday after the midterm elections, with the S&P 500 up about 1.58%, but it gave those gains back on Thursday as semiconductor shares continued to fall and correlations among stocks rose. Business Insider reported that the Nasdaq 100 entered an official correction on Thursday, and that Asian tech shares were hit hard on Friday, when South Korea's Kospi fell 9% in early trading, triggering a trading halt, and Japan's Nikkei 225 sank 7%.

The Mott analysis describes a volatility unwind that masked weakness beneath the surface. The 1-day VIX had risen to about 23 before the election, implying a move of roughly 1.4% for Wednesday, and once that event passed, options premiums decayed and hedges came off, lifting the index while technology shares fell. By Thursday's close the 1-day VIX stood at 36.8, and the author expects limited room for volatility to fall further, noting that the one-month implied correlation of 20 is high relative to recent months but low historically. The analysis flags CPI due Tuesday, November 10, and PPI after it as near-term catalysts, and it says the S&P 500 sits on an important support level that a break could push lower. Business Insider adds that investors fear Democratic election wins could bring tighter regulation of data centers and AI development, which could threaten the spending boom behind the rally.

Michael Kramer, a member and investment adviser representative with Mott Capital Management, wrote the Mott analysis, which presents his own views and is published for informational purposes only. He argued that the market could keep unwinding if Nvidia, Micron, and Broadcom stop working, and he said Thursday and Friday might prove to be an isolated event. Business Insider quotes Charu Chanana, Saxo's chief investment strategist, who said the sharp correction partly reflects a reassessment of future US infrastructure demand and crowded investor positioning in AI beneficiaries. She said the market is repricing future expectations rather than reacting to a sudden collapse in current demand, and that it may be the end of rewarding every company linked to AI equally.

Looking ahead, the sources point to the inflation data due next week and to the question of whether AI spending will pay off. Business Insider reports that investors increasingly want evidence of returns and may favor firms with strong finances and established customers over those relying on outside funding. Chanana described the sell-off as possibly not the end of the AI trade, while Kramer's analysis warned that mechanical unwinding could continue and that caution is warranted. Neither source offers a firm forecast beyond the coming days.

stories.Headline: Who Owns DeepSeek, The Chinese AI Company?
stories.Summary:
DeepSeek, a Chinese AI lab, drew global attention when it launched its R1 model in 2025, using a mixture of experts design to generate responses at a far lower cost than rivals. The app quickly grew popular, and the launch set off a global technology stock selloff that year. The company has since released its V4-Flash model, which the articles say is more than 90% cheaper to run than peer models such as Kimi K3, GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Fable 5. Its models are subject to censorship under Chinese law, which may limit future growth.

The company was founded by Liang Wenfeng, an electronics engineer from Zhejiang University, who funded its launch in 2023 with profits from his hedge fund, High-Flyer. In DeepSeek's second funding round it raised about $15 billion from backers including Tencent Holdings and CATL, and the articles say 27% of that funding is state-owned, with the China National AI Industry Investment Fund contributing about $150 million. Liang is one of four Chinese tech entrepreneurs the media have dubbed China's "fantastic four," and the company is reportedly considering an IPO on Shanghai's STAR Market. The market reaction to R1 was severe: NVIDIA lost $589 billion in market value in a single day, the largest single-day loss in the history of the U.S. stock market.

The articles tie DeepSeek's efficiency to its technical methods, including its mixture of experts architecture, which activates only the parts of a model needed for a task, along with optimization for cheaper GPUs, model distillation and reinforcement learning. Before U.S. export controls took effect in 2022, High-Flyer and other Chinese entities stockpiled NVIDIA GPUs, which DeepSeek later used. The U.S. has tried to limit China's access to such chips, and China has responded by advancing its homegrown chip manufacturing to reduce reliance on Western chips and tools. The articles suggest the wider AI industry could learn from these efficiency gains to ease the heavy resource demands of data centers.

stories.Summary:
Indonesia's government announced investment agreements worth a combined US$385 million in technology and downstream industries during a trip to London. The delegation included Finance Minister Suahasil Nazara, Bank Indonesia Governor Destry Damayanti, and Investment and Downstream Minister Rosan Roeslani, who attended the Indonesia Investment Forum 2026 in the United Kingdom on Thursday. The goal of the trip was to promote investment opportunities in the country as part of efforts to boost investment and reach economic growth targets. Finance Minister Suahasil Nazara has emphasized the need to grow investment by 7 percent to help reach the country's gross domestic product target. At the forum, Indonesia secured new partnership agreements in artificial intelligence, industrial estate development, and tin downstreaming.

These deals are intended to bring new technology and add value within the country. One agreement pairs Central Java industrial estate operator PT Kawasan Industri Terpadu Batang with European chip company Axelera AI to explore developing an AI ecosystem, with an investment value of $56 million. Separately, PT Jakarta Industrial Estate Pulogadung signed a $77 million investment agreement with asset management firm BlackInk Co-operation Ltd focused on using its industrial land. The government also announced a Letter of Intent from private investment firm Titanium Capital for a tin downstream project worth $252.1 million. The articles do not describe the terms of the letter beyond its value and sector.

The forum and the agreements were presented by the government as steps toward its investment and growth goals. The announcement came as officials sought foreign investment to support national economic targets. The articles do not say whether the agreements have been finalized or when the projects will begin construction. They also do not give further details on how the government plans to track progress on the 7 percent investment growth goal.

stories.Headline: The Artificial Intelligence (AI) Boom Is Far From Over. Here Are 4 Potential Long-Term Winners
stories.Summary:
Recent earnings reports from major AI companies have prompted Motley Fool analyst Prosper Junior Bakiny to argue that the artificial intelligence boom is not yet over. Writing on November 7, 2026, he points to corporations that are still spending heavily on AI infrastructure and says this suggests the trend could continue for years. He identifies four companies he believes are positioned to benefit over the long run: Nvidia, Microsoft, Advanced Micro Devices, and Broadcom. The article appeared on Motley Fool and was syndicated by The Globe and Mail the same day.

Nvidia is described as one of the biggest winners so far, with a runaway lead in graphics processing units despite growing competition. The author credits its CUDA software ecosystem with creating high switching costs that help protect its position. He notes that demand for its chips may not grow as fast as it has recently, but says the company has expanded into hardware and services that work alongside its processors. Microsoft is presented as having adapted after some investors worried AI would make its software obsolete. The article says its cloud business is booming, helped by its AI services and a large, rapidly growing cloud backlog.

Advanced Micro Devices is said to be gaining from soaring demand for central processing units, which the author links to AI agents, even though it trails Nvidia in graphics chips. The article reports excellent recent results in its data center segment and says the company has raised its 2030 addressable market guidance several times over the past year. Broadcom is portrayed as a rising force because it designs custom AI chips that corporations increasingly buy to diversify away from Nvidia. The author says these chips can be cheaper and more power-efficient than graphics processors, and that Broadcom counts Meta, Alphabet, and Anthropic among its AI customers. He acknowledges that its AI chip business carries lower margins than its software segment but argues the trade-off will pay off over time.

stories.Headline: George Kurtz Just Announced Incredible News for CrowdStrike Investors and the Artificial Intelligence (AI) Industry
stories.Summary:
On November 3, 2026, at CrowdStrike's Fal.Con conference in Europe, chief executive George Kurtz unveiled the AI Kill Switch, a new product that lets enterprises take full control of the AI agents running on their networks. The announcement came as the company keeps adding features to its Falcon platform to counter the threats that artificial intelligence creates. Articles from The Motley Fool, published on Yahoo Finance and AOL in early November, covered the launch and its implications for investors. The product is part of the Falcon Guardian platform, which the company describes as an AI Detection and Response tool.

The Kill Switch lets a human security decision maker immediately end a running agent at its source, cut off its network access, and stop it from running again. The articles say this is the first time enterprises will have that level of control over their agent fleets, and they note it works only because the Falcon platform is embedded across the network and its endpoints. Existing Falcon Guardian tools already track every input and output from trusted agents and inventory every AI application, so security teams can spot an unauthorized agent. The articles argue that this confidence in control could speed up how quickly businesses adopt AI agents, which often need deep access to sensitive data and can be compromised through prompt injection.

The articles attribute the announcement to CrowdStrike chief executive George Kurtz, who presented it at the Fal.Con event. The Motley Fool author, Anthony Di Pizio, frames the product as a potential game-changer for both CrowdStrike and the wider AI industry. The author is careful to add that CrowdStrike stock looks expensive, with a price-to-sales ratio of 46.6 as of November 4, compared with 23.1 for Palo Alto Networks and 6.3 for the Nasdaq-100. Di Pizio also says the company believes it can grow annual recurring revenue to $20 billion by fiscal 2036, a goal the article presents as a reason long-term holders might still do well.

The context offered is that CrowdStrike reported $5.84 billion in annual recurring revenue at the end of its fiscal 2027 second quarter, ended July 31, up 25 percent from a year earlier. The articles say AI products are driving that growth, with ARR from its AI Detection and Response offering nearly tripling from the prior quarter. The company also projects its addressable market will reach $325 billion by calendar year 2030. The articles do not say when the AI Kill Switch will become generally available, so the near-term effect on revenue remains unclear from these sources.

stories.Headline: Anthropic’s $1.5 Trillion IPO Could Expose the Biggest Risk Facing the AI Boom
stories.Summary:
Anthropic is reportedly seeking $80 billion to $100 billion in a public offering at a valuation near $1.5 trillion, down from earlier talk of about $2 trillion. The deal is being watched as a test of whether the AI infrastructure buildout can keep funding itself. Shares of CoreWeave, which rents out computing capacity, closed at $46.40 on November 6, down 47.54% in one month and 56.61% over the past year. The stock's slide has made it the most direct way for investors to bet on that question. The reporting was carried by Yahoo Finance and 24/7 Wall St. on November 8, 2026.

CoreWeave's balance sheet relies heavily on borrowed money. At the end of the second quarter of 2026, it carried $72.05 billion in total liabilities against $5.02 billion of shareholders' equity. Its operating income did not cover its interest costs, which reached $640 million in the quarter, up from $267 million a year earlier. Management guided third-quarter interest to between $860 million and $940 million. Free cash flow in the quarter was negative $5.743 billion, and the company covered that gap with $10.071 billion of financing.

The articles say the company's position would weaken if credit tightened, since it depends on open debt markets to fund its planned capital spending of $35 billion to $39 billion this year. Anthropic's own filings show about $895.4 billion in future computing and infrastructure obligations, including $69.8 billion due in the next 12 months, and warn that higher financing costs or tighter credit could delay contracted capacity. Reuters reported on November 5 that some investors wondered whether the roadshow could stay on schedule. The 10-year Treasury yield stood at 4.84%. CoreWeave also has concentrated customers, including about $22.4 billion in OpenAI commitments, depends on NVIDIA for its chips, and faces a securities fraud class action alleging it hid data center construction delays.

NVIDIA, by contrast, earns revenue from the same buildout without carrying comparable debt. In its fiscal second quarter of 2027 it produced $21.341 billion of free cash flow and $59.688 billion of net income, with a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.07. The articles note NVIDIA trades at about 38 times earnings, which they describe as expensive but supported by real profits. They say the key milestones to watch for CoreWeave are positive free cash flow and interest costs covered by operating income, and until it reaches them, the company remains a direct proxy for AI credit conditions with high financing risk.

stories.Headline: Dollar climbs on safe haven demand as AI rout saps Asian markets - CNA
stories.Summary:
The US dollar index climbed 0.77 per cent to 102.26 on Friday, November 6, 2026, as a stronger-than-expected US jobs report pushed it toward its biggest daily gain in nearly five months. The Labor Department said nonfarm payrolls rose by 165,000 in October, well above the 65,000 that economists polled by Reuters had expected, and the unemployment rate dipped to 4.1 per cent. The euro fell 0.67 per cent to $1.11437, and the Japanese yen weakened 0.47 per cent to 158.430 against the greenback. The move came as safe-haven demand lifted the dollar earlier in the day, after a selloff in AI-linked stocks spread across global markets.

The jobs data strengthened expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates at its December meeting. Market odds of a rise of at least 25 basis points rebounded toward 80 per cent after the report, according to the CME FedWatch Tool, up from about 67 per cent on Thursday. Treasury yields also rose, with the 10-year yield up 1.6 basis points to 4.85 per cent and the 2-year yield up 4.1 basis points to 4.52 per cent. Sterling dropped 0.71 per cent to $1.3355, on pace for its biggest daily fall since September 23, after the Bank of England raised rates for the first time in more than three years.

Fed officials speaking on Friday backed the case for tightening. New York Fed President John Williams said US growth has held up remarkably well through successive shocks, but that inflation is too high and must return to 2 per cent. St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said inflation remains a top concern in his talks with businesses, and San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly said the central bank will likely still need to raise rates further despite what she called a "painful" tech stock selloff. Earlier in the week, US equities had slumped, with the S&P 500 losing about $3 trillion in market value and the Nasdaq suffering its worst one-day percentage drop in 19 months, amid fears that tougher AI regulation after the US midterm elections would slow economic growth.

Those regulatory fears centre on Democrats, who plan to introduce a wave of new legislation on artificial intelligence systems and data-center development when they take control of Congress in January, according to lawmakers, congressional aides and advocates. In Japan, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi proposed using proceeds from the Bank of Japan's sales of exchange-traded funds to finance her flagship investment projects, as the AI-driven rout threatened tax revenue. Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda said underlying inflation should stay near the 2 per cent target but acknowledged "some upside risks." The articles do not say when the Fed's December decision will be announced.

stories.Headline: AI Could Make Filmmaking Costlier Than the 35mm Era, Korean Pioneers Warn at Taiwan Creative Content Fest
stories.Summary:
AI could make feature filmmaking more expensive than the 35mm era, according to two Korean AI production pioneers who spoke at the Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF) in Taipei. Kim Kwang-jib, founder and CEO of Studio Meta-K, warned that token fees on the most expensive commercial tools could top KRW500 million ($366,000) for a 100-minute film. He said AI companies are currently losing money and keeping prices low as a marketing move. If those costs rose roughly tenfold, he argued, they could exceed what Korean, Taiwanese and other Asian features now spend on live action and VFX.

Kim explained that every re-render is paid for again, so the total budget depends on how few rounds of revisions a project requires. He said that if a client sends 10 changes at once, the studio can re-render a single time, but if the same changes arrive one a day over 10 days, the studio must re-render 10 times. Lee Sang-wook, head of the AI Content Lab at MBC C&I, said budgeting is also hard because tools change weekly. His lab's 139-minute feature "Raphael" took about one year and four months to make, and it opens in Korean cinemas on Nov. 25.

Both speakers described the financial trade-offs of using AI in production. Kim said a Pizza Hut commercial that took about eight months and roughly KRW2 billion ($1.4 million) could be made in-house in about two weeks for around KRW30 million ($22,000). He said he does not think audiences will yet pay for fully AI films, so he favors a hybrid model in which AI generates large crowd scenes while leads are shot live. Lee said the lab's earlier AI shorts drew a cold market response, so it chose a cinema release because theatrical releases can move to streaming later.

The speakers also discussed jobs and the tools themselves. Kim said crews of hundreds on a single scene will become rarer, and that workers who learn AI will replace those who do not. Lee compared the shift to the arrival of sound and predicted new roles such as previsualization artists and continuity supervisors. The two companies also differ on open-source models, with Studio Meta-K using them for simpler shots and MBC C&I avoiding them because it cannot verify training data transparency. The session was moderated by Archin Yen, director and VFX supervisor at WWWIND Studio.

stories.Headline: ‘Pokemon’ Anime Studio OLM Trains AI Coloring Tool on Just Three Frames in Japan Government-Backed Project
stories.Summary:
OLM, the Japanese animation group behind the Pokemon anime, has built an AI coloring tool that learns a show's look from just three hand-painted frames, according to OLM Digital board director Yotsukura Tatsuo. He presented the tool at the Taiwan Creative Content Fest in Taipei. The tool came out of ANIMINS, a 15-month research project Yotsukura led under GENIAC, a generative AI program overseen by Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, which wrapped up in February. Because such systems usually need large training sets, OLM instead has an artist color three frames, after which the system learns the show's line shapes and palette in about 90 seconds and colors each remaining frame in roughly 15 seconds.

Yotsukura said the tool is not generative AI in the strict sense, and that training only on a production's own frames avoids using other people's work. It can adapt when a new creature such as a dragon appears, and OLM stresses that it fits into existing anime workflows. At proof-of-concept stage, he estimated it has cut painting workload by around 30%, although the people who check each colored frame have somewhat more to do. Toon Boom Animation, the Canadian maker of Harmony and Storyboard Pro, is working on the same problem, with its coloring tool in beta inside its Ember AI suite and in-betweening expected to follow within a couple of weeks. One Manila studio that tested the coloring tool reportedly cut the painting time on a 90-second scene from 15 hours to two or three.

OLM employs around 600 staff across Japan, Malaysia, Thailand and the U.S., and produces the Pokemon anime, Beyblade, Hanakappa and The Apothecary Diaries. Yotsukura, who also serves as CTO for the group's Malaysian and Thai arms, said the group is also testing AI for in-betweening and for anime-specific agents that could help with directing and license management. Toon Boom's product marketing director, Harry Ravelomanantsoa, said the creative work stays with the artist while mechanical tasks go to AI. Yotsukura agreed with that split and said AI can only do what it has learned. Charles Beirnaert, chief creative officer of Blue Spirit, said his studio uses no AI on its Netflix projects, which the streamer's guidelines restrict, and that AI is not meant to replace animators.

Yotsukura compared the arrival of AI to that of 3DCG, which took around 20 years to gain acceptance in anime, but said AI will move faster because its quality is already high. He said he thinks "not using AI" is probably no longer an option. Beirnaert's team used AI to recreate a pilot that took a team of about 20 roughly three months, with one person finishing the work within days. The article presents these accounts as the views of the speakers at the event, and it does not report any outcome beyond what they described.

stories.Headline: Opinion | US and China must join hands to measure rising AI tide
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is advancing so quickly that Washington and Beijing may not have a shared sense of how fast its capabilities are growing, according to an opinion piece by Marshall Li and Zhengfei Zhang published by the South China Morning Post on November 7, 2026. The authors argue that the next US-China talks on AI should start by asking whether both governments really understand this pace. They say the two sides need a common method for measuring progress before deciding how to respond. The piece notes that Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump are expected to meet in Shenzhen soon, with AI likely to stay high on their agenda.

The authors describe their ongoing exchanges on the technology as a positive sign, though they warn that governments may have less time to prepare for its consequences than they assume. They point to changes in creative and professional work, where AI is reshaping fields once thought hard to disrupt. In China, according to the article, more than 90 per cent of new microdramas released in the first eight months of the year were AI-generated, produced without cameras or live actors. A production that once needed as many as 100 people can now be finished in one week by a team of two to five. The authors add that AI has eliminated much of the well-paid work that actors once relied on.

The article frames the call for shared measurement as a responsibility of both governments rather than of any single party. It presents Li and Zhang as arguing that Beijing and Washington should work together to track how quickly the technology is progressing. The authors' central request is that the two governments first agree on a basis for judging AI's development and only then decide on policy. The piece does not describe any formal commitment or agreement reached by either government on this point. It instead positions the proposal as a step toward closing the gap between the speed of AI's advance and the speed of official responses.

stories.Headline: America’s AI Spending Boom Just Crossed a Staggering $1 Trillion Milestone
stories.Summary:
America's AI hardware imports have hit a pace of roughly $1.04 trillion a year, according to trade data for September 2026 reported by The Kobeissi Letter. U.S. imports of computers, computer accessories, and semiconductors rose $12.1 billion in that month to $86.9 billion, the second-largest monthly increase on record. The annualized figure assumes September's pace holds for a full year, which is a meaningful assumption drawn from a single month of data. Still, the year-over-year growth of 151% is far faster than the peak of about 34% seen during the dot-com boom. Since the start of 2024, these import categories have more than quadrupled.

Much of this equipment flows into data centers, where NVIDIA sits at the center of the order book. In its fiscal Q2 2027, NVIDIA reported revenue of $96.22 billion, above the $92.07 billion estimate and up 105.8% from a year earlier. Its Data Center revenue reached $89.02 billion, up 117%, and non-GAAP gross margin widened to 75.0% from 72.5%. Other suppliers are also reporting strong demand, including Dell with a record $95 billion AI backlog and Broadcom with AI chip revenue up 221%. Micron, Vertiv, and CoreWeave also cited large commitments and backlogs.

NVIDIA's management expects spending to keep climbing, and on its August 26, 2026 earnings call, it pointed to capital spending by the top five hyperscalers reaching nearly $800 billion in 2026 and $1.3 trillion in 2027. CEO Jensen Huang said demand is much greater than the company's ability to supply, and that its supply allows it to confidently deliver 70% of that demand. The cloud industry backlog was described as greater than $2 trillion. The stock has not followed the trade data, closing at $186.64 on November 6, 2026, down 21.4% over the past month. The article notes that gross margins are expected to bottom at 71% to 72% in the fourth quarter as memory costs rise.

The broader context is that AI spending is moving ahead of proven returns, which the article says leaves room for overcapacity if demand fades. NVIDIA's next earnings report will test its fiscal Q3 guidance of $108.0 billion revenue, plus or minus 2%, at a gross margin of roughly 74.0%. The company expects Vera Rubin to make up about 20% of Data Center revenue in that period. The article concludes that while the stock has fallen, America is importing AI hardware at a record pace, and most of that hardware is built to run on NVIDIA chips.

stories.Headline: AI safety advocates make gains after $110 million midterm fight
stories.Summary:
Candidates who favor stricter oversight of artificial intelligence won several key congressional races in the U.S. midterm elections, according to a report published by The Japan Times on November 8, 2026. The wins came with help from a pro-regulation political funding group called Public First, which is backed in part by Anthropic and was funded by Anthropic co-founder Dario Amodei and other AI safety advocates. The report notes that this happened as Americans have grown increasingly uneasy about the rapidly developing technology. Public First spent more than $63 million on the midterms to support candidates who share its goal of tighter regulation, based on the group's own figures. The article names Colorado's Manny Rutinel and California's Scott Wiener as two of the people who wrote some of the country's most sweeping state-level AI laws.

Both are expected to join the U.S. House after being elected with support from Public First. The group backed 17 congressional candidates, and ten of them won. The article does not describe any new federal rules or legal changes that would follow directly from these results. The report attributes the funding and the strategy to Public First and to Dario Amodei, who helped fund it along with other AI safety advocates. The article does not include a direct statement from Public First, Amodei or Anthropic about the results.

It describes the group as aimed at promoting stricter AI regulation, and it presents the outcome as a sign of how much influence the group has gained. The article does not say what legislation these incoming lawmakers plan to pursue. The article places the election results within a broader public debate over AI, in which voters are increasingly wary of the technology's rapid growth. It does not provide further details on how the new members will act once they take office in Congress. The article is brief, and it does not describe any next steps beyond the incoming House members' arrival in Washington.

stories.Headline: America’s Productivity Just Surged 3.6% — Is AI Finally Delivering on Its Promise?
stories.Summary:
Nonfarm business labor productivity rose at a 3.6% annualized rate in the third quarter of 2026, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics data cited in the reporting. That marked the third straight quarterly gain, following 2.1% in the second quarter and 1.4% in the first. Output grew 3.7% annualized while hours worked rose only 0.1%, meaning companies produced more without adding meaningful labor. Commentators tied this to the AI spending boom, though the data do not isolate AI's role.

Hourly compensation rose 2.9%, but productivity grew faster, so unit labor costs fell, with the index dropping to 124.39 from 124.6 in the second quarter. Corporate profits reached a $4.71 trillion annual rate in the second quarter, up 20.8% from a year earlier, according to the Bureau of Economic Analysis. Manufacturing profits climbed to $1.05 trillion from $812 billion in the prior quarter. Labor's share of nonfarm business output fell to 53.0%, the lowest in a series dating to 1947. Inflation-adjusted average hourly earnings for private workers were $11.26 in September, below $11.32 a year earlier.

The reporting notes that mining value added grew 13.7% and manufacturing 5.5% in the second quarter, outpacing the information sector's 2.7%, so heavy industry contributed alongside software and automation. A top Meta Platforms executive told the Financial Times that population decline makes AI productivity gains vital, arguing that output per hour is the main lasting route to economic growth as labor supply grows slowly. The articles frame this as a reason companies facing tight labor markets may lean on technology instead of new hires. Average hourly earnings reached a preliminary $38.00 in October, up from $36.85 a year earlier, while unit labor costs still rose 2.4% year over year.

The core PCE price index, the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation measure, rose 0.3% in September to a new high, and real GDP grew at a 3.4% annualized pace in the third quarter. The articles say one strong quarter will not convince the Fed that disinflation is certain. Two upcoming reports are highlighted: a revision of third-quarter productivity, where a gain holding above 3% and a fourth straight improvement would strengthen the AI argument, and hours worked, where continued flat hours alongside rising output would make the boom a profit story. If hours begin rising with output, the articles suggest workers may finally share in the gains.

stories.Headline: Wall Street Is Dumping AI Stocks Even as Business Booms. Something Doesn’t Add Up.
stories.Summary:
Shares of Advanced Micro Devices and Palantir have fallen sharply over the past month even though both companies just reported record quarters. AMD dropped 30.47% to $449.04, and Palantir fell 17.38% to $160.38, even after a rebound on Friday from a sharp selloff in chip stocks. The articles attribute the initial selling to worries about large AI spending commitments, debt financing and high valuations. They suggest that once institutions cut their exposure, leverage and options hedging may have pushed prices lower without any weakening in the businesses, though no one can yet say how much of the decline came from forced selling.

The comparison is framed around which stock better suits a retirement portfolio, where neither company pays a dividend, so all returns must come from share price gains. On valuation, the articles favor AMD: Palantir trades at 228 times earnings, 50.08 times book value and 176.12 times free cash flow, with an earnings yield of 0.44%, while AMD is priced at 109.97 times free cash flow and 11.69 times book, but its non-GAAP earnings per share of $2.09 rose 74%, faster than 45% revenue growth. On growth, Palantir wins: third-quarter revenue rose 95.9% to $2.313 billion, U.S. commercial revenue jumped 148% to $984 million, and full-year guidance was raised to $8.530 billion to $8.534 billion. AMD's Data Center revenue rose 97% to $8.546 billion, and CEO Lisa Su expects revenue to grow more than 80% in 2027.

On risk, the articles give Palantir the edge because of its balance sheet, which carries a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.031, net cash and $10.4 billion in cash and Treasuries. AMD's operating cash flow fell 44.33% to $1.2 billion, free cash flow dropped 70.86% to $554 million, inventory rose 35% to $11.46 billion, and total debt reached $7.08 billion after an August notes offering. The author concludes that AMD's profile better fits retirement priorities, since its earnings are growing into a lower valuation, while Palantir suits younger investors who can wait out a correction. Su is quoted saying demand exceeds supply, and the author describes AMD's cash flow dip as a working-capital cost of building inventory for customers including Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI and Oracle.

stories.Headline: TCL CSOT to Explore the Future of Displays in the AI Era at DTC 2026
stories.Summary:
The TCL CSOT Global Display Tech-Ecosystem Conference 2026, known as DTC 2026, will take place in Wuhan, China, on November 13, 2026. Organized by TCL CSOT under the theme "TRUE VISION, AI IN MOTION," the conference will showcase the company's latest work on Inkjet Printing OLED, APEX display technologies, AI applications, and next-generation display solutions. The announcement was distributed through PR Newswire and carried by several publications on November 8, 2026. It frames the event as a look at how displays can deliver rich colors and fine detail for varied usage scenarios as AI changes digital content and intelligent devices.

The articles describe the event as a platform for demonstrating and discussing these technologies rather than reporting any new outcome. The conference will examine how AI is reshaping content creation, device form factors, and human-machine interaction, and how those shifts are expanding the role of displays. TCL CSOT's Inkjet Printing OLED technology, which followed more than a decade of research and development, is moving from technical validation toward large-scale production. Its applications have grown from medical displays into IT and consumer products, including monitors and future intelligent devices.

At DTC 2026, the company plans to share further updates on this development and on its continued exploration of the technology. The APEX platform showcase will cover display experience, visual health, sustainability, and new form factors, linking development to real-world uses such as picture quality and viewing comfort. TCL CSOT is the organizer and is responsible for the content of the announcement, which the Straits Times notes was issued solely under its responsibility. Jun Zhao, Senior Vice President of TCL Technology and CEO of TCL CSOT, and Xiaolin Yan, CTO of TCL Technology and TCL CSOT, are expected to attend.

Science writer and Wenjin Book Award winner Weigang Wan is also expected to join the discussions. Their sessions are meant to examine how AI is reshaping display standards, product development, and user experience. The articles say the conference aims to offer an integrated view of the forces shaping displays and to encourage closer collaboration across the display industry. The organizers said more highlights from DTC 2026 would be announced soon.

stories.Headline: Dan Ives Sees A ‘Multiyear Tech Bull Market’ Despite AI Stock Rout — ‘This Was Just A... Scary Moment’
stories.Summary:
Dan Ives, the Wedbush and Yorkville analyst, said on Saturday that technology investors have overreacted to a sharp sell-off in AI-linked stocks. Speaking with Bloomberg, he said semiconductor stocks, hyperscalers and data center companies were hit hard after the U.S. midterm elections, which he called a painful shakeout. He still believes the broader tech bull market is intact. Ives made these comments in an interview published on November 8, 2026.

Ives said Democratic election victories and growing local opposition to data center construction were a major shock to tech investors. He argued that investors reassessed whether political resistance could derail the large infrastructure spending behind the AI boom. He also said concerns grew that tech companies could reach their peak capital spending sooner than expected. He acknowledged the spending trajectory is changing and suggested Big Tech's capital expenditure growth, once expected to peak around 2028 and 2029, could now peak as early as 2027. Ives added that this shift was being taken too far by investors.

Ives said the backlash could make it harder for technology companies to win over ordinary Americans, given fears of white-collar job losses and higher electricity bills. He believes companies will need to show concrete local benefits such as jobs, tax revenue and infrastructure investment. He pointed to projected AI infrastructure spending of $3 trillion to $4 trillion, arguing the investment cycle may last longer rather than end. He said fears of insufficient data center capacity were misplaced because chip demand and orders remained robust. He also said investors were starting to separate likely winners from losers, particularly among neocloud companies facing tougher competition.

Nvidia shares fell nearly 9% last week and AMD dropped over 11% for the week, despite an 11% gain on Friday. Ives said the ripple effects of AI spending reach companies such as Caterpillar, Lockheed Martin, energy firms and financial services providers. He believes political resistance may slow certain projects but will not stop the technology's advance. He described the recent turbulence as a white-knuckle roller-coaster moment. During Friday's after-hours session, the S&P 500, Nasdaq-100 and Dow Jones ETFs were modestly higher, while the Global X AI and Technology ETF rose 1.32% on Friday.

stories.Headline: How differences in economics, public policy, and cultural patterns could explain greater pessimism about AI in the West than in Asia and emerging economies (Gillian Tett/Financial Times)
stories.Summary:
The Financial Times columnist Gillian Tett published a piece on November 7, 2026, asking why Americans appear more pessimistic about artificial intelligence than people in parts of Asia and in emerging economies. The article's headline poses the question directly, but the text available to me is only the paywall page, so I cannot see its full argument. Accompanying coverage on Techmeme that same morning focused on a separate matter, a report that a Chinese executive linked to Megaspeed had been recruited by China's top spy agency. Taken together, these items show a moment when AI is drawing close attention from business, government, and the public. The Tett piece itself is framed as an explanation of a gap in attitudes rather than a single event.

The available sources do not spell out the economic, policy, or cultural factors that Tett identifies as explanations for the difference in attitudes. They also do not give any figures on public opinion in the West or in Asia that would show the size of the gap. What the sources do contain is reporting on the money flowing into the sector, including a roughly $11 billion funding round for OpenAI at a $1.25 trillion valuation and expectations that Anthropic would seek $80 billion to $100 billion in a public listing before Thanksgiving. Reports also said that some investors viewed the lower valuation of that listing as a possibility. These figures show the scale of commercial expectations, though they do not establish how ordinary people feel about the technology.

Responsibility for the espionage allegations rests with U.S. intelligence officials, who reportedly concluded that Alice Huang had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security. The New York Times and the Financial Times both reported that the officials believed she had sought to influence Nvidia's chief executive, Jensen Huang, and that Congressional committee leaders asked him for a closed-door briefing about his ties to her. Huang has not been quoted in these reports as responding to the claims. Commentators quoted on social media disputed how much weight to place on the reports, and the sources do not settle those disagreements. Whether the briefing takes place, and what follows from it, is not something the articles can predict.

stories.Headline: Big Tech, AI, and the quiet expansion of digital surveillance in Nigeria
stories.Summary:
The Federal Trade Commission in the United States published findings in September 2024 from an investigation into nine major social media and video-streaming companies, including Meta, YouTube, TikTok, and Amazon-owned Twitch. The report found that these firms gathered extensive information about users and, in some cases, people who were not users. That information covered personal details, interests, online activity, and data drawn from other sources. The investigation also flagged long data retention, weak privacy protections, and the use of personal data in automated systems, AI among them.

The report pointed to a basic imbalance between companies and the people whose information they hold. Firms can build a large store of knowledge about individuals, while those individuals often have little sense of how their data is used or how to limit certain uses. The article notes that AI makes this worse, since data can train models, sharpen recommendations and drive automated decisions. The more information a company can reach, the more important clear limits on collection and use become. The writer stresses that this is not necessarily a matter of malice, but of systems built to extract commercial value from data, which can push companies to collect more than people expect.

The article presents AI as a real source of opportunity, particularly in countries like Nigeria where access to resources and professional services is uneven. Students, small businesses and journalists can all benefit, and tools that support local languages and cultural experiences could widen access. Yet the writer argues that inclusion should also mean people understand the terms of use and keep meaningful rights over their information. Lengthy terms and privacy policies are often accepted without real understanding, and it is unclear in some cases whether prompts or uploaded documents are kept or used to improve models. Users need plain explanations of what is collected, why, how long it is kept and whether it serves purposes beyond the service itself.

The piece also examines how corporate data power could slide toward surveillance, noting that authoritarianism involves concentrated power that weakens accountability and rights, which is more than private data collection alone. Detailed personal profiles can support targeting, persuasion and behavioral prediction, and various actors may exploit them. Risks grow when data is shared without safeguards, when automated systems make consequential decisions without oversight, or when people cannot challenge how their information is used. The article adds that when a few companies dominate platforms, AI services and large data pools, users may have few practical alternatives. In Nigeria, the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 created the Nigeria Data Protection Commission, but the writer says enforcement, public awareness and accountability will determine whether the law protects people in practice.

stories.Headline: West Virginia sues Snap over children's safety, AI chatbot
stories.Summary:
West Virginia Attorney General JB McCuskey has filed a consumer protection lawsuit against Snap, the maker of Snapchat, according to an MLex report dated November 6, 2026. The suit alleges that Snap deceived West Virginia parents and children about how safe its platform is, even though the company allegedly knew young users were being exposed to sexual exploitation, harmful content and compulsive-use design. It also claims Snap rushed the launch of its "My AI" chatbot to children without adequate safety testing. The state further alleges that Snap misled families about what the chatbot does with children's private conversations and location data.

The lawsuit centers on the claim that Snap's public statements did not match what the company knew about risks to minors. According to the report, the complaint describes harms ranging from sexual exploitation to content that is harmful to young people, along with features that encourage compulsive use. The chatbot allegations focus on timing and disclosure, since the state says the product reached children before adequate safety checks were done. The articles do not say what remedies or penalties the state is seeking, nor do they give a dollar figure. Snap's response is not described in the coverage.

According to the MLex summary, the attorney general brought the case in his official role, and the allegations are framed as a violation of state consumer protection rules. The report describes the claims as the state's allegations and does not present them as findings. It also links to the complaint itself, which is the primary source for the specific claims. The reporting does not include any statement from Snap in reply to the suit.

The articles provide only limited context beyond the complaint itself. They do not say whether other states have taken similar action against Snap or whether the chatbot is subject to any separate regulatory review. The coverage also does not indicate when the court will schedule its next steps or what the company is expected to do next. Any further developments would have to come from later court filings or reporting.

stories.Headline: Nvidia’s $20bn AI chip pile-up - Asian Tech Roundup
stories.Summary:
Reuters has reported that around 600,000 Nvidia H200 AI chips are stranded in Hong Kong, awaiting shipment to mainland China. The high-end processors typically sell for $32,000 to $40,000 each, putting the total value near $20 billion. Because Beijing has not approved large-scale imports, the chips remain in the territory, even though Chinese AI companies are eager to buy them. The stockpile would be enough to supply three xAI Colossus-sized hyperscale datacentres.

Grey-market prices have reportedly tripled, with eight-GPU H200 servers offered in mainland China for more than $900,000 in October. At that valuation, the 600,000 chips installed across 75,000 eight-GPU servers would be worth more than $67 billion. The standoff is a test of Beijing's push for domestic firms to depend less on US technology while still matching its AI capability. Small shipments have been approved, but the authorities have not yet allowed large imports of the US-made processors.

The report does not name a single party taking responsibility for the holdup, but it places the decision with the Chinese government, which has been reinforcing a self-sufficiency strategy. The reporting describes the Chinese authorities as refusing entry to the chips while the country's AI companies press for them. Beijing has also urged the US and EU to reconsider tariffs on Chinese goods, linking larger purchases of American farm products to lower trade barriers. The articles do not say when or whether the impasse will be resolved.
