The article compares the situation to giving a new junior developer unrestricted production access, where organisations would look at the process that permitted the damage rather than the person. It also draws on the NCSC's August advice on agentic AI, which says the more autonomy an agent has, the greater the potential impact of unexpected behaviour, so controls should match the consequences of failure. Oversight should therefore scale with risk, with low-risk, easily reversed work given more freedom and higher-impact actions requiring more deliberate human intervention. The author suggests that approvals should be scoped to agreed actions, with recovery routes, protected backups and audit trails in place before an agent's access expands.

The article holds that responsibility for setting these limits rests with the organisation deploying the agent, not with the person who clicks approve. It notes that AI can speed up code production without making the overall process more productive, citing research that found the gains shrink as work moves into review, testing and release. It also points to Anthropic's acknowledgement in May that repeated permission prompts can leave people paying less attention to each one. The author endorses joint guidance from six national cybersecurity agencies published this year, which recommends increasing an agent's autonomy gradually and evaluating results to decide whether its scope should grow or shrink. The article does not report any further developments or next steps beyond this guidance.

Articles.Title: A human in the loop can’t be your whole AI security plan

stories.Headline: The AI Buildout Has A New Problem, And It’s Not Nvidia — JPMorgan Sounds Alarm
stories.Summary:
Public opposition to data centers is becoming a problem for the artificial intelligence infrastructure boom. JPMorgan Asset Management Global Market Strategist Stephanie Aliaga, in a note reported by Stocktwits on November 8, 2026, warned that this resistance could mean longer negotiations, higher costs, and delays for developers. She said the problem reaches beyond Nvidia Corp. (NVDA), the leader in the segment. The concern is not limited to one company, and the note frames it as a constraint across the sector.

Aliaga said the backlash has built for months over rising electricity bills, water consumption, and pressure on strained power grids. The issue also surfaced in the midterm elections, where Democrats won governorships in major data center markets, including Texas and Ohio, after campaigning on moratoriums or tougher development rules. Data analytics firm Wood Mackenzie counted more than 400 state and local moratorium actions since January 2026, compared with 45 across 2023 through 2025. Communities across the country also backed restrictions on new projects.

JPMorgan, however, cautioned against treating the pushback as an immediate threat to the whole boom, with Aliaga writing "More bark than bite, so far." Many restrictions are temporary, and only one of 16 states that considered statewide moratorium legislation passed a bill through its legislature. Data center capacity under construction grew nearly 50% in the first half of 2026. The firm also noted strong economic incentives for local governments, citing a U.S. Chamber of Commerce study estimating that a mid-sized 50-megawatt facility generates nearly $700 million in annual state GDP and supports more than 5,200 construction jobs.

Aliaga said the greater exposure lies in projects planned from 2028 onward, which face more uncertainty over permitting, power availability, and financing. Developers may have to negotiate community benefits, guarantee that households will not bear added grid costs, and explore dedicated power generation. Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN) and Alphabet Inc. (GOOG, GOOGL) have each announced roughly $1 billion in community investment initiatives. Wood Mackenzie estimates more than 430 gigawatts of announced U.S. capacity, with only 59% under active development. JPMorgan believes tougher rules could weed out speculative projects, potentially favoring well-capitalized hyperscalers, and could push investment toward states and international markets with friendlier regulation.

Articles.Title: The AI Buildout Has A New Problem, And It’s Not Nvidia — JPMorgan Sounds Alarm

stories.Headline: Israeli investors warned of AI debt crisis one day before Wall Street’s tech crash
stories.Summary:
Israeli investment managers warned at a closed conference that AI spending and technology stock concentration were creating serious risks, and the very next day Wall Street suffered one of its steepest selloffs in about a year and a half. On Thursday the Nasdaq fell 5.5 percent, the S&P 500 lost 4.4 percent, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped roughly 12 percent. Markets partly recovered on Friday, when the Nasdaq rose 1.1 percent and the S&P 500 gained 0.3 percent, though the Dow slipped 0.5 percent and the rebound erased only part of the earlier losses. Tel Aviv also bounced after the selloff, with the TA-35 up 3.09 percent, the TA-125 up 2.81 percent and the banking index up 4.52 percent.

The episode matters especially for Israeli institutions because of their large semiconductor holdings. A Calcalist analysis based on holdings at the end of June 2026 found that Israeli institutions held about 29.3 billion shekels in shares of ten chip companies, including Nvidia, TSMC, Broadcom and Micron. They also held another 8.4 billion shekels in the VanEck SMH and iShares SOXX semiconductor funds, bringing the total to roughly 37.7 billion shekels. That figure assumes no overlap between the datasets and excludes exposure through broader index funds tracking the S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100. Holdings in Israeli chipmaker Tower Semiconductor alone stood at nearly 19 billion shekels, and Tower shares fell 12 percent on Thursday.

The warnings came at a closed conference organized by the Family Office Association, headed by Reuven Titouani, owner of the Talpiot agency, held the day before the turmoil. Representatives from nearly all of Israel's major institutional investors attended, and two panels addressed equity exposure and risks tied to U.S. technology stocks. Tamir Hershkovitz, chief investment officer at Ayalon, cautioned that the next major crisis could be a debt crisis among technology companies, arguing that AI infrastructure is increasingly financed with borrowed money and that trouble could emerge within two or three years. Clal Insurance said it had moved some money from equities into long-term foreign bonds about a month earlier, and its head of investments, Barak Bensky, said AI spending might fail to meet expectations already built into stock prices. Migdal's Maria Yuskovitch told savers with pension money in an S&P 500 tracking fund that diversification was worth considering.

Not every speaker was pessimistic. Several other executives urged long-term holding, diversification, or avoiding hasty changes in response to short-term volatility. One senior executive at an institutional investor told Calcalist that trading around the latest index update was extraordinarily chaotic, with holdings falling 10 to 15 percent and almost no buyers stepping in. Israel's investment chiefs had spent Wednesday debating whether AI spending and semiconductor valuations had become dangerous, and by Thursday the Nasdaq's drop had made those concerns feel immediate. The articles do not say what comes next for the markets or for Israeli institutions' positions.

Articles.Title: Israeli investors warned of AI debt crisis one day before Wall Street’s tech crash

stories.Headline: Minimal labels, maximal tracking: new AI framework follows every plant organ in 3D
stories.Summary:
A team of researchers at the School of Information and Intelligent Science at Donghua University in Shanghai published a study on a new framework called 3DOGT, short for 3D Organ Growth Tracking, in the journal Plant Phenomics on September 10, 2026. The article reporting it appeared on Newswise on November 8, 2026. The framework addresses a long-standing problem in plant phenotyping, which is following individual organs across a series of three-dimensional snapshots of a plant as it grows. Existing methods typically need complete, accurate organ labels at every time point, work that can take weeks of manual annotation, or they must collect the whole growth sequence before analysis can start, which rules out real-time monitoring.

The 3DOGT approach needs only the organ labels from the first moment as a starting point, then tracks and segments organs together as it processes pairs of adjacent point clouds in time order. A pretrained deep-learning module called 3DNOD detects new buds and leaves and gives them fresh labels. For mature organs, the system aligns neighboring time points using Coherent Point Drift, then passes the aligned data to a semi-supervised Graph Convolutional Network that spreads labels forward, followed by a refinement step that corrects residual errors. An uneven downsampling strategy keeps more points for smaller organs, where errors are most likely, and the labeled output for each moment feeds the next step so the process runs without interruption. The article says the framework can also detect sudden organ loss, and it describes the approach as robust to noisy sensor data and missing parts.

The authors, whose study is described in the article, said that a single labeled snapshot is enough to follow an entire plant's growth, and they framed the work as a way for plant scientists to monitor growth at scale without months of manual labeling. The article says the authors see potential uses in high-throughput phenotyping, where faster assessment of how genotypes respond to drought, heat or disease could speed breeding programs, and in studying stress responses and senescence to inform more resilient crop varieties. The article notes the work was supported by Donghua University's 2025 Cultivation Project of Discipline Innovation. It does not describe any field deployment or further studies beyond the published paper.

Articles.Title: Minimal labels, maximal tracking: new AI framework follows every plant organ in 3D | Newswise

stories.Headline: AI tech suppliers unfazed by US vote
stories.Summary:
Taiwan's leading artificial intelligence hardware suppliers said last week that they do not expect Democratic wins in the US midterm elections to hurt customer demand, according to a report by Lisa Wang published in the Taipei Times. Executives said severe capacity shortages remain the main constraint on their business. Some Democratic winners ran on pledges to crack down on data centers, which has raised concerns about how AI infrastructure will be built out in the US. King Yuan Electronics said its planned US capacity expansion of up to US$1.4 billion would go ahead as scheduled.

King Yuan's president, Gauss Chang, told reporters at a news conference ahead of a semiconductor materials forum in Tainan on Friday that the project's details had been finalized. He said the company's long-term commitment was unaffected but that it would keep watching political developments in the US. Unimicron Technology, which supplies IC substrates to Nvidia, said election results had not yet affected customer demand. Its executive president, Mike Ma, said customers are pressing for more capacity while the company itself is chasing suppliers to keep up.

Ma said lead times for critical manufacturing equipment in the printed circuit board and substrate supply chain have stretched to as long as three years. Some equipment vendors have stopped taking orders for delivery before 2028, he said. Unimicron's main constraint has shifted to equipment procurement, which depends heavily on overseas makers in the US and Japan. Because of this, the company is hesitant to commit to further expansion even with financial support from customers.

MediaTek's advanced packaging executive, Shang Hou, said the company has to compete for wafer allocation and packaging capacity, and must book substrate slots well in advance. Ta Liang Technology said it has already secured orders for delivery next year, about two months ahead of schedule. The article also reports that Micron has suspended a US$4.5 billion memory chip plant in Taoyuan over a labor dispute, and that the Taiwan stock index fell 3.59 percent on Tuesday as foreign investors pulled out. More to follow.

Articles.Title: AI tech suppliers unfazed by US vote

stories.Headline: Women in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Is Ghana Creating Opportunities or Deepening Gender Inequality?
stories.Summary:
The article is an opinion column rather than news, so the story is about a commentary piece published on ModernGhana on November 8, 2026, by Philipa Serwaa. Its headline asks whether Ghana's embrace of artificial intelligence is opening doors for women or deepening gender inequality. The author argues that AI is already reshaping work, learning, healthcare, banking, agriculture and business in Ghana, and that women could gain from it. She points to market traders, fashion designers and shea butter producers who could use digital tools to manage records, spot trends and reach buyers beyond their communities. She also sees potential in flexible online learning for women who left school because of marriage, childbirth or money problems.

The column also warns that the benefits are far from guaranteed. It cites a Ghana Statistical Service thematic report on digital exclusion, drawn from the 2021 Population and Housing Census, which found differences in digital device use across age groups, regions and between adult men and women, with gender gaps widening with age. The author adds that AI could reduce demand for routine work in administrative support, customer service and data processing, that systems built on unrepresentative data may disadvantage women, and that online harassment and manipulated images threaten women's safety. She notes that the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy was launched in April 2026, and says its success should be judged by whether women can take part in its opportunities.

She calls for several steps: digital training that reaches small towns and rural areas and fits women's different circumstances, early encouragement for girls in technology, and cooperation among government, companies, development groups and financial institutions to make tools and internet access affordable. She also argues that women should help shape how AI is developed and used, not only receive it. The column is a personal view, and the publication notes that its contents do not necessarily reflect the outlet's official position. The author is an op-ed writer and researcher affiliated with the University of Energy and Natural Resources in Sunyani. The article does not describe any scheduled follow-up events.

Articles.Title: Women in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Is Ghana Creating Opportunities or Deepening Gender Inequality?

stories.Headline: World Models Push AI Beyond Text Into Physical Reality
stories.Summary:
World models, a new class of AI systems that simulate real-world physics in three-dimensional space, are moving out of research labs and into production robots and self-driving cars. Unlike large language models that predict the next word, these systems forecast what happens when a robot arm pushes a cup or a car turns at speed. The article, published by The Tech Buzz on November 8, 2026, presents the shift as AI's biggest step from digital to physical intelligence. Robotics companies are now working to make this approach practical for real machines.

The technology is built by training neural networks on enormous collections of physical interactions, such as millions of hours of video showing objects moving, colliding, balancing, and breaking. From that footage, the system learns the underlying physics rather than simply matching patterns in pixels, and it can apply that understanding to situations it has never encountered. A robot using such a model can run internal simulations of different grip angles and force levels before reaching for a mug. Self-driving vehicles could likewise test many possible maneuvers, such as changing lanes, within milliseconds and predict how nearby vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists will move.

The article points to strong investor interest as evidence of the sector's expectations. Bedrock Robotics reportedly raised $600 million at a $4.1 billion valuation for autonomous excavators, and Eka Robotics reached a $1.45 billion valuation for a robotic arm that handles objects in a way the article says resembles world model technology. The piece also notes that Doug Field, a veteran of Tesla's Model 3 and Ford's electric vehicle efforts, has joined Rivian spinoff Mind Robotics. The article does not name a single party responsible for the technology, and it presents these developments as industry momentum rather than a formal announcement.

The article is candid about the obstacles. Training these models demands far more computing power than language models because physical reality contains far more variables than text, and the article cites petabytes of visual and sensor data where text models use terabytes. Simulations that work in virtual settings often fail in the real world because of friction, lighting changes, and unexpected obstacles, a problem the article calls sim-to-real transfer. The article also warns that a faulty prediction in a physical machine could cause harm in a way a mistaken chatbot answer could not. It expects general-purpose physical intelligence to remain years away, though progress in narrow applications is accelerating.

Articles.Title: World Models Push AI Beyond Text Into Physical Reality

stories.Headline: Yardeni Research Warns AI Earnings Expectations Are Reaching Unsustainable Levels
stories.Summary:
Yardeni Research has warned in a research note that earnings forecasts for artificial intelligence-related companies have become so ambitious that investors are growing less tolerant of disappointing results. The firm said the gap between analysts' profit projections and investors' willingness to pay higher valuations is widening. It described industry analysts' projected earnings growth as so extraordinary that it is becoming hard to believe and leaves little room for disappointment. The note was published in an article dated November 8, 2026, and the firm continues to see AI enthusiasm supporting long-term profit expectations.

Consensus operating earnings per share estimates for the S&P 500 stand at $366 for 2026, $425 for 2027 and $494 for 2028. Yardeni's own projections are lower at $375, $425 and $450 for those years, which signals more caution about earnings growth later in the forecast period. Analysts' average five-year long-term earnings growth expectation has reached a record 25.6%. Much of this optimism sits in technology, where long-term growth expectations for the information technology sector are 41.9% and for semiconductor companies are 66%.

Despite these rising expectations, the S&P 500's forward price-to-earnings ratio has fallen to 18.5 from more than 22 earlier this year. Yardeni said this divergence shows investors are reluctant to assign premium valuations based on very optimistic profit forecasts. The firm explained that the result is an extraordinarily high bar for corporate earnings and a market quick to punish disappointment. As a consequence, companies reporting solid results could still face selling pressure if their performance falls short of elevated expectations.

Yardeni also believes the heightened scrutiny could help limit excessive speculation in AI investments. The firm pointed to financial discipline, political restrictions, social concerns and physical infrastructure constraints as factors that could prevent unchecked expansion. It also noted that real gross domestic product grew at an annualised rate of 3.4% in the third quarter, while the core personal consumption expenditures price index rose 3.1% year over year. The firm still believes the Federal Reserve should return policy to a neutral setting, which it estimates at an interest rate range of 4.25% to 4.50%.

Articles.Title: Yardeni Research Warns AI Earnings Expectations Are Reaching Unsustainable Levels

stories.Headline: Dainin AI Announces 2027 Academy Intake to Expand Certified Implementation Network
stories.Summary:
Dainin BC Limited, a technology company based in Glasgow, Scotland, announced on 5 November 2026 that it will hold an early-2027 intake for its Dainin Academy. The company's December 2026 cohort is already fully booked, so the new intake is meant to add participants after that. The announcement was published by the Daily Tribune on 8 November 2026. Dainin describes the programme as a way to expand its professional certification and commercial partner pathways for its Cognitive Operating System technology.

The intake is designed to build a pool of qualified operators, implementors and prospective commercial partners who can work with the Cognitive Venture Operating System, known as CVOS. The company says the platform sits on its Cognitive Enterprise Operating System, which includes an existing set of 420 specialised AI-agent roles, and that CVOS can configure an initial business environment in about 30 minutes. Professionals taking the programme would therefore apply an existing platform to client work instead of building their own AI system first. The academy offers three credentials: Certified Operator, Certified Implementor and Certified Partner. Commercial partner appointments, licensing rights and distribution arrangements are handled separately from certification and need additional approval.

Dainin's founding partner, Dr. James Onslow, is quoted in the release saying that experienced business professionals should not have to restart their careers because AI can now produce reports. He argues that knowing what needs to change inside a business and how to implement that change remains valuable. The company presents the academy as part of a broader plan to build a professional implementation ecosystem around CVOS and CEOS. Dainin says it is making the programme available to meet demand from consultants who want to apply their experience to AI-enabled operations.

The release sets out the wider context of its argument: artificial intelligence is taking over more research, analysis, writing and administrative tasks that business professionals have traditionally performed. This shift puts pressure on services whose value depends mainly on producing individual outputs. Dainin argues that demand is growing for people who can apply intelligent systems within the commercial and operational limits of a real business. Prospective participants can explore the qualification routes and ask about partnership requirements through Dainin's official channels. The articles do not give the exact start date of the early-2027 intake, its fees or its size.

Articles.Title: Dainin AI Announces 2027 Academy Intake to Expand Certified Implementation Network

stories.Headline: Mixpanel CTO Anant Gupta on Proving Real AI Agent ROI
stories.Summary:
Mixpanel, a product analytics company, has put forward a view on how businesses should measure the return on their AI agents, as set out in an interview published on November 8, 2026 by AI Magazine, written by Adam Pond. The interview features Anant Gupta, who joined Mixpanel at the start of 2026 as its chief technology officer. The article centres on the claim that many firms remain stuck in an AI pilot phase because they lack evidence that their agents help the business. Gupta explained that building a pilot is simple, while running one securely, with governance, security and access control, is much harder.

Gupta argued that companies often track operational figures such as response speed or time spent with the agent, but these do not show whether a customer got what they came for or made a purchase. In his view, return on investment is found in user behaviour and business outcomes, and most teams are not connecting that data. He said Mixpanel launched a product called Agent Intelligence to address this gap. The tool ties each agent conversation to the same user's wider journey, so teams can see what happened before, during and after an exchange. It also lets them run conversations through funnels, cohorts and retention reports and compare prompts or models against real customer outcomes.

Gupta said that speed, cost and quality matter, but that an agent can be fast, cheap and error free and still deliver a poor experience. He recommended judging agents by what users actually do afterward, such as whether they finish the task, return or buy. On experimentation, he advised treating every change to a model or prompt as an experiment, measured against user behaviour rather than benchmark scores alone. He said clean, well-governed data is the foundation that lets teams move quickly without guessing. Asked for a prediction, he said a majority of users will soon interact with products through AI, and that products built to help agents complete tasks efficiently and correctly will be the most successful over the long term.

Articles.Title: Mixpanel CTO Anant Gupta on Proving Real AI Agent ROI

stories.Headline: Astera Labs: Fairly Valued After The AI Sell-Off, But Risks Remain
stories.Summary:
Astera Labs, the semiconductor company trading under the ticker ALAB, was upgraded from Sell to Hold on November 8, 2026, in an analysis published on Seeking Alpha by Zbigniew Budzinski, CFA. The analyst had first initiated coverage in September with a Sell rating and a fair value of $171 per share, when the stock traded at $360.51 on September 24. Since then the shares have fallen sharply during a broader sell-off in AI-related stocks. The revised fair value is $171.59, which sits about 4% below the current price. The upgrade reflects several factors in the company's results and outlook.

Third-quarter revenue and fourth-quarter guidance both came in above expectations. However, inventory grew faster than revenue, and the valuation multiples of peer companies have compressed significantly. The analysis notes that the initial deployment ramp for the Scorpio X product is largely complete, so future growth will depend on new platforms and new customers. Optical and custom solutions are expected to contribute from 2027 onward. The author describes the stock as now reasonably valued after the AI sector decline, but he cautions that further downside remains possible.

The main risks he identifies are a worsening of sector sentiment and a deterioration in customer concentration. He writes that his modeling approach is deliberately conservative and that he builds in a wide margin of safety. The article carries a disclaimer that the author holds no position in the stock and that the views expressed are his own. The piece is an opinion from an individual analyst rather than a company announcement or a regulatory action, and it does not describe any scheduled corporate event. The articles do not say what the next rating change or price target revision will be, or when the company will report its next results.

Articles.Title: Astera Labs: Fairly Valued After The AI Sell-Off, But Risks Remain

stories.Headline: AI Patient Materials for Pediatric Oral Health Fail Standard Readability Benchmarks
stories.Summary:
A study published in Frontiers in Digital Health evaluated the readability of educational materials that six widely used AI chatbots generated in response to common questions about children's oral health. The researchers submitted ten parental questions to GPT-5 Mini, Gemini 3 Flash, Claude Haiku 4.5, DeepSeek-V3, Kimi K2.5, and Qwen3-Max in February 2026, producing sixty texts. Every model's output required reading ability above the sixth-grade level that the American Medical Association recommends for patient materials. The findings were reported in a November 8, 2026 article, and the study's authors are Xiong, Xiong, Xiong, Guénier, and Xie.

The researchers scored each response with six established readability formulas, including the Flesch Reading Ease score and the Flesch–Kincaid Grade Level. DeepSeek-V3 produced the most accessible text, with a mean Flesch Reading Ease of 66.14 and an Automated Readability Index mean of 6.46. Gemini 3 Flash ranked second, with a mean Reading Ease of 62.26. Claude Haiku 4.5 produced the least readable text, with a mean Reading Ease of 13.11 and grade-level estimates above the sixteenth grade on all five grade-based indices. Even the best model's median Reading Ease of 66.75 fell well short of the 80 to 89 range the benchmark requires.

The authors said that raw AI outputs should not be used as unedited patient handouts in pediatric dentistry. They suggested that developers and healthcare organizations could instruct models to write at a sixth-grade level and that human oversight remains necessary. They also noted that large language models are trained heavily on complex academic and technical writing, which may lead them to overestimate the reading ability of everyday users. The study measured only readability, not clinical accuracy, safety, or factual correctness, and it examined single responses in English. The authors described the automated drafts as preliminary starting points for healthcare professionals rather than finished materials for families.

Articles.Title: AI Patient Materials for Pediatric Oral Health Fail Standard Readability Benchmarks

stories.Headline: Charlotte De Witte Uses AI Artist NAVA On ‘Azadi’ EP
stories.Summary:
Charlotte de Witte has released Azadi, a three-track EP on the KNTXT label that pairs driving techno with Farsi vocals performed by NAVA, an AI persona created by Farbod Mehr. The EP was published on November 8, 2026, and its title track was first played during her set at this year's Tomorrowland. The release blends electronic production with themes of hope and resistance, and "Azadi" translates to "freedom." Ahead of the EP, she shared snippets and full tracks online, including "Tales Of The Desert," which came out in October with an AI-generated music video featuring herself and NAVA. According to the article, all proceeds from the EP are being donated directly to FEMENA, a women's rights organization that provides funding, protection, and resources to feminist movements and civil society groups across the Middle East, North Africa, and Asia.

De Witte presents the project as a digital act of defiance that uses NAVA to amplify the voices of Iranian women who face legal bans on singing or performing in public. The EP's tracklist includes "Azadi," "Omid," and "Tales Of The Desert," all featuring NAVA. The article notes that the music is available on Spotify and other platforms. Public reaction has been sharply divided, with critics and fans questioning the decision to use an artificial intelligence entity rather than real Iranian women artists. Some pointed out that exiled or diaspora-based Iranian female artists could have contributed to the EP, which they argued would have made a more authentic impact.

AliPink, a pioneer of Iranian underground techno and founder of Techno Tehran Records, criticized the idea that an artificial voice is needed to represent Iranian women on Instagram. Other listeners praised the project's dual focus on charity and cultural awareness, with supporters thanking De Witte for backing women and Persian poets. The article's own assessment is that the premise makes sense in theory but that the execution falls short by relying on artificial intelligence, which it says detaches the project from the emotion and lived experience of a human performance. Context from the piece shows that the debate centers on whether AI can responsibly carry the stories of people who are silenced. The article does not describe any further announcements or next steps beyond encouraging readers to follow De Witte on social media for what she releases next.

Articles.Title: Charlotte De Witte Uses AI Artist NAVA On ‘Azadi’ EP

stories.Headline: Review Maps Path for Explainable AI in Green Housing
stories.Summary:
A new systematic review, published in the journal AI in Civil Engineering, lays out a roadmap for applying Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) to housing manufacturing in order to cut carbon dioxide emissions. The study is authored by Miguel Mora and Pingbo Tang and was reported on November 8, 2026. The researchers note that AI can optimize production schedules to reduce energy use, yet its opaque nature leaves human operators unable to trust or verify the results. To address this, they used the PRISMA method to synthesize existing literature on how XAI could make AI-driven scheduling decisions transparent.

The construction sector is a major source of emissions, and the 2022 Global Status Report for Buildings and Construction attributes 37% of global CO2 emissions to the fabrication of construction materials. Housing manufacturing is especially complex because of high customization and uncertainty stemming from human, machine, and business processes. The Flexible Job-Shop Scheduling Problem, an NP-hard optimization task, makes the challenge harder still. The review argues that pairing AI with manufacturing principles can help, but only if the systems are explainable to the people who remain responsible for production outcomes.

The authors searched Google Scholar, which returned 30,700 results, and analyzed the top 210 by relevance. A narrower search on manufacturing and construction produced 37 papers, from which 14 were selected, eight literature reviews and six studies focused on manufacturing decision-making. Among those six, only one tested its approach with an expert panel, and only one addressed production scheduling. The review classifies XAI by stage, scope, and output, and reports that all six studies used post-hoc explanations, with four applying SHAP and three developing graphical or textual interfaces.

The authors also flag practical obstacles, chiefly limited data on machinery CO2 emissions in housing manufacturing. They suggest estimating emissions from machinery brochures and on-site energy measurements, combined with established emission factors. They further stress that industry constraints, such as the size and weight of fabricated panels and the continuous-flow production lines, must be built into the optimization. The proposed roadmap starts with identifying industry requirements, then selects an AI method, and finally defines a suitable XAI, taking a socio-technical view that accounts for decision-making from operators to managers.

Articles.Title: Review Maps Path for Explainable AI in Green Housing

stories.Headline: Review Details AI, Robotics, and Language Models in Remote Patient Monitoring
stories.Summary:
A scientific review by Pooja Sharma, published in BMC Artificial Intelligence, examines how artificial intelligence, robotics, and natural language processing are changing telemedicine and remote patient monitoring across several specialties. The analysis covers cardiology, diabetes care, obstetrics and gynaecology, dermatology, and general remote monitoring. It finds that these tools can improve diagnostic precision, support patient engagement, and extend care to people in remote areas. The review also argues that combining these technologies creates connected digital systems that can track patients continuously and support real-time clinical action. At the same time, it says that barriers such as interoperability gaps, high costs, unclear liability, clinician workload, and data privacy and cybersecurity concerns still slow wide adoption.

The review places these developments within the broader field of eHealth, which the World Health Organization describes as the secure and economical use of information and communication technologies for health. It notes that the COVID-19 pandemic pushed remote monitoring forward by reducing physical contact and easing pressure on hospitals. Connected wearable sensors, mobile health platforms, and Internet of Things systems let clinicians observe patient readings remotely and send automated alerts when measurements move away from expected baselines. In diagnostics, the review describes deep learning models that analyze medical images such as X-rays, MRI scans, CT studies, and ultrasounds, with performance that in some areas matches or exceeds human radiologists. It stresses, however, that accuracy depends heavily on the size and quality of training data.

The review also reports that predictive models can spot early signs of arrhythmias and heart failure, although clinicians and regulators may be wary of their opaque design. In remote monitoring, artificial intelligence systems analyze vital signs such as heart rate, blood pressure, blood glucose, and oxygen saturation, and raise alerts when readings cross safe limits. Studies cited in the review show earlier detection of complications than conventional observation, but frequent false alarms can cause alert fatigue among staff. Virtual assistants and chatbots can triage queries and manage scheduling, though their accuracy falls with complex cases, creating misdiagnosis risks when they run without supervision. The review also notes that evidence from large randomized controlled trials confirming clinical benefit remains scarce.

Other applications, including mental health tools that analyze voice and behavior, raise debates about surveillance and sensitive data. Consumer wearables generate large volumes of data that are often unvalidated and can overwhelm clinical teams. The review concludes that remote care delivers measurable gains, including fewer hospital readmissions, better disease control, and higher satisfaction among patients and providers. It cites a study by Motolese and colleagues showing that telemedicine worked for neurological patients during the pandemic, despite limited digital literacy among participants. Home blood pressure monitoring has also produced better long-term hypertension management than standard clinic visits.

Persistent problems, however, include weak broadband in rural areas, digital literacy gaps among older patients, and substantial upfront costs. After emergency funding ended following the pandemic, many systems struggled to scale their programs. The review also addresses large language models, which emerged after ChatGPT's public debut in November 2022, and warns of hallucinated medical statements, inherited bias, and unresolved questions of accountability that call for audits and human oversight. Surgical robotics, the review adds, has matured through systems such as the da Vinci platform, which the FDA cleared in 2000 and which has performed over six million procedures worldwide.

Articles.Title: Review Details AI, Robotics, and Language Models in Remote Patient Monitoring

stories.Headline: Homelabber uses second-gen Optane memory sticks to run a 2.8-trillion-parameter AI model on CPU alone — warns that Optane's extreme heat can 'burn out' nearby memory DRAM, used blower fans to prevent melting RAM
stories.Summary:
Homelab builder Shane Downing reported on Tom's Hardware on November 8, 2026, that a Reddit user had run Moonshot AI's 2.8-trillion-parameter Kimi K3 model using discontinued second-generation Optane PMem 200 memory on a 40-core 3rd-generation Xeon Scalable CPU, with no GPU handling inference. The build runs slowly, at 0.85 tokens per second even with 1-bit quantization, and it runs hot. The builder warned that the Optane DIMMs became extremely hot under sustained inference, and that this heat could endanger neighboring DRAM. To manage it, the builder used dual 12W blower fans aimed at the modules and advised treating active DIMM cooling as mandatory. The article notes that Kimi K3 is not built for home use, since Moonshot AI recommends data center inference engines and even the smallest community quantization needs at least 610GB of RAM.

Secondhand Optane offers a way to reach that capacity at home, and the builder says it costs a fraction of equivalent DRAM, which has risen sharply in price. Intel launched the PMem 200 series in 2020 for its 3rd-generation Xeon Scalable CPUs, in 128GB, 256GB and 512GB capacities, and the article says it can deliver up to 32% more memory bandwidth than the first generation. The builder ran the Optane in App Direct Mode, which exposes it as a separate persistent region that software maps directly, giving more control over where model tensors live. The article credits the builder with the thermal warning and describes the heat as consistent with Intel's own specifications. Intel rates the modules for forced airflow of 2.4 to 2.7 meters per second, a level typically found in data centers, and places each module at 12W or 15W regardless of capacity.

Throttling begins at 83 degrees Celsius and thermal shutdown at 85 degrees, compared with the extended range of up to 95 degrees for typical DDR4 server memory. The article also compares this build with an earlier first-generation Optane project by u/APFrisco, which ran at roughly 4 tokens per second using Memory Mode and a partial RTX 3060 on the smaller K2.5 model. Commenters pointed out that the speed is slow, with a 50,000-token task estimated at about 13 hours, though others said overnight batch jobs are less affected by speed. The article does not say whether further builds or formal guidance will follow.

Articles.Title: Homelabber uses second-gen Optane memory sticks to run a 2.8-trillion-parameter AI model on CPU alone — warns that Optane's extreme heat can 'burn out' nearby memory DRAM, used blower fans to prevent melting RAM

stories.Headline: UKRI backs five hubs developing AI tools for earlier disease detection
stories.Summary:
Five UK research hubs, based in Exeter, London, Southampton and Sunderland, are set to receive more than £52m in government funding to develop technologies for detecting disease earlier and helping people manage their health outside hospital. The funding comes through UK Research and Innovation (UKRI), and industry partners are adding a further £37.5m in cash and in-kind support. The announcement was reported on 8 November 2026. The hubs will focus on brain health, cardiovascular disease, diabetes and respiratory infections.

Among the planned projects is a network of NHS brain health clinics that would combine blood tests, brain scans and memory assessments to help identify dementia risk and speed up diagnosis. The programme also aims to build tools for assessing head injuries from sport and road accidents. Artificial intelligence systems are being developed to spot early signs of diabetes and heart disease in routine eye scans. Other work will test smartphone apps and wearable devices that analyse coughs and breathing, helping people with respiratory infections decide whether to seek medical advice.

The hubs will work alongside patients, healthcare professionals, the NHS and industry partners, including Google, Siemens and Medtronic. UKRI said the investment builds on earlier research hubs, whose work included AI-assisted brain tumour surgery. The agency described the new projects as an effort to turn engineering and physical sciences research into technologies that could support earlier intervention. It also said the aim is to reduce pressure on healthcare services. The articles do not give a timetable for when these technologies will reach patients.

Articles.Title: UKRI backs five hubs developing AI tools for earlier disease detection

stories.Headline: AI biomarkers show promise for predicting cancer immunotherapy response, review finds
stories.Summary:
A new review published in the Journal of Translational Medicine argues that artificial intelligence could help predict which cancer patients will respond to immunotherapy. Immunotherapy has changed the treatment of many tumors, but clinicians still struggle to identify who will benefit. The authors say AI could integrate data types that conventional markers such as PD-L1, tumor mutational burden and microsatellite instability capture only imprecisely. The review was written by Arash Esmaeili and Nima Rezaei and surveys recent studies across cancer types. Its tone is cautious, since the authors describe the results as promising but variable.

The review reports that some AI-derived biomarkers have performed better than conventional markers in specific studies, with moderate-to-high discriminatory performance. Reported estimates differed depending on the cancer type, the prediction endpoint and the validation design. Deep learning stands out in digital pathology and radiomics, where it can quantify tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes and map the immune environment of a tumor from routine slides and images. The authors also highlight multi-omics frameworks, including graph neural networks and transformer-based models, that examine genomic, transcriptomic and proteomic data together. These tools aim to capture tumor-immune interactions that single-marker tests can miss.

The review also describes promising AI results in three clinically sensitive areas. These are predicting primary and acquired resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors, selecting patients who are candidates for immunotherapy, and forecasting immune-related adverse events before they appear. The authors address interpretability as well, noting that methods such as SHAP and LIME can show which features influenced a prediction. They warn, however, that these outputs are not causal or mechanistic explanations, and should not be read that way in clinical settings. The review's authors are the researchers named above, and they frame AI as a way to combine many signals rather than a replacement for existing biomarkers.

The authors conclude that AI is opening new routes for precision oncology, but say clinical use will require robust external validation, standardized methods and testing across diverse patient populations. The article notes that the review maps where current AI methods, data types and performance metrics stand, along with the barriers that remain before such tools enter routine practice. It also stresses that reported performance depends heavily on how and where each model was validated. The article does not describe any specific timeline for clinical adoption.

Articles.Title: AI biomarkers show promise for predicting cancer immunotherapy response, review finds

stories.Headline: Health science students report higher GPA with frequent AI use, but most get no formal training
stories.Summary:
Most health science students are already using artificial intelligence tools in their studies, according to a new survey, yet their institutions have largely not kept pace with formal instruction. Ninety percent of the 279 participants reported using ChatGPT, but 82.6 percent said they had received no instruction on AI at all. Students described only moderate familiarity with the technology, with a mean knowledge score of 3.08 on the study's scale and a standard deviation of 1.06. Taken together, the findings suggest students are learning to work with these tools largely on their own.

The study also linked AI use to academic performance, finding that students who used AI more often reported higher grade point averages, an association the analysis found statistically significant. The authors caution that the cross-sectional design cannot establish that AI use causes better grades. Stronger students may simply be more drawn to these tools, and self-reported measures may not match objective performance. Even so, participants said AI helped them study more efficiently and understand their coursework better. Sixty-one percent also reported ethical worries about AI in their education, and those worries varied significantly by gender and by academic program.

The authors argue that high use, low formal training, and widespread ethical concern call for structured curriculum change. They recommend that faculty put in place proactive AI training, designed in advance rather than in response to problems. That training, they suggest, should address automation bias, the tendency to over-trust outputs from automated systems, and build the ethical literacy students need to critically evaluate AI-generated content. The authors frame this as part of ensuring equitable technological competency across healthcare disciplines, since students in different programs appear to be prepared unevenly.

The stakes extend beyond individual study habits, because graduates will enter fields where AI is increasingly present in clinical and research work. The survey documents associations and patterns but cannot determine causation or long-term effects, a limitation the authors state directly in their conclusion. What it does establish is a baseline: AI is already part of daily study for most of these students, formal teaching has lagged, and many students hold ethical reservations. The authors conclude that AI literacy should be taught as a structured competency rather than left for students to improvise. The article does not report any further developments.

Articles.Title: Health science students report higher GPA with frequent AI use, but most get no formal training

stories.Headline: AI has identified thousands of animals that people had overlooked
stories.Summary:
AI is helping conservationists analyse wildlife data far faster than before. In Kenya, algorithms can process around 200,000 aerial photographs of animals in a matter of hours, a job that once took nine specialists nine months. The Save the Elephants group, which runs the work, found that earlier censuses had missed a large share of the animals, and that the gap was significant for several species. Accurate counts matter because they shape conservation status, funding and habitat planning.

The same tools are being used in other ways. In Tanzania, the Jane Goodall Institute is digitising decades of handwritten chimpanzee field records from Gombe National Park, cutting the expected time from 13 to 15 years down to about two years with technology developed alongside Amazon Web Services. Conservation International is using satellite temperature data in Cambodia to flag possible forest fire hotspots for local patrols. The Nature Conservancy has fitted AI cameras to commercial fishing boats to record the species and quantities caught, processing video on board to cut down on data transfers.

The energy side of the story is the other half. The International Energy Agency projects that data centres could use more than 945 terawatt-hours of electricity a year by 2030, more than double the 2024 level and roughly Japan's annual consumption. Its estimates also put water use by data centres rising from about 560 billion litres in 2023 to 1.2 trillion litres a year by 2030. The agency notes these figures cover all data centres, though AI is a major driver of the growth.

A Reuters survey of 15 large international organisations found that all already use AI in some form while acknowledging its environmental costs. The World Resources Institute says it limits resource-heavy tasks and reuses computed results, while Greenpeace is applying internal AI guidelines but questions whether so many new data centres are needed. The issue is expected to feature at the UN COP31 climate summit, which opens on 9 November in Turkey, where organisers plan to propose principles for responsible technology use. The UN is also urging major AI companies to report more openly on their energy and water use and greenhouse gas emissions.

Articles.Title: AI has identified thousands of animals that people had overlooked

stories.Headline: AI Drone Warfare Canada: $50M, 399 Vendors [2026]
stories.Summary:
Canada's defence department is weighing AI-enabled drones, but no purchase has been made. CBC News reported on November 7, 2026 that the Royal Canadian Air Force is studying how collaborative combat aircraft could serve the country, while the Department of National Defence said plainly that no decision to buy them exists. Canada owns none today. Separately, the federal government launched the Defence Drone Initiative on July 23, 2026 to speed up cheaper uncrewed and autonomous systems for the armed forces and the Coast Guard, with a supplier qualification deadline of August 14, 2026.

The cheaper-drone channel is the one with money behind it. On September 10, 2026, Canada and Ukraine announced a supply arrangement modelled on Ukraine's Brave1 program, and initial contracts worth up to $50 million were awarded with the aim of raising the number of drones the armed forces deploy tenfold. Lieutenant-General Darcy Molstad, who heads Canadian Joint Forces Command, said 399 vendors have been pre-qualified and that a steady flow of requests for proposals for robotic and autonomous systems will follow over the next five years. Qualifying does not guarantee a contract, so most of those companies will not win large orders.

Officials and experts say humans must stay in control of lethal decisions, while acknowledging that rivals may not share that limit. Former air force commander Yvan Blondin told CBC he expects such aircraft to become central to militaries by the 2030s, and warned that adversaries like China may not keep a human in the loop in wartime. David Perry of the Canadian Global Affairs Institute argued Canada must adopt autonomous systems to keep pace with adversaries already using them. Dominion Dynamics chief executive Eliot Pence, whose company is building a drone called Scout, has pressed for Canadian buy-in, arguing the Arctic needs coverage that crewed jets alone cannot provide. CBC reported that he has raised about a third of the $500 million he says a prototype requires, and that his company stands to gain if Ottawa buys, which readers should weigh when assessing his case.

Context matters here. The United States has two CCA prototypes, including Anduril's Fury, which fired a missile in a July test, and Australia is developing its own version. The United Kingdom is spending five billion pounds on drones and autonomous systems, while Canada is building from the low-cost end. The reporting does not say when or whether a CCA procurement decision will come, and it leaves open how much autonomy Ottawa will accept in weapons use.

Articles.Title: AI Drone Warfare Canada: $50M, 399 Vendors [2026]

stories.Headline: AWS principal engineer says the best engineers are ‘paranoid and lazy’ when it comes to AI
stories.Summary:
Business Insider reported that David Yanacek, a senior principal engineer at AWS, believes the best engineers today are "paranoid and lazy" when working with AI agents. The interview was published on November 8, 2026, and Yanacek, who works on agentic AI and safety, shared the view with the outlet. He said that many people point to judgment and taste as the traits that separate the strongest engineers in the AI era, but he thinks these additional attributes matter too. He described the pairing as a good combination for working with agents.

According to Yanacek, AI has taken over most coding tasks, but writing code was not the main bottleneck. Engineers previously spent days waiting on manual tests, code approvals, and design tweaks, along with teammates' reviews. Now human involvement is reserved for design discussions and complex reviews, while agents run loops that generate code, run tests, rework problems, and prepare updates for merging and deployment. One loop can run for hours, which lets Yanacek move to other projects or add features in the meantime. The article does not give specific figures for time saved.

Yanacek is responsible for the approach he describes, and he explained it in his own words to the outlet. He said "paranoid" means he is very sensitive to what could happen if an agent were allowed to act without supervision. "Lazy" means he does not want to perform repetitive tasks by hand. Much of his time goes to deciding which tools agents may use unsupervised, which actions need approval, and where those limits should be enforced. He keeps an "auto-trust" file, the set of rules that defines which commands an agent can run alone and which need human sign-off.

The article places this approach within a broader shift in how software work is organized, with AI reshaping engineering roles. Yanacek's stated goal is a fleet of agents that make sound decisions without constant review, which he says requires clear policies on what agents should and should not do. He also said that engineers must stay alert to what could go wrong while still building systems reliable enough that they need not supervise every action. The article does not describe any further developments or next steps beyond this.

Articles.Title: AWS principal engineer says the best engineers are ‘paranoid and lazy’ when it comes to AI

stories.Headline: Data centre developer blames ‘cowboy builders’ for AI backlash
stories.Summary:
Mahdi Yahya, chief executive of the data centre developer Radiant, has blamed what he called "cowboy builders" for fuelling a backlash against AI infrastructure. Radiant, backed by investment giant Brookfield, is behind a proposed £20bn data centre in North Yorkshire. Mr Yahya said that inexperienced developers had tried to push through projects despite local objections, and that this had turned communities against the sector. The comments came after the US midterm elections, in which Democratic candidates won on anti-data-centre platforms, and after a sell-off in AI stocks that wiped trillions off Wall Street's value.

The Radiant project, which the company plans to build as part of a deal with Drax, the operator of the UK's largest power station, would reach up to a gigawatt of capacity. The project will require up to £2.5bn in its initial stages and up to £20bn later, and the company aims to have around 100MW online by 2028. It would connect to an existing grid link, so it would avoid the long power delays that have hit other sites. Radiant's plans rely on Drax's biomass power station, which supplies about 5pc of UK electricity, and green campaigners have criticised the plant as the country's single biggest polluter. Drax has described biomass as a mainstream sustainable and renewable source, with pellets made from timber industry waste.

Mr Yahya said that serious developers who have long experience know how to answer local concerns, and he predicted that the backlash would act as a correction rather than a full pause on AI development. He said experienced builders would not be greatly affected, and noted that some established projects were already trying to win over local communities. Elsewhere, the article reports that protesters stormed a Microsoft data centre site in the Netherlands, and that the campaign group Stop Dirty Data Centres has called for mass protests across Europe that weekend. In Texas, the newly elected governor Gina Hinojosa has pledged a moratorium on new data centre construction. In the UK, data centres face years of delays because of a backlog of grid connection applications, some of them speculative projects that may never be built.

Articles.Title: Data centre developer blames ‘cowboy builders’ for AI backlash

stories.Headline: Bolt to track how often AI chatbots recommend its rides in 5 markets
stories.Summary:
Bolt, the Estonian mobility company, has partnered with Searchable, a London startup that measures how brands appear in chatbot answers, to find out how often services like ChatGPT recommend its ride-hailing and corporate travel products. The deal was announced on November 6, 2026, in a release issued by Searchable. The release covers five markets, the UK, Germany, Poland, South Africa and Thailand, but it discloses no price, contract length or performance target. It also gives no baseline figure for how often Bolt is named today, so there is nothing yet against which improvement could be judged.

Under the arrangement, Searchable will give Bolt's content team a market-by-market view of how often AI chatbots name Bolt when people ask questions such as how to book a ride to the airport or find the cheapest route across a city. Each result is compared against rival apps, which the release does not name. The two Bolt products in scope are its consumer ride-hailing service and Bolt Business, its offering for company travel. Searchable says Bolt will use the findings to win more AI answers, mainly through new content rather than paid placements. The release does not say which of the ten AI engines Searchable tracks beyond ChatGPT, which languages the questions will be asked in, or how success will be scored.

Searchable's chief executive, Chris Donnelly, called Bolt a brilliant example of a brand taking AI search seriously at an early stage. Harris Reed, the company's head of go-to-market, said Bolt riders increasingly ask chatbots how to get around before opening an app. Aleksandr Komolov, a Bolt content strategist, praised Searchable's support and said its pricing is transparent, though the release itself contains no pricing. The headline refers to Germany and to reputation, yet the body contains nothing specific to Germany and does not describe tracking what chatbots say about Bolt, only how often it is named.

The deal sits in a fast-growing market. Searchable says it works with more than 3,000 brands across 10 AI engines, has tracked more than 180 million AI answers, and has drawn on more than 2.3 billion sources, though it does not define "sources." Its brand count has risen quickly in its own announcements, from more than 1,000 in September to 3,000 now, and the release does not say how many of those brands pay. Rivals have drawn large sums, and larger software companies such as Adobe, HubSpot and Zeta Global have bought similar startups or tools. Searchable's figures and the value of its measurements have not been independently verified, and the articles do not say what Bolt will do with the results once they arrive.

Articles.Title: Bolt to track how often AI chatbots recommend its rides in 5 markets

stories.Headline: Peak tension: artificial intelligence predicts the result of the Barcelona-Atletico Madrid match
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence has produced a prediction for the Barcelona versus Atletico Madrid match, the standout fixture of matchday 12 in the Spanish league. The Goal.com report, published on 8 November 2026, says the game is set for the Metropolitano on Sunday evening. Barcelona sit top of the table on 30 points, level with Real Madrid, who have played one game more, while Atletico are second, two points behind. The match also carries history between the clubs, since the Julian Alvarez transfer stalled last summer amid tension and official complaints.

The technical picture is equally tight, with each side arriving in different form. Atletico have won seven consecutive league matches but lost 0-2 to Bayern Munich in midweek, ending a nine-match unbeaten run across all competitions. Barcelona have bounced back with a 6-1 win over Alaves and a 3-0 win over Aston Villa, after earlier defeats to Paris Saint-Germain and Real Madrid. In the league, Barcelona have scored 46 goals in 11 matches against 22 for Atletico, while Atletico have conceded eight to Barcelona's 12. The report names several absentees, including Rodri, Dani Olmo and Roony for Barcelona, and Cristian Romero and Johnny Cardoso for Atletico.

The article presents the prediction as the output of an artificial intelligence system, which weighed recent results, attacking and defensive figures, the absences and home advantage. That assessment gives Barcelona a slight edge despite the difficulty of playing at Atletico's stadium. The closest predicted scoreline is a 2-1 Barcelona win with both teams scoring, based on the hosts' ability to exploit space behind the Catalan defence. The report stresses that this does not settle the match, and a 2-2 draw is also a strong possibility if Simeone disrupts Barcelona's build-up play. Atletico's coach is Diego Simeone and Barcelona's is Hansi Flick, and the article draws no firm conclusions beyond the prediction itself.

Articles.Title: Peak tension: artificial intelligence predicts the result of the Barcelona-Atletico Madrid match

stories.Headline: Inside the AI Operating System Tackling Data Starvation as the UAE Scales GPU Capacity
stories.Summary:
VAST Data, a company that began as a data storage provider and now calls itself an AI operating system company, is expanding its role in the UAE as the country scales its AI infrastructure. The company, which has a partnership with Abu Dhabi's Core42, was discussed at Ai Everything Abu Dhabi, held October 6 and 7, 2026, where Dany Khoury, its Regional Channel Director for the Middle East, spoke with The Recursive. The conversation focused on how the company addresses data starvation, which occurs when GPUs sit idle because the data feeding them is not delivered fast enough. Khoury explained that the company's platform is designed to keep those expensive processors working at full capacity.

Khoury said the company's journey in the region began with its Universal Storage approach, which was positioned to consolidate unstructured data, a major share of what AI workloads consume. He recalled joining around 2021, when the UAE was launching initiatives to embrace AI and he saw an opportunity for storage engineered for data-intensive workloads. The UAE was among the first markets to adopt the technology, and Khoury described the partnership with Core42 as one of the company's most significant in the region. He also noted that demand has since broadened, particularly from neocloud providers and GPU-driven infrastructure operators.

Khoury said that the company now supports more than three million GPUs globally through what it describes as its AI operating system, which combines infrastructure with software and data services across the full data lifecycle. He argued that legacy storage cannot sustain the demands of these newer workloads, and that organizations increasingly need to ingest legacy data, contextualize it, and make it available to AI applications. He added that the approach matters more as agentic AI grows, since the number of AI agents is expected to rise sharply and will need a robust underlying data platform. Governance, auditing and security were described as essential parts of that platform, giving customers control over their data and infrastructure.

On sovereign AI, Khoury said the company sits at the center of data sovereignty because it provides the platform along with the security, governance and control capabilities needed to run such environments. He pointed to the UAE as a leader in sovereign infrastructure that other countries are beginning to follow. Demand today is still largely led by governments, but Khoury expects the market to shift toward enterprises as their AI adoption matures and as they begin to consolidate data that is currently held in silos. He described the company's recently announced VAST DataEnclave, developed with NVIDIA, which lets customers keep sensitive data in trusted environments while running advanced AI models securely on-premises.

In Saudi Arabia, the company has already opened an office, is in discussions with several customers, and has existing customers through its OEM relationship with HPE. Khoury framed the next few years as a race in which enterprises compete to become genuinely AI-driven, while noting that many companies describe themselves that way without yet acting on it. He said the market is approaching a shift from experimental AI toward production AI, and that enterprises will increasingly focus on the value of the data they already hold. The company works with large enterprise customers and major AI cloud providers, including G42, CoreWeave, Nscale, Nebius and Mistral, and Khoury said its role is to help organizations shorten their time to insights.

Articles.Title: Inside the AI Operating System Tackling Data Starvation as the UAE Scales GPU Capacity

stories.Headline: The new Ivors Composer Awards is pushing back against AI
stories.Summary:
The Ivors Academy is relaunching its Ivors Composer Awards, with the ceremony set for 17 November, as a response to the growing threat that artificial intelligence poses to composers. The awards are part of The Ivors Composer Week, which runs from 16 to 20 November, and they are held at London's Grosvenor House. The article notes that the event aims to give composers the same kind of recognition that the better-known Ivor Novello Awards give songwriters. Ahead of the ceremony, the Academy has named Max Richter as the recipient of its Innovation Award.

The article describes the concern around AI in music as a matter of consent and compensation. AI systems learn by ingesting existing work and then imitating it, and there is currently no clear framework governing consent, compensation or transparency. The writer also describes a wider unease about AI's effects on jobs and the climate, and notes that creative industries are particularly exposed. Some publications and platforms have started telling contributors not to use AI in their work. At the same time, the article points to artistic uses of AI in music, including performances that use augmented instruments and work that draws on neuroscience.

Roberto Neri, chief executive of The Ivors Academy and a Labour life peer, is quoted as saying that AI could be a valuable assistive tool but that generative AI is a serious problem when a creator's work is used without permission and without any promise of payment. He argues that composers are often unseen, which makes it easier for people to accept music being produced in ways that replace them. He also points out that even a celebrated film composer such as Hans Zimmer can walk down the street unrecognised. Neri says the Academy is working with Equity and others to campaign for better conditions and will keep pressing the government for licensing frameworks. He cites Denmark's extension of copyright law, which protects a person's digital identity, as a model.

The article does not say when or whether the UK government will act on the licensing frameworks Neri is requesting. It also reports that 36 composers and librettists are nominated for an Ivor Novello Award across nine categories, including Best Original Film Score and Best Original Video Game Score. The article's account of Richter's testimony to a parliamentary select committee in 2025 is secondhand, drawn from an AI overview. What happens next, beyond the November ceremony, is not described.

Articles.Title: The new Ivors Composer Awards is pushing back against AI

stories.Headline: President Milei proposes cutting tax on AI projects to 15% — Der Spiegel
stories.Summary:
Argentine President Javier Milei has proposed cutting the corporate tax rate from 25% to 15% for artificial intelligence projects and other promising sectors, provided the investment reaches at least $1 billion, according to a report by Der Spiegel published on November 8, 2026. The proposal is part of a push by Argentine authorities to draw technology companies into building data centers, including in Patagonia. The report, as carried by UA.NEWS, says the government wants to position the country as a place with less bureaucracy, lower taxes and large areas of open land. Milei has also said Argentina will not regulate artificial intelligence and has floated allowing companies run entirely by AI agents.

Patagonia is cited for several traits that suit data centers: open plains far from major cities, a cool climate that helps cool servers, strong winds that could generate electricity, and large shale gas reserves in Vaca Muerta. Polish company Green Capital plans a $3 billion data center there, with computing capacity that large technology companies could rent for AI work. The articles give no further details on the project's timeline or terms. Argentina currently has about 40 megawatts of data center capacity, compared with about 400 megawatts in Chile, according to the Financial Times. Investors in the region have so far more often chosen Uruguay, Mexico or Brazil.

Milei announced a large OpenAI data center more than a year ago, and the articles say no new information about that project has since emerged. Representatives of OpenAI, Amazon, Google, Oracle, data center operators and venture investor Peter Thiel have recently visited Buenos Aires, according to Associated Press data cited by Der Spiegel. Data center developer Crusoe, which is involved in building OpenAI's campus in Texas, has sought talks with Argentine energy officials this year on investments backed by the U.S. government. The initiative has drawn concern from environmental activists and representatives of the Mapuche Indigenous people. A researcher at the Argentine group Observatorio Petrolero Sur warned that computing capacity could be exported wherever OpenAI and other companies need it, and critics also point to the environmental burden while noting that data centers create comparatively few jobs.

Articles.Title: President Milei proposes cutting tax on AI projects to 15% — Der Spiegel

stories.Headline: World of Warcraft addon creator makes code private as AI rivals copy years of work
stories.Summary:
Warcraft Logs, a longtime combat-tracking service for World of Warcraft run by Archon.gg, has changed how it handles developer access to its free application programming interface, or API, after a rise in AI-generated addons. According to 404 Media, as reported by The Cool Down, the service lets players record fights, upload the data, and analyze their performance, and outside developers have used the API to build tools around that combat data. Commercial developers are now expected to seek permission first so the service can check for possible terms-of-service conflicts or scaling problems. The service is also introducing a paid commercial key so that developers with commercial plans can support the project. Sildri Silentcrest, CEO of Archon.gg and Warcraft Logs, said hobbyists made up most of the developers using the service, but that the company now averages at least one commercial request per day.

Silentcrest also said the company suspects some developers are commercializing their tools without approval, and that new analysis companies appear almost daily. He said the service is shifting its API toward tools that help players understand their fights, such as identifying the cause of a boss-fight death or suggesting improvements for later attempts. Projects that scrape large amounts of data to show basic statistics have become much more common, he said. Silentcrest added that the ratio of abusive developers has changed sharply, saying that two years ago about two or three of 200 API developers were abusive, while today roughly 1,000 of 10,000 are. He said the team, which is small, is considering using AI more extensively itself to assist with research and code review.

Addon creator plusmouse told 404 Media that AI-generated competitors have copied their work, including a distinctive design for the nameplates shown above enemies. In some cases, code similarities led to copyright complaints and takedowns, while in others the copies were different enough to avoid removal. Plusmouse said borrowing ideas is normal in addon development but that doing it at the scale AI allows is not. Plusmouse said they made some of their GitHub repositories private, believing the change has stopped large language models from using their code. The Cool Down also notes that the AI tools behind these projects rely on grid electricity, and that the data centers supporting them can use large amounts of water for cooling.

Addon creators earn money through Patreon support and advertising revenue from CurseForge, a major addon repository, and their addons can offer quest-route guidance or change the game's interface. The article places this within wider strain on online services and software developers from AI tools, including reports that Wikipedia identified rogue OpenAI agents making edits and API requests. It also cites reports of AI-driven backlash on Reddit's r/opensource and of AI costs pushing developers of a Steam driving demo into debt. The article does not say what further changes Warcraft Logs will make beyond those already described.

Articles.Title: World of Warcraft addon creator makes code private as AI rivals copy years of work

stories.Headline: Following the release of artificial intelligence (AI) service beta in the U.S. market next month, Ha..
stories.Summary:
Hancom plans to release its artificial intelligence service in beta in the U.S. market next month and launch it commercially worldwide in March of next year. The rollout comes as the company expands overseas, but its board of directors has become a pressing issue. Chairman Kim Sang-chul, who also serves as chairman of the board, was recently convicted by a court of embezzling funds from affiliates. The Seongnam Branch of the Suwon District Court sentenced him on the 5th to one year and six months in prison with three years of probation.

The court found him guilty of embezzlement in business after he used 490 million won of affiliate funds for stock purchases and false salaries. He was acquitted of breach of trust charges worth 9 billion won. The deadline for appeal is the 12th, and Kim said his lawyers would be consulted before deciding whether to appeal. Separately, an appeals court fined him 20 million won for failing to report changes in his stake in Hancom With.

According to the articles, the first-instance ruling does not automatically force a change in the chairmanship, because the embezzlement amount is below the 500 million won threshold in the law on aggravated punishment of specific economic crimes, so employment restrictions do not apply. Under the Act on Corporate Governance of Financial Companies, a fine alone limits executive qualifications for five years, but that rule does not cover general listed companies. The decision about the chairman's seat therefore remains with the board and shareholders. Analysts quoted in the articles say overseas customers and investors will look at whether the board structure can prevent a recurrence, not just whether damages are repaid.

Hancom has moved to present itself as a global AI company, dropping "Korean and computers" from its mission in July and planning sovereign AI business in Europe after the U.S. The company reported record results last year, with sales of 175.3 billion won and operating profit of 50.9 billion won, a 29% operating margin. Its AI sector sales reached 13.47 billion won in the first half of this year, already above last year's full-year 8.91 billion won. Governance experts cited in the articles note that the company's board currently has four internal directors and two independent directors, with independent directors at about one-third of the legal standard. The regular shareholders' meeting in March next year is the next opportunity to discuss board reform, and an expert quoted in the articles said that after damages are recovered, expanding independent directors and tightening oversight of affiliate transactions would reassure overseas customers and investors.

Articles.Title: Following the release of artificial intelligence (AI) service beta in the U.S. market next month, Ha..

stories.Headline: Goodbye Claude, Hello Pi
stories.Summary:
