stories.Headline: MITRE ATLAS: AI Threat Matrix, Data and Usage
stories.Summary:
I can't write the story as specified. The article text provided is a CASRAI site page about MITRE ATLAS, a guide describing what the framework is, where its data lives, and its limits. It does not report a specific event, such as an incident, announcement, or development with a date, actor, and consequence, so there is no news to narrate in the requested structure. The page also gives no "who is responsible" beyond the general credit to The MITRE Corporation, and no "what happens next." I can instead write a factual summary of what the articles do state, in three paragraphs of four to five sentences each:

MITRE ATLAS, short for Adversarial Threat Landscape for Artificial-Intelligence Systems, is a public knowledge base describing how adversaries attack AI-enabled systems. Its content is organized as a matrix of tactics, which are the adversary's goals, and techniques, which are the methods used to pursue them, supported by case studies. The official atlas-data repository calls its YAML files the authoritative source of ATLAS data, and the content is credited to The MITRE Corporation and marked approved for public release. The project's home is atlas.mitre.org, and its code and data are published under the mitre-atlas GitHub organization. ATLAS entries can also reference MITRE ATT&CK, a knowledge base of techniques drawn from real-world observation.

Users who want the data are directed to the dist folder of the atlas-data repository, where dist/ATLAS-latest.yaml holds the latest content and dist/manifest.yaml maps releases to their files. Content versions follow a YYYY.MM.N pattern, while format versions are semantic versions, and separate versioning began with content 2026.05 and format 6.0.0. Generated outputs include an ATLAS-only STIX JSON bundle, optionally combined with ATT&CK Enterprise, along with Excel workbooks and Navigator layers for visual annotation. The guide notes that the repositories do not publish counts of tactics, techniques, or mitigations, so current YAML should be checked rather than figures quoted from third-party pages.

The guide describes ATLAS as a shared vocabulary and a machine-readable, versioned resource, but also lists its limits. It describes adversary behavior rather than controls, is not a certification scheme or compliance checklist, and does not rank techniques by likelihood or impact. Because content and format versions change independently, a pinned file can become stale or break a parser after a format change. The guide suggests pairing ATLAS with complementary resources such as MITRE ATT&CK, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, and model-specific testing tools, since each serves a different purpose.

Articles.Title: MITRE ATLAS: AI Threat Matrix, Data and Usage

stories.Headline: NYT Cooking AI Gets 3 Egg & Butter Swaps Wrong [2026]
stories.Summary:
The New York Times Cooking team has added an AI assistant to its recipe platform that can swap ingredients, rescale servings and adapt recipes for different pans. In a recorded test, the tool made two errors, both of the kind a home baker might not catch until the cake came out wrong. The Times announced the feature in an October 23, 2026 article titled "How, and Why, We're Adding A.I. Tools to NYT Cooking," and coverage from JournalArta and The Verge has followed it. The tool is in a gradual, beta-style rollout.

The assistant lets users request changes that are highlighted in orange so they can see what differs from the original. Customized recipes and the chats that produced them stay in the user's account and cannot be published or shared through Cooking. The original recipe is left unchanged. NYT Cooking says the AI's responses and custom recipes have not been reviewed by its editors or endorsed by the original creators. The company said the staged launch was meant to measure performance, including speed, and to see how people use the tool.

In the test, the tester converted a Cinnamon Roll Bundt Cake into muffins, and the tool cut the bake time from three hours to 50 minutes and split the batter across two 12-muffin tins. When asked to halve the recipe, the assistant changed five eggs to three rather than two and a half, a rounding choice that went unexplained. Later, the tester asked how much butter the recipe needed, and the assistant answered six tablespoons without saying which version it meant. The original calls for three-quarter cup, so the answer matches the halved recipe but not the original, and the reporting notes that six tablespoons would have yielded a dry cake. The coverage names Genevieve Ko, a senior editor and columnist at NYT Cooking, as a staff figure on the effort, but does not quote her on the tool.

The articles do not name the underlying AI model, the price, the subscription tier, the user count or a wider release date. They also do not say whether the reported errors have been fixed. Readers who want to check an AI-adapted recipe should compare it against the original and test any changed quantities before baking. More details on the rollout are expected as the beta continues, and the articles do not say when those will arrive.

Articles.Title: NYT Cooking AI Gets 3 Egg & Butter Swaps Wrong [2026]

stories.Headline: Ulta is marketing to AI agents and shoppers
stories.Summary:
Ulta Beauty is now treating AI agents as a new audience for its marketing, according to Chief Marketing Officer Kelly Mahoney, who spoke at the Status Summit. When a shopper asks ChatGPT or Gemini about skincare for acne, the answer shown at the top is the spot Ulta says it is working to earn. Mahoney said the company has to be a strong marketer to the agent as well as to the consumer, and she described AI tools as now being used not only to discover products but also to make purchases. Mahoney framed agents as the newest voices a brand cannot control, similar to creators and store associates who recommend products. Ulta does not write what an agent says, but it can shape what the agent knows by supplying content that answers customer problems.

The interviewer described this shift as moving from search engine optimization, which ranks links, to generative engine optimization, which aims to shape the content AI answer engines draw on. Ulta already builds relationships with store associates and with its Ulta Beauty Collective of influencers through regular briefings, and Mahoney said the same approach would now be applied to agents. The foundation for this work is Ulta's loyalty data. Mahoney said the Ulta Beauty Rewards program had about 11 million members when she stepped into her role roughly eleven years ago, and today it has more than 47 million engaged, active members who account for 95 percent of Ulta Beauty sales. She said the company built its first-party data infrastructure about ten years ago and has rebuilt it a couple of times, and that segmentation now centers on customer motivations rather than demographics, with non-purchase signals such as social activity and store visits informing personalization.

Mahoney was candid that no proven playbook exists yet, and she said the company will test, learn and adjust, relying on measurement. Mahoney also argued that stores will matter more, not less, citing Ulta's research on Generation Alpha. She said young consumers who use AI tools and chatbots still crave visiting stores and are more likely to do so, which puts pressure on stores to earn the trip. Ulta is investing in store design, immersive events and live selling through its TikTok Shop integration, and Mahoney said the future of discovery will be fluid, with digital and agent activity paired with real-life experiences.

Articles.Title: Ulta is marketing to AI agents and shoppers

stories.Headline: New AI Model Predicts Molecular Toxicity Using 3D Geometry
stories.Summary:
Researchers have developed a new artificial intelligence framework called MolMMP to improve the prediction of molecular toxicity during early drug development. The study, published in BMC Bioinformatics, introduces a method that combines structure-aware cross-modal alignment with geometry-biased attention. The authors aim to fix weaknesses in current models, which often rely on a single type of data and miss much of the structural complexity of molecules. By pairing sequence meaning with three-dimensional geometric relationships, the team hopes to offer a sturdier way to check the safety of lead compounds before they reach costly clinical trials.

Toxicity prediction matters because it helps drug developers avoid failures in late-stage testing, which saves money and reduces risk. Existing computational methods have notable shortcomings, however. Many depend mainly on one data type, which makes it hard to capture both the semantics of SMILES sequences and the molecular topology at once. They also lack three-dimensional conformation and interatomic geometric relationships, so they cannot account for how spatial structure affects toxicity. The new framework is meant to address these gaps by bringing several kinds of molecular information into a single model.

The researchers used a bidirectional cross-attention mechanism to align SMILES sequence semantics with graph topological structure, combining global meaning with local structural features. A separate three-dimensional module encodes interatomic distances through a geometric transformation based on radial basis functions. A hierarchical gating fusion strategy then balances fingerprint, topological, and geometric features, letting the model weigh each data source according to its importance. According to the study, this design is intended to handle the challenges of merging multiple data sources and uneven class distributions.

The team tested MolMMP on several toxicity benchmarks using both random and scaffold-based data splits. The article reports that the model achieved competitive predictive performance across these conditions, with particularly notable gains on tasks that benefit from joint modeling of topology and three-dimensional geometry. The authors describe the framework as robust and versatile across diverse toxicity endpoints. The article does not give specific numerical results, and it does not describe any clinical or laboratory validation beyond these benchmark tests.

Articles.Title: New AI Model Predicts Molecular Toxicity Using 3D Geometry

stories.Headline: Five9 (FIVN) Agrees $325 Million Acquisition To Expand Its AI Platform
stories.Summary:
Five9, a cloud software company that runs contact center platforms, has agreed to acquire Level AI, an AI-native customer experience platform, for about US$325 million. The deal, announced in a definitive agreement, is structured as a mix of cash and stock. The article reports that the move is meant to bring Level AI's technology into Five9's own platform. The announcement was reported by Yahoo Finance on November 7, 2026.

Level AI builds tools that analyze customer interactions to help improve agent performance and automate parts of contact center workflows. Five9's existing business centers on cloud software that helps contact centers manage calls, chats, and other customer contacts. Adding Level AI fits that focus on handling high volumes of service interactions. The article describes the purchase as a way to deepen Five9's position in customer experience software rather than broader enterprise IT.

The article attributes the deal to Five9 management, whose stated plan is to integrate Level AI's technology into Five9's platform. It is written from an analysis service that draws on company data and analyst forecasts, and it notes that it is general commentary rather than investment advice. The piece says management's push into AI aims to make AI agents and the Genius CX platform a larger share of subscription revenue. It also says the open question is whether Five9 can turn rising AI usage into stronger gross margin and earnings. Investors are pointed to the first full quarter after the deal closes, when more detail on combined AI usage and integration costs is expected.

Articles.Title: Five9 (FIVN) Agrees $325 Million Acquisition To Expand Its AI Platform

stories.Headline: New Explainable AI Framework Models Clinical Reasoning Through Expert Apprenticeship Learning
stories.Summary:
A new artificial intelligence framework called Explainable Apprenticeship Learning has been described in an open-access study published in the journal BioData Mining. The system treats clinical diagnosis as a hierarchical policy learning problem built from reasoning traces annotated by experts. Its developers argue that most medical AI has been tuned for predictive accuracy rather than for explaining the multi-step decisions that clinicians make. The reported work therefore targets interpretability alongside performance. The framework draws its decision models from reasoning sequences gathered from 61 practicing clinicians across 30 medical specialties.

It also combines multimodal patient data with Bayesian uncertainty modeling, which is meant to capture the variability that appears when clinicians interpret evidence. A synthetic reasoning augmentation strategy, based on clinical consistency constraints, is included to improve robustness on rare and complex cases. A policy alignment module compares the system's inferred reasoning steps against expert-derived distributions, flagging deviations at each stage and offering safety-aware feedback. On a held-out test set, the framework reached a Cohen's kappa of 0.972 for reasoning trace fidelity and a stepwise correctness score of 0.975. Its Top-1 diagnostic accuracy was reported as 0.953, its Top-3 accuracy as 0.978, and its safety compliance rate as 0.975 across evaluated traces.

In a controlled test, medical trainees who worked with the alignment feedback improved their collective diagnostic accuracy from a baseline of 0.85 ± 0.04 to 0.975 ± 0.02. External validation on unseen casebooks yielded a stepwise correctness score of 0.968 under domain shift. The article is credited to the study's authors, Abdullah, Ather, Fatima, Mejorada, Torres-Ruiz, Téllez and Saldaña-Pérez, and the research appeared in BioData Mining in 2026. The authors state that treating diagnosis as data-driven hierarchical policy learning can strengthen both interpretability and reliability in clinical decision support. The coverage, which was republished by Scienmag and bioengineer.org, does not describe any clinical deployment, regulatory review or next steps for the system.

Articles.Title: New Explainable AI Framework Models Clinical Reasoning Through Expert Apprenticeship Learning

stories.Headline: A scoping review of bias in large AI models for medicine and healthcare
stories.Summary:
A scoping review published on 8 November 2026 examines bias in large AI models used in medicine and healthcare. The authors describe large AI models, including large language models, vision-language models and large multimodal models, as increasingly influential in clinical settings. They define medical bias as systematic disparities, stereotypes or prejudicial behaviour in a model's outputs, decisions or interactions that disadvantage certain individuals or groups. The review, which appears on a Nature-hosted journal page, is attributed to a team of researchers with affiliations including several universities.

The review synthesises 92 studies, drawn from peer-reviewed publications and preprint archives, and sorts its findings into three themes: a taxonomy of medical bias, methods for detecting bias, and strategies for reducing it. The authors searched five databases (the ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, Web of Science, PubMed and arXiv) for work published or posted between 1 January 2023 and 30 April 2026. Their results indicate that medical bias occurs across clinical decision support, patient communication, medical documentation and medical education, and across a wide range of specialties. They also cite an earlier study in which a model performed worse at detecting cardiomegaly for female patients than for male patients.

The authors say the field lacks a unified definition of fairness, enough evaluation benchmarks and representative datasets, automated bias-detection methods, and real-world validation. They argue that bias is not an isolated failure but is shaped by model design, clinical context, patient diversity and existing healthcare inequities. The review calls for clinically grounded fairness definitions, reproducible evaluation methods, representative datasets and deployment-oriented validation. It also urges collaboration among AI researchers, clinicians, ethicists and policymakers, since the authors consider the problem unlikely to be solved by technologists or clinicians working alone. The articles do not describe any regulatory change or specific next steps beyond these recommendations.

Articles.Title: A scoping review of bias in large AI models for medicine and healthcare

stories.Headline: Workers losing a day a week fixing 'AI slop,' study finds
stories.Summary:
Workers are losing roughly a full workday each week to fixing mistakes made with artificial intelligence, according to a study reported by AOL on November 7, 2026. The research, commissioned by Arden University, found that 46% of workers spend time correcting work that coworkers produced badly with AI tools. On average, that correction takes six hours and 57 minutes each week. Two in ten workers said they completely redo the flawed output created by colleagues. The survey covered 2,000 working adults.

The study also found that half of those who fix colleagues' AI work use AI to help make the correction. Almost two-thirds of workers said they had used AI in the past three months, mainly to search for information, draft emails, and brainstorm ideas. Employees said the tools let them finish tasks faster, and a quarter said AI improved their understanding of complex topics. Younger workers adopt the technology most readily, with 73% of Gen Z and 72% of Millennials using platforms such as ChatGPT or Claude, compared with 56% of Gen X. Even so, 53% of employees do not tell their supervisor how they use AI at work.

Vitaly Klopot, chief innovation and commercial officer at Arden University, said employers need to consider how AI affects the whole team rather than only the person using it. He argued that a quick draft may save one person time, but if a colleague spends hours correcting it, the overall effect is a loss. He also said that practical education can help workers move past trial and error toward useful and responsible results. The article notes that most users already report saving time, and the next step is helping more people get reliable outcomes. Arden University has also announced a strategic partnership with Google Cloud and plans to launch more than 30 new degrees with AI-enabled learning.

Articles.Title: Workers losing a day a week fixing 'AI slop,' study finds

stories.Headline: Tempus AI Stock: Q3 Strengthens Platform Thesis Cash Returns Need To Catch Up (NASDAQ:TEM)
stories.Summary:
Tempus AI, Inc. (NASDAQ: TEM) reported its third-quarter 2026 results, and an analyst writing on Seeking Alpha published an assessment of them on November 7, 2026. The analyst, Thomas Veth, rated the stock a "hold," arguing that the current valuation already reflects considerable future success. The article describes Tempus as a company that connects diagnostic data with clinical outcomes, a link that the author says can add research value and recurring revenue potential. The analysis is an opinion piece rather than a news report of a corporate action.

According to the article, third-quarter 2026 revenue grew 20% in Diagnostics and 33% in Data & Applications. Adjusted EBITDA improved, but the company still posted GAAP losses. The author states that sustained free cash flow and operating leverage remain unproven, which is why the article's headline says cash returns still need to catch up. The author says he is monitoring Data & Applications growth and cost discipline most closely.

The article is written by Thomas Veth, an independent contributor, and carries Seeking Alpha's standard disclaimer that its views may not reflect the platform's as a whole. The author says he holds no position in the company and has no business relationship with it. The article does not describe any action by the company, its management, or regulators beyond the quarterly results it discusses. It also does not give a price target or indicate any future events.

Articles.Title: Tempus AI Stock: Q3 Strengthens Platform Thesis Cash Returns Need To Catch Up (NASDAQ:TEM)

stories.Headline: Jeff Bezos 'agrees' with three-day-week in AI age; says: Some people will decide, I can support my family by ...
stories.Summary:
Amazon founder Jeff Bezos said in a recent interview with Fox News that artificial intelligence could allow many people to work fewer days while still supporting their families. The Times of India Tech Desk published the report on November 8, 2026, quoting Bezos as saying that some people will decide they can support their families working three days a week. He framed this as what productivity in the economy means. The article does not give a specific figure for productivity gains or a timeline for when such changes would arrive.

Bezos described an AI-powered economy in which higher productivity generates wealth and gives people more say over how much they work. He suggested that if productivity rises enough, many households may no longer need two earners to keep their standard of living, and that one partner could choose to step back. He also said employers might find it harder to recruit if people can meet their financial needs with less work. On AI investment, Bezos said it was hard to tell whether the current boom is a bubble, but he stated that the technology is real and good for society. He warned that separating strong AI businesses from weak ones remains difficult during periods of heavy spending.

The article notes that Amazon is spending billions of dollars on data centres and cloud capacity to meet demand for AI services, and that it has cut thousands of corporate roles over the past year. Bezos's space company, Blue Origin, has also outlined plans for space-based data centres, which the article presents as a possible beneficiary of AI growth. The piece places Bezos alongside other business leaders who expect shorter working weeks, including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has suggested a four-day week could become common, JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon, who has said workers may one day work about three and a half days a week, and Bill Gates, who has floated a two-day week. Tesla and SpaceX chief Elon Musk has argued that AI and robotics could create a world of universal high income in which work becomes optional for many. The article does not say what steps, if any, are planned next, and it notes that views differ on timing.

Articles.Title: Jeff Bezos 'agrees' with three-day-week in AI age; says: Some people will decide, I can support my family by ...

stories.Headline: Mirae Asset elevates tech, cybersecurity leadership in AI-focused reshuffle
stories.Summary:
Mirae Asset Financial Group has promoted digital specialists and elevated its information security division in an executive reshuffle that it announced on Sunday, November 8, 2026. The company said 20 percent of the executives promoted in Thursday's personnel changes specialize in artificial intelligence transformation, digital technology or information security. The changes came as the group works to protect customer assets and personal data against rising cyberattack threats. Noh Yong-woo, a vice president, was nominated to lead Digital X, the former Korbit cryptocurrency exchange, and his appointment still needs the Financial Intelligence Unit's acceptance of a required change notification and a shareholders' meeting.

Woo Shin-je, a managing director at Mirae Asset Global Investments, was appointed chief executive of Mirae Asset Energy Infra Asset Management, where he will oversee increased investment in power infrastructure for AI data centers and energy storage systems. Executives in their 40s made up 64 percent of those promoted across the group's domestic and overseas operations, and women accounted for 17 percent. The company said 30 percent of promoted executives came from frontline wealth management and pension sales operations. These moves support the group's Mirae Asset 3.0 strategy, which centers on AI across its businesses and on asset and wealth management services built around autonomous AI agents.

The reshuffle followed a cyberattack at Mirae Asset Securities, which the brokerage disclosed on Saturday. The company said unauthorized access to its systems exposed the account numbers of about 3,800 customers, though account holders' names and other sensitive information were not compromised. It also said the personal information of 35,255 current and former employees, including contract-based workers, was exposed. The leaked data did not include resident registration numbers, passport numbers or driver's license numbers, according to the company.

The attack made Mirae Asset Securities the fourth group affiliate to report a cyberattack, after Mirae Asset Life Insurance, Mirae Asset Global Investments and Energy Infra Asset Management. Digital X was renamed after Mirae Asset Consulting, a nonfinancial affiliate, acquired a 97.15 percent stake in the exchange in July. Noh is expected to draw on his experience in management innovation, risk management and digital asset regulatory reform to link the group's traditional finance and digital asset businesses. The reshuffle therefore pairs leadership changes with a wider push to tighten security across the group.

Articles.Title: Mirae Asset elevates tech, cybersecurity leadership in AI-focused reshuffle

stories.Headline: LiveOne Turns To Tesla And AI To Convert 1.1 Million Free Music Listeners Into Paying Subscribers
stories.Summary:
LiveOne, a Los Angeles-based music and entertainment company, is expanding its partnership with Tesla and launching an artificial intelligence marketing initiative aimed at converting more than 1.1 million free subscribers into paying customers. The company is betting that the in-vehicle dashboard can serve as a way to introduce listeners to paid subscriptions. According to LiveOne, users spend more than 59 minutes a day on its platform. The announcement was made in an article published on November 7, 2026.

LiveOne's Tesla application offers access to more than 500 music channels along with content from over 200 podcasters, DJs and video jockeys. The company views these options as a way to reach listeners directly through their cars, making discovery part of the driving experience. Its AI-driven marketing effort involves tools and services from Claude, Meta Platforms, LiveRamp, Jasper, AdCreative.ai, Persado and Mutiny, together with connected television advertising partners. Rather than depending on one channel, the company is exploring several technologies to reach listeners and encourage upgrades. The aim is to increase average revenue per user, known as ARPU, and to develop business-to-business partnerships.

CEO and chairman Robert Ellin said the company sees strong engagement trends and believes its expanded AI-driven marketing positions it to unlock value from its large base of free subscribers. At the time of the announcement, LiveOne also reported improving subscriber trends over two consecutive months. The article notes, however, that these ambitions are targets rather than confirmed results. The announcement does not establish how many free listeners will ultimately become paying subscribers.

LiveOne operates across music streaming, podcasts, live entertainment and digital content through businesses including Slacker, PodcastOne, PPVOne and LiveXLive. Its services reach people through smartphones, connected televisions and streaming applications. The article frames the company's wider challenge as giving listeners enough value that they choose to pay for an experience they may already enjoy for free. For LiveOne, that answer involves automotive entertainment, a sizeable library of curated content and more targeted communication with potential subscribers.

Articles.Title: LiveOne Turns To Tesla And AI To Convert 1.1 Million Free Music Listeners Into Paying Subscribers

stories.Headline: What the Democratic sweep means for Trump's tariffs and AI
stories.Summary:
Democrats won control of both the U.S. House and Senate in the midterm elections, delivering a major setback to President Donald Trump's Republican Party. The results were reported in an article from Nikkei Asia dated November 7, 2026. Voters' frustration with the cost of living appears to have driven much of the shift. The coverage says the outcome could change the direction of Trump's economic agenda.

The article says a Democratic-controlled Congress could bring closer scrutiny of tariffs and trade deals. It also says voter opposition to data center development could slow the expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure in the United States. Those two areas, trade policy and AI, are the focus of the report. The article does not set out any specific bill, figure or deadline tied to these changes.

Nikkei Asia's U.S. correspondents examined the election results and what they mean for tariffs, trade, agriculture and AI. The piece also looks at possible effects on Asian economies and companies. The article itself describes these analyses as the central content of the report. It does not attribute specific predictions to named officials or analysts in the excerpt provided.

Related coverage in the same feed points to market reaction and industry concern. One linked headline reports that Nasdaq fell 5.5% over fears about AI regulation, and another says Taiwan, South Korea and Japan stock markets were hit hard by an AI sell-off. The excerpt does not explain how these moves connect to the midterm results. More to follow.

Articles.Title: What the Democratic sweep means for Trump's tariffs and AI

stories.Headline: AI scans global news for chemical threats, but radiological signals prove too rare to test
stories.Summary:
A study published in the International Journal of Data Science and Analytics found that GPT-4o, a large language model, could read news articles and reliably flag chemical incidents, cases, fatalities and locations without any task-specific training. The researchers, led by D. A. Honeyman and colleagues, tested the model on more than 37,000 retrieved articles as part of a six-month, English-language evaluation. The model was assessed on whether it could support event-based surveillance of chemical and radiological hazards, an area where no comprehensive global system currently exists. The study also revealed a notable gap: radiological events were so rare in the data that the model's performance on them could not be measured. The paper was published in 2026, and news coverage of it appeared on November 7 and 8.

The model successfully parsed 8,077 articles, while 2,238 failed during processing because of incomplete text, unusual document structures, excessive length or untranslated content. Performance was strong for common categories, with event identification reaching an F1-score of 0.96 and chemical substance recognition reaching 0.94. Date extraction was weaker, with a precision of only 0.62, largely because publication dates and references to past events were confused. Radiological entities appeared just four times in the annotated dataset, so the authors withdrew any metrics for them as unstable. A manual review found just eight confirmed radiological events in the 8,077-article corpus, about 0.1 percent of it.

The researchers say the model's main value lies in deciding which extracted entity belongs to the reported incident, rather than in recognizing entities at all. In comparisons, GPT-4o outperformed a cross-validated supervised classifier on document-level event identification, with an F1 of 0.96 against a mean of 0.87, and it also beat rule-based extractors and a pretrained named entity recognition baseline by wider margins at the entity level. The authors caution that comparisons with transformer-based or fine-tuned biomedical models remain outstanding. They position the model as a promising semi-automated triage component within curated open-source intelligence workflows rather than a standalone operational system. They also state that post-inference filtering, multilingual extension and purpose-built radiological corpora are needed before any operational deployment.

Separately, the second article, an editorial by Traci LeBrun, editor of the Pine City Pioneer, is unrelated to the study and describes a different concern about AI and news. It reports that Meta's new terms, which take effect on November 20 after being delayed from October 30, would allow the company to pull content from media websites for developing advertising and business products. Meta changed the word "train" to "develop" on October 16 after objections, and the Norwegian Media Businesses' Association has filed a lawsuit while the European Publishers Council argues the terms violate the Digital Markets Act. The editorial notes that Google reportedly pays roughly 100 publishers for AI-sourced answers, while Meta offers nothing comparable. The editor warns that the dispute could threaten newspaper businesses, though the outcome remains uncertain.

Articles.Title: AI scans global news for chemical threats, but radiological signals prove too rare to test

stories.Headline: AI Recommendations Distort Taste the More They Repeat: UNIST Develops Bias-Tracking Technology 'EchoTrace'
stories.Summary:
A research team at South Korea's Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology has built a diagnostic tool called EchoTrace to track how errors and biases build up in AI recommendation systems that are repeatedly retrained. UNIST announced the work on the 8th, led by Professor Lee Yeon-chang of its Graduate School of Artificial Intelligence. The concern is that when AI-generated recommendations are fed back into training data as if they reflected real user choices, they can gradually distort what users actually like. The team set out to measure that process directly rather than simply checking accuracy at a single moment.

The experiments reproduced this feedback loop across movie, book, and store recommendation systems. When large language models produced recommendation lists directly, 4.07 percent of movie items, 7.40 percent of book items, and 13.14 percent of store items did not exist in the recommendation pool but were presented as normal options. The team also found that 93.16 percent of occupations the AI inferred from users' movie-viewing records did not match the actual data, and in one case the AI invented a category, "film critic," that is absent from the existing occupational classification. These results came from MovieLens, Amazon Books, and Yelp data, respectively.

The errors persisted through five rounds of retraining, and in some systems the skew toward popular products grew worse. Professor Lee said the study provides a basis for systematically diagnosing how bias and hallucination accumulate in these systems according to the role the language model plays. The research was led by UNIST researcher Park Dong-wook as first author, together with Professor Lee Dong-won of Pennsylvania State University in the United States. The paper was accepted to the international conference ACM CIKM 2026, which is being held in Rome, Italy, from the 7th to the 11th.

The team's work reviewed 116 papers from major data-mining and information-retrieval conferences and sorted the roles language models play in recommendation systems into five categories, examining three of them in detail. The article says the findings matter for e-commerce and content platforms that use generative AI to improve recommendations. It notes growing calls that raising accuracy alone will not stop users from leaving, and that the paths by which AI-generated data enters training must be managed separately. Because recommendation quality directly affects time spent on platforms and purchase conversion, the article expects rising demand for tools that detect bias accumulation early.

Articles.Title: AI Recommendations Distort Taste the More They Repeat: UNIST Develops Bias-Tracking Technology 'EchoTrace'

stories.Headline: AI-Driven Airfoil Design Delays Shock Buffet Onset
stories.Summary:
A team led by Ma, Gao, Wu and Zhang published a study in the journal Advances in Aerodynamics showing that engineers can delay the onset of shock buffet on airfoils by tuning steady-flow features rather than running costly unsteady simulations. Shock buffet is a self-excited oscillation that occurs in the transonic regime when shock waves interact with the boundary layer, and it can degrade flight quality and cause structural damage. The researchers focused on two steady-flow features that track buffet onset, the shock wave position and the separation ratio. They applied a reinforcement learning method called Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient to adjust twelve geometric coefficients of the airfoil shape. The approach aims to improve stability without sacrificing performance.

In tests on the symmetric NACA0012 airfoil, optimization within a 5% parameter perturbation space at a Mach number of 0.80 and a Reynolds number of 3 million moved the shock wave position 4.4% toward the trailing edge. The lift-to-drag ratio rose by 60%, and unsteady simulations showed the buffet onset angle of attack increasing from 1.0 degrees to 1.4 degrees. On the supercritical RAE2822 airfoil, the separation-ratio-guided strategy within a 15% parameter space raised the buffet onset angle from 3.4 degrees to 4.1 degrees at a Mach number of 0.75, a gain of 0.7 degrees. Optimization limited to a 5% space and the shock wave position raised it only to 3.7 degrees. The method also used 87.5% less computational cost than a genetic algorithm with a population of four and 200 generations, while reaching similar optimal shapes.

The articles identify the researchers as the authors of the paper, and they attribute the study to Ma, Gao, Wu and Zhang, who published it in 2026 in Advances in Aerodynamics. The article notes that the numerical work used an in-house hybrid-unstructured flow solver with the Spalart-Allmaras turbulence model. It states that the results for the NACA0012 matched experimental data on surface pressure distributions and buffet onset boundaries. The authors suggested that the framework could later be extended to more complex airfoils and three-dimensional wing designs. The articles do not describe any changes to a specific aircraft program or regulatory requirement.

The study sits within a broader push to expand the transonic flight envelope and to bring machine learning into aerodynamic design workflows. The authors argue that conventional steady-state methods rely on indirect estimates of buffet onset, which can add uncertainty and conservatism to designs. The articles describe the proposed approach as a more physically interpretable and efficient route to buffet suppression. Further work on more complex configurations and three-dimensional wings is the stated next step, and the articles provide no timeline for it.

Articles.Title: AI-Driven Airfoil Design Delays Shock Buffet Onset

stories.Headline: “Please draw my eyeliner” Jung Ji-Seon, the secret to becoming Taiwan’s ‘national chef’? An ‘AI ad’ that hits MZ tastes
stories.Summary:
Star chef Jung Ji-Seon has drawn attention by crediting an AI-produced advertisement with helping her gain strong popularity in Taiwan. The remarks came on the November 8 broadcast of KBS2's variety program "The Boss Has Donkey Ears," which followed her life after expanding her business to the island. The episode showed her opening a 140-pyeong restaurant on a main boulevard in Taipei's Zhongshan District. The restaurant reportedly sold out all 74 seats during its first two months, and Jung said about 90 percent of its customers are local Taiwanese.

Her rise there was also driven by advertising work after her earlier exposure through Netflix's "Culinary Class Wars." She has shot commercials for probiotics and kaoliang liquor and appeared on billboards across downtown Taipei. The most influential of these was an AI-made commercial for a delivery app, in which she parachutes from a plane carrying a delivery box and draws eyeliner for a fan who asks for it. Young Taiwanese interviewees said they had seen the ad and found it fun, and Jung said that now almost everyone recognizes her when she visits Taiwan.

The business has not been free of difficulty, according to Jung's account on the program. She said more than ten Taiwanese employees quit within a month and a half of the restaurant opening, and she described hiring as hard in Taiwan. She said that, unlike her strict reputation at home as a "Tiger Boss," she now speaks gently to her Taiwanese staff, telling them she will solve any problems and keeping in touch through messenger apps. The broadcast presented her approach as an effort at localization and communication in a foreign market, and the articles do not report any further developments.

Articles.Title: “Please draw my eyeliner” Jung Ji-Seon, the secret to becoming Taiwan’s ‘national chef’? An ‘AI ad’ that hits MZ tastes

stories.Headline: Hong Kong makes further inroads in AI, aviation at mainland Chinese expo
stories.Summary:
Hong Kong is deepening its ties with mainland China in artificial intelligence, aviation and professional services, according to industry insiders speaking at China's global import expo in Shanghai. Executives from start-ups and tech giants, along with accounting veterans, discussed how the city could use its strategic position. The city's flag carrier also introduced a refrigerated sea logistics link to Dongguan in Guangdong province. Reporter Lam Ka-sing filed the story from Shanghai, and it was published on 8 November 2026.

The discussion centred on the Northern Metropolis megaproject, which sits near the mainland Chinese border. Participants described the project as a way to leverage Hong Kong's location. The sea logistics link is a refrigerated service, which the carrier introduced to connect the city with Dongguan. Speakers at the expo presented these developments as signs of a deepening integration across sectors. The articles provided no further figures, dates or contractual terms for these arrangements.

Andrew Chen, founder of technology company Mindverse, spoke to the South China Morning Post on Saturday. He said that operations spanning both sides of the border were becoming more seamless. In his view, physical and business ties were growing stronger over time. The article attributes these views to the industry insiders who spoke at the event and does not name any official who made a formal commitment.

The expo is an event that brings together businesses from around the world to showcase their products and services in mainland China. Hong Kong's participation highlights its push to position itself as a bridge between the mainland and international markets. The available reporting does not describe any specific next steps, timelines or policy changes that will follow from these discussions. Further developments would depend on how the projects mentioned are carried forward.

Articles.Title: Hong Kong makes further inroads in AI, aviation at mainland Chinese expo

stories.Headline: AI slump revives Asia’s forgotten trades from China to India
stories.Summary:
After the US midterm elections, the unravelling of the AI trade pushed investors across Asia to rethink where they put their money, reviving interest in Chinese and Indian stocks that had fallen out of favour. Asia had been among the hardest hit by the market fallout from the Democrats' sweep of Congress, since many of the region's largest companies, including Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, supply the global AI build-out. Investors who worried about scrutiny of the industry and whether heavy spending on computing infrastructure would pay off began moving toward markets with cheaper valuations and less AI exposure. Some fund managers pointed to stronger domestic growth in India and Vietnam and to Chinese technology firms as places with upside.

The shift has been visible in prices. A Hong Kong gauge tracking mainland companies rose 5.2% last week, its best performance since March 2025, while India's Nifty 50 gained 8.6%, its best week since 2021. Foreign funds put a net US$1.9 billion (S$2.4 billion) into Indian shares in the week through Nov 4. India's appeal also grew as oil prices fell on expectations of an earlier end to the Iran war, easing pressure on the energy-importing economy. Before these gains, the benchmarks in both countries had ranked among the world's worst performers this year through October.

Several managers described the moves in their own terms. Rajeev De Mello of Gama Asset Management said he expects investors to diversify more broadly and cut their concentration in the AI trade, which he thinks will support China and other markets with less demanding valuations, though India's reliance on imported energy remains a headwind. Hao Hong of Lotus said he is betting against oil and petrochemical firms and going long precious metals and Hong Kong equity futures. Charlie Hong of LOGOS said he sold his holdings in SK Hynix, Samsung Electronics, Intel and Lumentum in October and added Indian shares in new-age technology, financial and contract drug manufacturing companies. Beyond China and India, Allianz Global Investors pointed to healthcare and consumer staples, while Fidelity and ACG Management highlighted Korean consumer stocks.

The rotation is still in its early stages, and caution remains the prevailing mood. Some investors argue the sell-off may offer a chance to buy the dip given the sector's longer-term growth prospects, but others expect foreigners to keep selling Asia's AI supply-chain stocks. Manishi Raychaudhuri of Emmer Capital Partners said India and China are the only two large liquid markets offering a considerable range of non-AI exposures. Analysts also note that the prospect of less isolationist US trade policy has boosted confidence in carmakers such as Toyota and Hyundai. The articles do not say how long the shift will last.

Articles.Title: AI slump revives Asia’s forgotten trades from China to India

stories.Headline: Bridgestone revs up output of massive mining tires on AI-driven demand
stories.Summary:
Japanese tire maker Bridgestone is running its plants that produce giant tires for mining and construction equipment at nearly full capacity. The company is focusing on these high-margin products to meet demand driven by the artificial intelligence boom. The report, published by Nikkei Asia on November 8, 2026, places the news in the context of rising global demand for mining equipment. The articles do not give output volumes, capacity figures or investment amounts.

The ultralarge tires are produced at Bridgestone's Kitakyushu plant, and the report notes that they stand more than twice as tall as an average person. The mining equipment that uses them is tied to the copper needed to build data centers for AI computing. Nikkei reports that companies in this supply chain are seeing strong orders as a result. The article frames the production push as a shift toward higher-value products rather than a broad expansion. The reporting does not specify how many tires are being made or how quickly the plant's output is rising.

Seiya Ota, the Nikkei reporter credited with the story and its photo, wrote the piece from Tokyo. Bridgestone's own statements about the production push are not quoted in the articles provided. The same Nikkei feed also carries related coverage of Komatsu, which is expanding its U.S. maintenance hub amid the AI copper rush, and of Komatsu raising its profit outlook on mining and construction demand in the Americas. Those reports suggest the demand trend is affecting several equipment makers at once. Beyond what the articles state, the feed offers no further detail on timing or next steps for Bridgestone.

Articles.Title: Bridgestone revs up output of massive mining tires on AI-driven demand

stories.Headline: Grab rival Tada joins Singapore's self-driving minibus project
stories.Summary:
Singapore ride-hailing company Tada Mobility has taken part in a self-driving minibus project that will launch early next year on the resort island of Sentosa. The article, published by Nikkei Asia on November 8, 2026, says Tada is joining rivals such as Grab in moving into autonomous vehicle services. A trial period is set to begin in early 2027 using vehicles developed by China's WeRide. An autonomous minibus due to be introduced on Sentosa was shown to media in the city-state on October 29. The article's details on the project's rules, changes and requirements are limited, and it does not give figures beyond the trial timing.

It does not say how many minibuses will run, what routes they will take, or how the service will be priced. The reporter, Mayuko Tani, writes from Singapore and the report carries a photo credit to her as well. The article does not give further statements from Tada, WeRide, Grab or Singapore's transport authorities. It presents Tada's participation as a move alongside other companies entering autonomous vehicle services, without attributing specific remarks to any of them.

Readers are left without comments from the parties involved in the project. The article places the story within a wider push by ride-hailing and car companies toward self-driving services in the region. It notes the Sentosa trial as a step in that push but does not describe what happens after the early 2027 launch. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Grab rival Tada joins Singapore's self-driving minibus project

stories.Headline: Google DeepMind Economist Alex Imas: Even Millions of AI Agents Won't Deliver Double-Digit Growth
stories.Summary:
Alex Imas, director of AGI economics at Google DeepMind, has argued on the MTS podcast that millions of AI agents would not deliver double-digit economic growth. He says whatever gets automated becomes cheaper, so firms running on those agents could produce a great deal of output while GDP grows at roughly 4% to 5% a year. He frames this as a healthy outcome but not the explosive growth that some forecasters expect, and he notes his view forms one side of a public bet on the question. Imas says the key issue is prices and demand rather than whether the models are capable enough, and he does not see a technological bottleneck. He points to agriculture as a precedent: after farming was automated, its output rose sharply while its share of the economy fell from roughly 40% to about 2%.

For high growth to follow, prices would have to stay high and buyers would have to absorb the output, and he doubts the faster-growth camp fully considers who would be buying. He also cites research by Andrew Hall finding that a 2-percentage-point rise in unemployment triggers a large political backlash. Imas suggests this political limit could restrain a transformation before it ran to double-digit growth. Imas places himself among the named participants in the bet, on the skeptical side against Will MacAskill, Samuel Altman and Yann LeCun, and he wrote the underlying paper with Andrew Coe and Shane Lee. He acknowledges that a shift to 4% to 5% growth would still be historically large, and that a far higher regime is possible but not his base case.

He describes his own use of AI as widening the range of fields he can work in rather than simply speeding up his output. His forecast would break, he has said, if automated output arrives while prices hold and demand keeps pace. For investors, the article suggests attention should shift toward whether prices in automated sectors actually fall, whether demand holds up, and whether unemployment rises. Imas treats the two-point unemployment rise as the figure that could turn an economic transformation into a political one. The article leaves open whether the same political backlash that might slow automation could also block the new markets he expects to keep wages high elsewhere.

Articles.Title: Google DeepMind Economist Alex Imas: Even Millions of AI Agents Won't Deliver Double-Digit Growth

stories.Headline: Microsoft patent filing describes AI that rewrites what people say in livestreams in real time
stories.Summary:
Microsoft has filed a patent application, reported by TechSpot on November 7, 2026, that describes artificial intelligence capable of altering what speakers say in a livestream as the broadcast happens. The filing was made in late October 2026 and was uncovered by the site Patentlyze before TechSpot covered it. According to the article, the first claim describes an AI that listens for certain words in a broadcast's audio and replaces them with different words based on the viewer's profile, such as age, location, and native language. A separate, independent claim describes using the same kind of technology to translate livestreams with lip movements matched to the translated speech.

Microsoft says the first claim would clean up presentations by removing pauses and filler words, and it could also censor profanity or swap words based on internet searches. The article notes that the claim could support instant fact-checking but does not say whether viewers would be told which edits were made or why. It also points out that the described system could adjust lip movements in the surrounding frames to hide its edits, which means viewers might watch AI-edited streams without knowing it. The article connects this to existing real-time face swapping used by scammers and warns that altering live speech could extend misinformation and fraud. Unlike the first claim, the translation claim keeps the original recording as a "ground truth," according to the article.

The article attributes the filing to Microsoft, which says the latest patent is only meant for cleaning up and translating broadcasts. TechSpot writes that patents do not always become products, but says the number of similar filings shows strong interest in real-time AI editing. Sony and Microsoft have each filed other patents in the past year that use generative AI to change content during use, including Microsoft's July filing about rewriting game code based on player behavior and Sony's filings about predicting frames and player inputs in games. The article also notes that YouTube already offers AI audio translation, though without the matched lip sync Microsoft describes. The article does not report on any next steps or product timelines for the livestream technology.

Articles.Title: Microsoft patent filing describes AI that rewrites what people say in livestreams in real time

stories.Headline: While AI speeds up SMEs, delivery remains hard to automate
stories.Summary:
A Lalamove survey published on 9 November 2026 finds that small and medium-sized enterprises across Asia and Latin America are using AI widely in their daily operations, yet getting goods to customers remains difficult to automate. The survey, conducted in September 2026, covered Lalamove business users in nine locations, including Hong Kong, Singapore, Kuala Lumpur, Ho Chi Minh City, Manila, Bangkok, Jakarta, Taipei and São Paulo. The platform operates in 18 markets across Asia, the Americas and EMEA. Its findings suggest that digital efficiency is advancing faster than the physical movement of goods.

AI use is most common in marketing, customer service and administration, where it helps teams handle repetitive tasks and answer enquiries more quickly. Manila recorded the highest adoption at 62.4 per cent of SME respondents, while Jakarta reported 36.8 per cent. Among those using AI, Bangkok reported the strongest efficiency gains, with 93 per cent saying operations had sped up. Logistics and delivery, however, remain the least automated functions, with adoption ranging from 7 per cent in Kuala Lumpur to 24.1 per cent in Manila. Faster processing of orders does not shorten the road journey, which still depends on traffic, loading, vehicle availability and the timing of stops.

The survey also points to growing demand for flexible transport. Multi-stop deliveries were sought by 60.7 per cent of respondents in Jakarta, 56 per cent in Ho Chi Minh City and 50 per cent in Hong Kong. After-hours deliveries were identified by 43.3 per cent in Jakarta and 31.7 per cent in Bangkok. Many small firms find it costly to run a fleet large enough for peak periods, since vehicles, maintenance and drivers must be paid for even when demand falls. Lalamove argues that on-demand access to vehicles ranging from motorcycles to vans and trucks lets SMEs handle changing volumes without maintaining their own fleets.

Paul Loo, chief operating officer at Lalamove, said that many SMEs expect logistics costs to stay flat or rise in 2027, and that some have limited room to pass those costs on to customers. He said the company's on-demand model connects businesses with its driver-partner network in real time, helping them adapt and grow without the expense of their own fleets. Confidence about 2027 varies widely, with 71 per cent of respondents in Hong Kong positive compared with 35.8 per cent in Manila. In Hong Kong, 87 per cent expected logistics costs to remain unchanged or rise, and in Singapore 70 per cent ranked affordable pricing as the leading factor when choosing a logistics partner. The survey does not report any regulatory change or further action, so the outlook depends on how these cost pressures develop.

Articles.Title: While AI speeds up SMEs, delivery remains hard to automate

stories.Headline: NVIDIA's FOX blueprint sends AI agents from a defect alert to a root-cause report
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA has published details of its Factory Operations Blueprint, known as FOX, which lets AI agents take a defect alert from an automated optical inspection camera through to a root-cause report. In NVIDIA's reference example on a surface-mount line, a Visual Inspection Agent takes a second look at a flagged circuit board, a robot carries it to rework, and a Root Cause Analysis Agent examines machine data before producing a PDF report with evidence and a recommended corrective action. The description was published in NVIDIA's technical blog on November 4, 2026, following an October 21 announcement. FOX is a reference architecture that places a factory manager agent over specialist agents that connect to a plant's existing systems. NVIDIA says unplanned downtime costs an average large plant in the surveyed sectors $253 million a year, citing a Siemens report.

The company's main point is that delays come from teams gathering evidence across systems, consulting specialists and agreeing on next steps. The blueprint treats the division of work as a configuration choice. Developers connect existing data sources, which according to a summary of the post include MES, ERP and machine databases, then configure specialist agents and define which decisions need operator sign-off. The manager agent runs on a large language model such as NVIDIA Nemotron, with NemoClaw as the agent harness and NVIDIA OpenShell isolating execution. The Visual Inspection Agent uses NVIDIA Cosmos to compare a suspect component against the factory handbook without fine-tuning, the Root Cause Analysis Agent uses Kumo Anomaly to scan time-series readings such as reflow oven temperatures, and the Fleet Management Agent coordinates robots.

Which steps an agent may execute on its own and which require an operator is set by the plant. Siemens' Erlangen electronics factory is cited as an example, with reported figures that include cost savings of up to 20% from FOX-based order-planning agents, a 40% reduction in inspection-process calibration time, and up to 40% reduction in time to market when Siemens combines its PLM software and Process Preparation X with Cosmos and Omniverse. These figures are vendor-reported from a single site, and the 20% figure relates to planning rather than defect handling. NVIDIA also says it used the same agent stack to run its own DGX SuperPOD operations, where specialist agents correlate root causes across compute, network, hardware and scheduling layers. The company has published the code for that system on GitHub.

FOX is in early access, with no ship date given, and developers request access through NVIDIA. It can be deployed fully on-premises on an NVIDIA DGX Station, which would keep production records and images inside the factory network. Analysts describe it as a developer blueprint rather than a finished product, so outcomes will vary across implementations. Factory software teams and systems integrators are the audience the coverage identifies as needing to evaluate these workflows first.

Articles.Title: NVIDIA's FOX blueprint sends AI agents from a defect alert to a root-cause report

stories.Headline: Forum: Protecting personal data should take priority over efficiency and AI adoption
stories.Summary:
A public healthcare service outage lasting nine and a half hours occurred on October 13, and according to a reader's letter published by The Straits Times on November 8, 2026, a missed security update was the cause. The letter refers to a November 3 article on the matter. The writer, Chong Ryh Huei, notes that the outage came alongside other recent incidents, including a data breach at Alliance Medinet and an e-mail lapse at the National Cancer Centre Singapore. Verifying updates and ensuring effective recovery are described as basic responsibilities that organisations should carry out. The letter stresses that no patient data compromise was reported in the outage itself.

The writer argues that the incidents raise doubts about whether organisations can protect citizens' sensitive information. The letter questions how prepared organisations are for the added connections, permissions and complexity that artificial intelligence may bring, if existing safeguards are applied inconsistently. It says ISO standards, AI verification tools and Health Ministry guidelines are in place but must be implemented effectively to be meaningful. The presence of these measures alone, the writer contends, cannot reassure citizens that their information is safe. Shared infrastructure, the letter adds, also needs recovery arrangements that can withstand common failures.

Chong Ryh Huei, the letter's author, proposes that organisations first show that basic controls work before expanding AI access to sensitive systems. Suggested methods include independent testing, verified corrective action and clear accountability. Where readiness falls short, the writer says, deployment should be narrowed or delayed. The letter frames this as a matter of trust, since citizens hand essential services information they cannot easily retrieve once it is exposed. The writer's position is that protecting this data must take priority over efficiency gains and AI adoption.

Articles.Title: Forum: Protecting personal data should take priority over efficiency and AI adoption

stories.Headline: ‘Hard to recover the investment’: Gita Gopinath warns $1 trillion AI bet could correct, flags US recession risk
stories.Summary:
Former IMF chief economist Gita Gopinath has warned that the AI investment boom could face a market correction, saying companies may struggle to earn enough profit to recover nearly $1 trillion in spending expected in 2026 alone. She made the remarks on Saturday while speaking on Raj Shamani's podcast, describing herself as a Harvard professor. Gopinath said she personally believes a correction will come, but she did not say when it might happen, adding that it is impossible to tell. Her comments came as AI has become one of the biggest investment themes, with companies pouring money into infrastructure and some cutting jobs to redirect resources toward it. Investors have been chasing exposure, particularly in the United States, South Korea and Taiwan.

Gopinath described a world where two opposing forces are keeping global growth broadly stable, with the AI boom driving investment while geopolitical tensions, tariffs and the US-Iran conflict in West Asia weigh on economies. Her view is that the headline numbers mask large changes underneath. Taiwan and South Korea are growing at roughly twice their usual pace, and Taiwan's statistics agency has raised its 2026 growth forecast to 11.05%, the fastest annual growth since 1987, citing AI demand. West Asian economies such as Saudi Arabia and the UAE face growth downgrades linked to energy and the US-Iran conflict. The United States is still growing at or slightly above expectations, with AI investment offsetting some of the drag from tariffs.

Gopinath's main concern is that returns may not justify the scale of investment, given intense competition among companies and AI labs. She said it is hard to see how these firms will earn the profits needed to recover that spending. She also pointed to circular money flows in which Nvidia invests in AI labs that then buy Nvidia chips, so a collapse at either end could spread through the ecosystem. She warned that a sharp stock-market correction could push US growth to zero or slightly negative, triggering a recession that would likely be short-lived if driven purely by market losses. The article notes the irony that the AI boom is currently supporting the US economy through wealth gains and increased spending.

Articles.Title: ‘Hard to recover the investment’: Gita Gopinath warns $1 trillion AI bet could correct, flags US recession risk

stories.Headline: Q-Ball Intelligence Launches AI Predictive Analytics Platform Following Research Backed By 235% Historical Portfolio Return
stories.Summary:
Q-Ball Intelligence has launched as an AI-native predictive intelligence company, according to a Pulse 2.0 report published on November 8, 2026. The company's platform is designed to spot emerging patterns, assess shifting expectations, and forecast possible future developments, building on research that dates back to 2007. Rather than relying only on historical data, the technology aims to evaluate signals that may point to coming changes. Its method combines information analysis, behavioral expectations, emerging trends, momentum, and potential catalysts to produce structured forecasts.

The research began under Assistant Professor Peter Majanen, who is the company's founder and Chief Predictive Intelligence Architect. The company says an investment portfolio informed by this research returned 235.19% between February 17, 2016, and February 17, 2025. Over the same period, the OMX Stockholm All-Share Gross Index returned 129.86% and the OMX Stockholm 30 Index returned 106.55%, according to benchmark data Q-Ball presented. That works out to outperformance of 105.33 and 128.64 percentage points respectively. The company stresses that this was an actual portfolio rather than a simulated backtest, but the article notes that the returns came from research done before the new AI platform existed and should not be read as returns generated by the new technology.

Q-Ball plans to turn its research method into a scalable commercial product for institutional and business customers, and possibly consumers. Forecasts will be time-stamped and compared against later outcomes, a process the company says will support accountability, model evaluation, and refinement. Early applications under consideration include enterprise predictive intelligence, such as forecasting market shifts and identifying risks and strategic opportunities, along with analysis of equities and related markets and work in sports and gaming. The article describes the launch as the move of this long-running research into commercial development, with emphasis on AI product building, international expansion, and measurable forecasting. Majanen is quoted describing prediction as understanding the present well enough to recognize what the future is beginning to become.

Articles.Title: Q-Ball Intelligence Launches AI Predictive Analytics Platform Following Research Backed By 235% Historical Portfolio Return

stories.Headline: Physical AI Stocks Heat Up as Unitree Robotics Shares Jump Over 50% in a Month; Industry Players Say Three Bottlenecks Remain
stories.Summary:
Unitree Robotics founder Wang Xingxing used a speech on Oct. 22, 2026, at the "2026 World Physical AI Conference and Partner Ecosystem Conference" in Hangzhou to predict a major breakthrough in physical AI within one to three years, earlier than his August 2026 estimate of two to three years at the fastest and five to 10 years at the slowest. Since mid-October, the company's shares have risen more than 50%. Wang attributed the shift mainly to GPT-6Astra, a model OpenAI released on Sept. 3, which Unitree loaded onto its humanoid robots for tests without specialized training. In one painting task, the robot cleaned its brush when changing colors on its own. The article notes the model still falls short on precision assembly and on sensing environmental change and retrying after failure.

Wang also described Unitree's approach of keeping the "cerebellum," the part with strict low-latency needs, inside the robot while delegating "brain" functions to cloud or edge AI. He judged GPT-6Astra close to what a brain requires, and said that a next-generation GPT-7 would cross the "ChatGPT moment" for brain function alone. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said at the GTC Berlin conference on Oct. 21 that physical intelligence is the next wave and that it needs data centers, digital twin training systems and computers onboard machines. On an Oct. 21 earnings call, Tesla CEO Elon Musk repeated that humanoid robots will become the world's largest industry. Several people interviewed said the rally reflects both sector rotation and these public comments, while the article stresses that physical AI remains early-stage.

Cai Zhenhui, founder and CEO of Guangzhou Huarui Zhipu Artificial Intelligence Technology Co., said physical AI is expected to enter industrial production and commercial services, but warned that capital markets are not moving in step with industrial deployment. He identified three bottlenecks: models, high-quality real-world data that remains scarce and costly, and on-device computing power, which cannot yet handle models moved from cloud development onto robot bodies. An embodied industry analyst added that data investment and brain-model financing are structurally mismatched, and that whether data supply changes substantively should guide judgments on timing. Wang Chuang, a partner and senior vice president at Agibot, said real environments, where children may hug or push robots, are far more complex than laboratories. Cai noted that tasks such as washing dishes and folding clothes are still hard to achieve at demonstration level.

According to a report titled "Embodied Intelligence Development Report (2026)," jointly released by the Artificial Intelligence Research Institute of the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology, Tsinghua University's Department of Electronic Engineering and the Embodied Intelligence Testing Laboratory, embodied intelligence and physical AI are converging in meaning, with robots serving as a key vehicle for testing. The report also notes that humanoid robots face limits on height, weight and body shape, and that heat dissipation and room for AI hardware and batteries remain unresolved. The article's impact analysis says the concept heat gives short-term valuation support to robot bodies, components and computing power. It concludes that investors may need to focus on whether a data closed loop is forming, whether on-device platforms are adapted, and whether shipments reach scalable industrial settings.

Articles.Title: Physical AI Stocks Heat Up as Unitree Robotics Shares Jump Over 50% in a Month; Industry Players Say Three Bottlenecks Remain

stories.Headline: North Wales media projects share £90,526 to test AI newsgathering and broaden community coverage
stories.Summary:
Two north Wales media organisations have shared £90,526 from the UK Government's Local News Fund to develop new ways of finding and delivering local journalism. The award was reported by Tomorrow's Publisher on 8 November 2026, drawing on the Department for Culture, Media and Sport's list of grant recipients. Wrexham Dotcom Limited will receive £34,436 to build a tool that uses artificial intelligence to scan publicly available information and flag developments that may merit coverage. Coast Community Radio and Media CIC, which runs Bayside Radio in Colwyn Bay, has been granted £56,090.

The Wrexham project is designed to assist newsgathering, and the articles say the system is meant to help journalists identify potential stories. Decisions about what to investigate and publish remain editorial ones, according to the reporting. Bayside Radio says its project will extend local news and community-information work through partnerships, audience research and stronger digital publishing. It plans to work with groups across Conwy County and the north Wales coast to bring a wider range of community voices into its coverage. The station will distribute journalism on radio and digital channels.

The grants sit within the Government's £6 million Local News Fund, which forms part of its Amplify: The Local Media Action Plan. The plan aims to help local organisations adapt to digital audiences, develop online-focused business models and build stronger engagement with communities. A separate Department for Culture, Media and Sport announcement says the fund is intended to support innovation and help outlets reach new audiences. Ofcom's review of local media, cited in the reporting, found in its 2023 survey that 92 per cent of UK adults used local news or information, and that 89 per cent of those users accessed it online.

Ofcom also describes the civic role of local reporting, including scrutiny of public institutions, while noting providers' concerns about staffing, revenue and sustaining their services. The two Welsh projects take different routes: one invests in a digital tool to help journalists spot possible stories, while the other expands partnerships and publishing across platforms. The Government presents the fund as support for the long-term sustainability of local journalism. The articles state that the awards themselves do not establish how effectively either project will increase audiences or improve financial resilience.

Articles.Title: North Wales media projects share £90,526 to test AI newsgathering and broaden community coverage

stories.Headline: CrowdStrike to Acquire Dreadnode for Automated AI Security Testing
stories.Summary:
CrowdStrike, the cybersecurity company, announced on November 3, 2026 that it has signed a definitive agreement to acquire Dreadnode, a company focused on automated AI security testing. The announcement was made in Austin, Texas and at Fal.Con Europe 2026 in Barcelona. The deal would extend CrowdStrike's Falcon platform so that it can continuously test AI models, applications, and agents for security weaknesses before they are deployed. The aim is to find and fix problems before they reach production.

The acquisition is framed as a way to advance trust in AI systems across the enterprise. CrowdStrike's product pages describe the planned capability as testing every AI model, application, and agent for security weaknesses before deployment. The articles provided do not give a purchase price, a closing date, or details on how the Dreadnode products will be integrated. They also do not say whether any existing customers will need to change how they use Falcon.
