stories.Headline: It’s Time to Teach Students to Be Drivers of AI, Not Passengers
stories.Summary:
This is an opinion column rather than news, so the breaking-story format does not apply, and I have written it as a four-paragraph piece in my own words. Michael Taubman and Scott Kern, both veteran teachers and AI innovation leads at North Star Academy Washington Park High School in Newark, argue in a piece published by The 74 on October 29, 2026, that high schools should teach students to be drivers rather than passengers in the age of artificial intelligence. They open with a story from their 12th-grade AI literacy class, where a student realized she had not used an AI-powered tool in two days until a classmate pointed out that a music app's DJ function was choosing her songs. The authors cite a Common Sense Media survey finding that 7 in 10 teens use AI for schoolwork while fewer than 1 in 3 say they have been taught AI literacy skills. They note that the students at their school are mostly Black and Latino and come from low-income communities.

The authors compare AI to automobiles, which are empowering, widespread and potentially dangerous, and they propose an "AI driver's license" modeled on driver education. Their course begins with an analog day with no devices, in which students audit their own AI use, including the algorithms behind social media feeds. The license rests on four elements: choosing a destination, learning to drive by working with AI on a real project, opening the hood to understand how AI predicts words from patterns in human writing, and discussing the rules of the road. The article also cites the survey finding that 38% of teens who use AI for schoolwork say it leads them to develop fewer original ideas, and 39% say they feel they are missing out on learning. Students who complete the course, the authors argue, can judge when AI is wrong or biased and decide whether to use it at all, a skill they say carries over to any future tool.

Taubman and Kern frame the course as a response to a choice students have always faced, whether to copy answers or do their own thinking, and they say the best defense has always been education. Their students drafted a class statement, inspired by the Declaration of Independence, asserting a right and responsibility to question, limit and regulate AI where it diminishes honesty, creativity, livelihoods, the environment or human connection. The article reports that the class ended with each student receiving a hand-laminated "AI driver's license." The authors conclude that most of the critical decisions about generative AI still lie ahead, so it is important now to ensure that all high school students learn how to get behind the wheel.

Articles.Title: It’s Time to Teach Students to Be Drivers of AI, Not Passengers

stories.Headline: International Workshop Explores AI Biomarkers and Equity in Breast Density Screening
stories.Summary:
The eleventh International Breast Density Workshop met in Līhue, Kaua‘i, Hawai‘i, bringing together clinicians, researchers, and patient advocates from fourteen countries. The proceedings, published in Breast Cancer Research, examined imaging biomarkers, tissue biology, and individualized cancer risk management. Investigators presented eighty-five abstracts, and the biennial series, started in 2002, organized its 2025 conference around five thematic tracks. Participants also took part in a pre-diagnosis risk board modeled on multidisciplinary tumor conferences.

Dense breast tissue remains the strongest common predictor of breast cancer apart from age, according to the proceedings. Women in the highest quartile of dense breast volume face a four-fold to six-fold higher likelihood of developing the disease than those in the lowest quartile. Dense tissue also lowers mammographic sensitivity by masking tumors, which can produce false-negative results. Notification rules in the United States, Canada, and Australia now require that patients and physicians be told about breast density. The articles say that standardized measurement, biological confounders, and causal pathways remain unresolved after three decades of study.

Several sessions reported new findings. Dr. Gils described long-term results from the randomized DENSE trial, in which supplemental magnetic resonance imaging reduced interval cancers across three screening rounds in women with extremely dense breasts. Dr. van Grinsven reported promising accuracy for abbreviated breast magnetic resonance protocols in high-risk women. Dr. Mahmoud documented significant racial differences in background parenchymal enhancement, and the workshop concluded that such imaging biomarkers must be validated across diverse populations before they can be assumed to perform the same way for everyone. Dr. Mainprize introduced Mammatus, an automated tool that measures masking directly from mammograms.

Several speakers said the field's tools need further work before wide use. Dr. McCarthy showed that the qualitative BI-RADS categories and commercial percentage measures are confounded by body mass index, which leads to fewer supplemental screening recommendations for Black women and more for Asian women. McCarthy proposed age-adjusted density metrics or absolute dense volume as less biased alternatives. Dr. Strand reported that three commercial artificial intelligence algorithms gave Asian women with breast cancer significantly lower detection scores. Presenters agreed that wider deployment of these methods will require rigorous standardization and validation across racially and ethnically diverse patients.

Articles.Title: International Workshop Explores AI Biomarkers and Equity in Breast Density Screening

stories.Headline: Computational Workflow Translates AI Tree Sketches into Deployable Tensegrity Pavilion
stories.Summary:
Researchers led by Alberto Pugnale, Gabriele Mirra, Jack Halls, Michael Minghi Park, Michael Mack, and Sofia Colabella introduced FloaTree, an experimental workflow that turns artificial intelligence sketches of large trees into deployable tensegrity structures. The study was published in the journal Architectural Intelligence. The team validated the approach through a series of prototypes that grew from a two-module physical test to an eight-module pavilion erected in Switzerland. That pavilion won the 2024 International Association for Shell and Spatial Structures Design Competition and Exhibition of Innovative Lightweight Structures in Zurich.

The project addresses the decline of large, old trees, which provide nesting, perching, and sheltering habitat for birds and other wildlife, especially in dense cities. An earlier 2022 study by Mirra and colleagues trained an AI agent to generate three-dimensional line abstractions of large trees, and those lines preserve branching cues useful to wildlife. The team chose tensegrity structures, which hold isolated compression struts within a continuous network of prestressed cables, because they can mimic branching forms and fold into compact bundles for transport. Tensegrity was pioneered by Kenneth Snelson in 1948 and later popularized alongside Buckminster Fuller.

The design was generated automatically in Rhinoceros 3D and Grasshopper, then checked with Karamba3D simulations. The initial 12-module model showed that 14.8 percent of its 114 steel cables were slack and that the cantilever deflected 54 centimeters, so the team applied dynamic relaxation in Kangaroo2 and then a genetic optimization in Octopus. The optimized form eliminated compressed cables and reduced maximum deflection to 3.13 centimeters. The team also scaled the model down by 25 percent to meet travel limits.

Four prototyping phases followed, and the final pavilion had 75 steel cables and was packed into no more than six pieces of standard checked luggage. In Zurich, a four-person crew erected the eight-module structure within two days without scaffolding, ladders, or heavy hoisting gear. The article reports that an unexpected combination of rainfall and temperature swings overnight caused a primary timber strut to buckle at its notched joint after erection. The authors describe this as a trade-off between low-tech timber fabrication and tensegrity mechanics, and the article's account of the failure's analysis and any follow-up is cut off in the source text.

Articles.Title: Computational Workflow Translates AI Tree Sketches into Deployable Tensegrity Pavilion

She said the two companies are helping customers protect AI applications, agents, and the AWS infrastructure powering them so they can build and scale AI with confidence.

stories.Headline: Which Routing Does Each MoE Model Use? DeepSeek, Qwen, Mixtral, Llama 4, gpt-oss Compared
stories.Summary:
Two articles from November 8, 2026 cover very different corners of open model work. The first, a MarkTechPost piece, compares how ten open Mixture-of-Experts models route tokens to their experts. It notes that expert counts range from 8 to 384 and top-k from 1 to 8, and that some models keep an always-on shared expert while others drop it. The sources it cites were checked on November 7, 2026.

The comparison is organized around five routing settings: expert count, experts per token, shared experts, the gating function and the load-balancing method. Mixtral 8x7B uses 8 experts with top-2 and a softmax over the selected scores, while gpt-oss-120b uses 128 experts with top-4 and does not disclose its balancing method. DeepSeek-V3 uses a sigmoid score with an auxiliary-loss-free bias, and DeepSeek-V4-Pro raises its expert count to 384 while lowering top-k to 6. Qwen3-235B-A22B uses 128 experts with top-8, and Llama 4 Maverick routes each token to one of 128 routed experts plus one shared expert.

The article attributes these details to each model's Hugging Face configuration files, model cards and technical reports. It notes that the Qwen3.6 and Llama 4 materials omit gating details, and that gpt-oss and Llama 4 omit their balancing methods. The author also says that Kimi K2 keeps the DeepSeek-V3 router design while raising routed experts to 384, and that the Kimi K2 report found higher sparsity lowered loss at fixed active compute. The article's stated takeaway is that configuration files make routing auditable, but labels such as "17B active" can hide quite different routers.

The second source, a GitHub repository called llama-modchip at version 2.4.0, takes a different angle on the same model family. Its README claims it can run the 284-billion-parameter DeepSeek-V4-Flash on a CPU workstation with 64 GB of RAM and no GPU, reporting a 56.56 GiB checkpoint on disk and 57.61 GiB peak resident memory at a 256K context. The project reports 44.36 tokens per second for CPU prefill and between 9.1 and 14.7 tokens per second for generation. It requires a custom quantization type, GGML_TYPE_Q2_0, so the models will not open in unpatched llama.cpp, Ollama or LM Studio. The README lists installation through a single script or a pre-compiled binary bundled with its Hugging Face repositories.

stories.Headline: alphaXiv Guide: arXiv Discussion & AI Tools
stories.Summary:
I can't write this as a breaking news story, because the article does not report a news event. It is an operational guide to alphaXiv, a platform built on top of the arXiv preprint server, and it describes how the platform works rather than something that happened on a given day. The only date in the piece is when the guide was last updated, 7 November 2026, so there is no event with a who-did-what-and-when to report. What I can offer is a summary of what the guide describes, written in three paragraphs of four or five sentences each: alphaXiv is an independent, open-access web platform that adds an interactive layer on top of arXiv preprints, letting readers annotate text, discuss methods and query paper contents.

The guide says users can switch an arXiv address to alphaxiv.org to reach the same paper with community comments, highlight passages to start threads, and use built-in AI assistants that answer questions grounded in the paper's text. Developers can also connect external AI research agents through open-source tools and Model Context Protocol clients. The platform is maintained by alphaXiv Inc. and was developed by researchers and engineers who originated at Stanford University AI groups, supported by an advisory group that the guide lists by name, including figures from Stanford, UC Berkeley, Carnegie Mellon and Google DeepMind. Its scope mirrors arXiv, with the strongest adoption in computer science and machine learning, though any arXiv paper can be discussed on it.

The guide also notes that alphaXiv is not affiliated with arXiv or Cornell University and that comments do not change the official arXiv record. The guide lists strengths and limitations. Among the strengths it names are centralized discussion on the manuscript itself and faster post-publication feedback. Among the limitations it names are that comments are hosted on alphaXiv's proprietary infrastructure rather than permanently archived with arXiv, and that discussion depth varies, with niche papers often having few or no annotations.

stories.Headline: As AI Threatens Tech Workers, Their Workplaces Become Sites of Class Struggle
stories.Summary:
Tech workers have been pushing back against their employers over military contracts, immigration enforcement, and the Israeli occupation of Palestine, and the fight has grown more intense as artificial intelligence threatens their jobs. The account comes from an interview with JS Tan and Clarissa Redwine, tech worker leaders and authors of the book Against Tech Oligarchy: Workers Resistance in the World's Most Powerful Industry. Their book traces the movement over roughly the last two decades, including campaigns and strikes at companies such as Kickstarter and The New York Times. The workers' early actions were aimed at exposing the gap between tech firms' public values and their contracts with the military, police, and ICE.

They often relied on open letters, and one example they describe is a campaign at Google over Project Maven, an AI system used to analyze military drone footage, which ended with the company agreeing not to renew its contract. The tech bosses' response, according to Tan, came in stages. After the Federal Reserve ended its zero-interest rate policy to fight inflation, the companies lost cheap credit and billions of dollars in market value, and they responded with mass layoffs, return-to-work orders, and heavier workloads for remaining staff. Tan points to Elon Musk's takeover of Twitter, where he fired 80 percent of the workforce and attacked teams focused on human rights, AI ethics, and content moderation.

Redwine describes how workers then turned to unionization using what she calls the Recognition Playbook, which means mapping coworkers, training organic leaders, building a supermajority, and filing for elections with the National Labor Relations Board. She says the bosses answered with their own union-busting tactics, including firing visible organizers, hiring consultants, and using return-to-office orders to push out workers. The authors also say the strike at The New York Times in 2024 was largely a failure, because management had prepared the platform to run without staff, and because contracts with no-strike pledges barred the newsroom from joining. Redwine argues that labor law constrains unions, and that most major breakthroughs in the labor movement came from illegal strikes.

Tan says AI is splitting the tech workforce, with most workers likely to lose their jobs or be de-skilled, while a smaller group of AI engineers holds strong bargaining power because employers value their skills. He says many of the affected workers are becoming more class-conscious and concerned with affordability, and that a growing movement against data center construction creates both openings and tensions, since building trades workers are currently gaining jobs from that construction. The authors say new organizing methods will be needed that go beyond the Recognition Playbook and beyond shop-floor issues. The articles do not describe specific plans or dates for those efforts beyond the book's publication and the continuing debate over strategy.

Articles.Title: As AI Threatens Tech Workers, Their Workplaces Become Sites of Class Struggle

stories.Headline: The brain-as-computer metaphor shaped modern AI but may be misleading the consciousness debate
stories.Summary:
Three leading consciousness researchers, Anil Seth, Ned Block, and Giulio Tononi, have argued in a commentary for Nature that today's AI is not conscious and probably cannot be on silicon hardware. Their piece pushes back on the idea that running the right computations is enough for consciousness, a central assumption in the debate. They are responding to figures such as Richard Dawkins and Geoffrey Hinton, who consider AI systems possibly already conscious. The authors also address a study Anthropic published this year, which reported internal processing patterns in its Claude model that resemble properties of consciously accessible information processing, a reading the company itself does not treat as evidence of subjective experience.

The commentary builds on a 2023 report, "Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence," by Patrick Butlin, Robert Long, and 17 other experts, including Yoshua Bengio. That team derived a checklist of 14 indicators drawn from leading neuroscientific theories and tested several current systems, including GPT-4. They concluded that none was a strong candidate for consciousness, a point on which the new authors agree. However, the report found no obvious technical barrier to building future systems that meet more indicators, and it assumed, for pragmatic reasons, that consciousness depends only on the type of information processing, a view known as computational functionalism. The report itself acknowledged that its indicators would be unreliable if consciousness depends on properties of living organisms, a view it attributed to Seth among others.

The Nature authors argue that consciousness is what disappears in dreamless sleep or under general anesthesia, and that it is distinct from intelligence, which means carrying out functions. They cite the human cerebellum, which holds nearly four-fifths of the brain's neurons and handles precise, fast, learned movement without any conscious involvement. They attribute the confusion between intelligence and consciousness to people's tendency to project human qualities onto things, and to language models trained on human text that often describes thoughts and feelings. They also reject computational functionalism outright, tracing its roots to Alan Turing's 1936 work and to the 1943 artificial neuron model of McCulloch and Pitts, and argue that the brain's material is inseparable from its function. Their view is that the position is "fatally flawed," and that any evidence the material matters counts against consciousness in today's AI.

The authors conclude that researchers should assume by default that AI is not conscious, and that advocating for AI welfare or AI rights wrongly diverts resources from beings that can actually feel. They warn that granting rights to systems that only appear conscious could make them harder to control when oversight matters most. Anthropic, for its part, has said there is no scientific consensus on whether AI systems could have conscious experiences, and it launched a model welfare research program in April 2025 as a precautionary measure. The article notes that false attribution of consciousness is already causing confusion, citing the 2022 dismissal of Google engineer Blake Lemoine after he claimed the LaMDA chatbot was sentient.

Articles.Title: The brain-as-computer metaphor shaped modern AI but may be misleading the consciousness debate

stories.Headline: Hugging Face Papers: Guide to AI Research on HF
stories.Summary:
This is not a breaking news story, and the article is a long explainer rather than a report of an event, so the requested "what happened, who did it and when" structure does not map cleanly onto it. The only dated facts are that the guide was last updated on 7 November 2026 and published on 8 November 2026 by CASRAI's Editorial Board, and that Hugging Face Papers is a platform run by Hugging Face, Inc. The article carries enough detail for three paragraphs, so I have written it as an explanatory summary of the guide instead. The guide, published by CASRAI on 8 November 2026 and last updated on 7 November 2026, explains Hugging Face Papers, a platform that links arXiv preprints to models, datasets and demonstration applications on the Hugging Face Hub. It is aimed at AI researchers, computational linguists and open-source developers who want to track new preprints, link their model weights and datasets, and verify authorship.

The platform's daily feed traces back to curation work by Ahsen Khaliq, and Hugging Face formalized that feed as a Hub feature in May 2023. After Meta retired Papers with Code in July 2025, the guide says Hugging Face Papers became the main destination for community-curated machine learning literature. Hugging Face, Inc., founded by Clément Delangue, Julien Chaumond and Thomas Wolf, develops and runs the platform. The guide describes three main functions: a daily trending feed ranked by date, upvotes and discussion, artifact linking that connects papers to Hub repositories and Gradio demonstrations in Spaces, and author profiles that let researchers claim their papers.

It notes that about 95 percent of paper links on the Hub come from arXiv, and it gives steps for searching by title or arXiv identifier, indexing a new paper at a URL based on its arXiv identifier, and linking a model by including the paper reference in its repository card. Authors claim authorship from the paper page, and requests are checked against institutional email addresses or by platform moderators. The guide also says that papers can be submitted within 14 days of their arXiv posting. The guide lists strengths and limits, and it is careful to say that Hugging Face Papers is a discovery and aggregation layer rather than a peer-reviewed journal.

Its strengths include quick links from preprints to runnable code, feed updates within hours of arXiv release, and browser-based testing through Spaces. Its limits include heavy dependence on arXiv, ranking that can favor popular generative AI topics over niche or negative results, and variable quality in community-uploaded artifacts. The guide also compares the platform with Papers with Code, arXiv Sanity Preserver, AlphaSignal and Semantic Scholar. The article does not describe any further changes or announced next steps for the platform.

Articles.Title: Hugging Face Papers: Guide to AI Research on HF

stories.Headline: OpenEHR Conference Demonstrates Advances in Clinical Data Interoperability and Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
A scientific supplement published in BMC Proceedings on November 8, 2026 gathers thirteen peer-reviewed abstracts accepted to the scientific track of the EHRCON25 openEHR International Conference, which was held in Barcelona in October 2025. The collection covers short papers and posters on health information systems built around openEHR archetypes, semantic data modeling, artificial intelligence, and conversions between data standards. Instead of relying on isolated proprietary databases, the work tests whether archetype-based architectures can structure clinical narratives, modernize older hospital systems, harmonize multi-center research registries, and support automated querying. The contributions come from academic medical centers, regional health authorities, public health bodies, and software teams working on standardized health records.

Several projects report measured results. Researchers from Better Ltd built a retrieval pipeline that links free-text clinical notes to archetypes, and on 800 narrative queries it reached an archetype recall of 0.73, compared with 0.53 for the Clinical Knowledge Manager Resource Finder and 0.44 for zero-shot GPT-4.1 prompting. A separate team developed Text2AQL, an assistant that turns plain-language questions into Archetype Query Language statements, and it produced syntactically valid queries in 81.9 percent of 1,274 tests. Other studies describe a multi-agent framework linking openEHR with HL7 Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources, an on-device assistant that runs small language models on a smartphone using local health records, and a template set for genomic variant reporting. The articles also describe a translation of the World Health Organization's antenatal care guidance into openEHR templates, in which 98 percent of its 879 data elements aligned with existing archetypes.

The authors do not present these tools as finished. The antenatal template, for instance, was judged limited as a primary longitudinal record and decision-support framework, so a further mapping phase is needed. The oncology study at Isala found that setup was laborious, documentation was sparse, ICD-10 codes did not map cleanly to SNOMED CT, and existing archetypes lacked coverage for adaptive radiotherapy and dose-volume parameters. The on-device assistant also sometimes left out critical emergency instructions, and the Clinnova pipeline relied on custom version attributes because REDCap lacks native form versioning. The articles describe these as ongoing hurdles rather than settled problems, and they point to further mapping, refinement, and testing as the next steps.

Articles.Title: OpenEHR Conference Demonstrates Advances in Clinical Data Interoperability and Artificial Intelligence

stories.Headline: PMLR: Machine Learning Research Proceedings Guide
stories.Summary:
The article is an explainer guide rather than breaking news, so it contains no discrete event, actor or date of action to report. It describes the Proceedings of Machine Learning Research (PMLR), an open-access series that publishes peer-reviewed proceedings from machine learning and AI conferences such as ICML, AISTATS and COLT. The guide says the series was formerly called JMLR Workshop and Conference Proceedings and was restructured under its current name on April 10, 2017. It is run by an editorial board of computer science researchers, with Tegan Emerson, Hoel Kervadec and Neil Lawrence listed as current Series Editors.

The guide explains how volumes are produced, with conference organizers submitting a proposal, building a repository from a Jekyll template and compiling a master BibTeX file. Each paper must carry a citation key in the form lastnameYY, with the camera-ready PDF matching that key, and supplementary files following a lastnameYY-supp.pdf pattern. Editors then submit a pull request that passes automated checks before deployment. The guide notes that PMLR charges no article processing fees, authors keep copyright under open licenses such as CC-BY, and individual authors cannot submit papers directly, since submissions come only through participating conferences and workshops.

The guide describes the series as maintained by volunteer editors and open-source tooling, which it says can lead to variable delays between a conference closing and its volume appearing online. It also says PMLR publishes only electronically, so institutions wanting print copies must use third-party services. The guide compares PMLR with NeurIPS Proceedings, OpenReview venues, IEEE Xplore and Springer LNCS, noting differences in access models and author costs. It does not describe any pending changes or upcoming decisions affecting the series.

Articles.Title: PMLR: Machine Learning Research Proceedings Guide

stories.Headline: IJCAI: AI Conference and Publishing Guide
stories.Summary:
The International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI) has introduced a Primary Paper Initiative, a submission fee policy that starts with the IJCAI-ECAI 2026 cycle in Bremen, Germany. The CASRAI guide, last updated 7 November 2026, describes the policy as a way to address rising submission volumes and to fund peer-review sustainability. Under it, a USD 100 fee applies to Main Track, Survey Track, and Special Track submissions, but the fee is waived for a "primary paper," meaning a manuscript where none of the co-authors appear on any other paper submitted to that conference cycle. The guide does not say when or by whom the policy was announced beyond citing IJCAI's own 2025 materials.

The policy also sets out where the money goes and what else changes for authors. The guide states that 100 percent of proceeds from non-primary paper fees go to the Peer Reviewers Recognition Policy, which funds honoraria, registration subsidies, and formal recognition for program committee reviewers. The Journal Track, Sister Conferences Track, Competitions, Demos, and Doctoral Consortium are exempt from the fee. Separately, the guide notes that the review process runs in two phases, with an early summary rejection screen by two program committee members before full review, and that authors resubmitting work rejected at another peer venue such as NeurIPS, ICML, or AAAI within the previous 12 months must declare that venue and upload past reviews.

IJCAI is a non-profit academic organization governed by a Board of Trustees and a permanent Secretariat, and the guide credits the conference with a CORE A* ranking, placing it in the top roughly four percent of computer science venues. The guide lists upcoming meetings, including IJCAI-ECAI 2026 in Bremen from 15 to 21 August 2026 and IJCAI 2027 in Kyoto, Japan, from 7 to 13 August 2027, followed by a satellite symposium in Hengqin, China, from 15 to 17 August 2027. Looking ahead, the guide describes the conference's two-site format for 2027 and its annual schedule, which has run every year since 2015. The guide itself was written and maintained by the CASRAI Editorial Board, and the sources it cites are IJCAI's own call for papers and primary paper pages.

Articles.Title: IJCAI: AI Conference and Publishing Guide

stories.Headline: Generative Artificial Intelligence Tools Accelerate Design Tasks but Diminish Creative Autonomy
stories.Summary:
Researcher Shin Young Jang published a controlled study in the journal Fashion and Textiles examining how generative artificial intelligence affects digital textile design. The study followed thirty-four third-year undergraduate fashion design students at a South Korean university who completed matched pattern design tasks using both traditional vector software and Adobe Illustrator's Firefly-powered text-to-vector generation. Each student produced twenty designs across five product categories, and afterward completed a fifty-item survey while eighteen of them also took part in follow-up interviews lasting 45 to 60 minutes. The work was framed against a wider debate about how automated tools affect cognitive engagement and creative authorship. Its findings point to a trade-off that the author treats as the central result.

The generative tools substantially reduced the perceived difficulty and workload of the tasks. Intrinsic task difficulty fell from 3.68 to 2.09 on a five-point scale, and overall mental workload dropped from 4.21 to 2.15. Students also rated the workflow as far more efficient, at 4.06 compared with 2.29 for traditional tools. However, editability fell from 3.91 to 2.47, since students found the machine-generated vector structures cumbersome to correct, often preferring to start over. Ideation was easier to begin with prompts, but the number of distinct ideas did not meaningfully increase, and the outputs tended to converge on a narrow aesthetic.

The outcomes were weaker across the board. Perceived creativity and originality dropped from 3.94 to 2.68, aesthetic value from 4.09 to 2.74, and overall task satisfaction from 3.91 to 2.26, while the ability to articulate personal style fell from 4.24 to 1.53. Sixteen participants said the system made key choices for them, leaving them as curators, and fourteen reported anxiety about translating visual intentions into text prompts. The author argues that automation removed the productive struggle that builds design understanding, and that freed cognitive resources did not shift into deeper engagement, since measured engagement showed no significant difference between workflows.

The study's authors propose a pedagogical framework of sequential exploration, refinement, and reflection, in which generative tools are used mainly for initial brainstorming while students manually rebuild outputs and document their prompt histories. They also suggest process-based grading and, for professional teams, prompt libraries and transparent decision pipelines. The author recommends future research on multimodal interfaces that accept sketch and style references, and on a wider range of learner profiles. The study's own methodological limits, which the article notes but which were not fully stated in the portion available, temper how far these findings can be generalized.

Articles.Title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Tools Accelerate Design Tasks but Diminish Creative Autonomy

stories.Headline: AAAI: AI Society & Conference Guide
stories.Summary:
The articles describe an operational guide to the Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence, published by CASRAI and last updated on 7 November 2026. The guide does not report a discrete event, such as a new rule or an incident, that happened on a particular day. Instead it explains the society's governance, its flagship conference and the process authors follow to submit and review papers. Read as a whole, it is a reference document rather than breaking news, so there is no single actor or date that can be stated as the trigger for a story.

The guide sets out what the society does and how its main venue works. AAAI was founded in 1979 as the American Association for Artificial Intelligence and took its current name in 2007. Its annual AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence is run through OpenReview, where submitting authors must register an abstract by a late July deadline and upload a full paper by an early August deadline, both stated as Anywhere on Earth time. Papers move through a tiered committee of reviewers, senior reviewers and area chairs, with an author rebuttal window once initial reviews are released. The guide also says the 40th conference, AAAI-26, was held in Singapore from January 20 to January 27, 2026.

The articles attribute the governance and procedures to the society itself, citing AAAI's mission, conference schedule and OpenReview configuration materials as sources. The society is led by an elected President, President-Elect, Past President and a Board of Councilors, and its first president was Allen Newell. The guide also reports comparisons with other venues, noting that NeurIPS focuses more narrowly on machine learning while AAAI covers both machine learning and classical artificial intelligence. Those comparisons are the guide's own assessment and are not attributed to any outside body. The articles do not describe any pending change, dispute or next step that would make this a developing story.

Articles.Title: AAAI: AI Society & Conference Guide

stories.Headline: How Generative Artificial Intelligence Is Transforming Spatial-Temporal Data Mining
stories.Summary:
Researchers led by Qianru Zhang and Hongzhi Yin published a comprehensive review in Data Science and Engineering on how modern generative artificial intelligence is reshaping spatial-temporal data mining. The survey, drawing on work from academic institutions across several regions, sets out a structured taxonomy and an end-to-end pipeline for assessing how large language models, diffusion models, masked autoencoders, variational autoencoders, and generative adversarial networks are replacing older modeling approaches. The authors did not run new physical experiments or collect field data. Instead, they analyzed how machine learning methods have developed for complex geographic and temporal systems, from urban traffic to climate observations. The review explains that conventional deep learning models, such as standard recurrent and convolutional networks, face three main limits in real-world settings.

They need large volumes of densely labeled data, which is costly to gather across sensor networks. They also generalize poorly to unseen scenarios, altered road layouts, or local extreme weather. Because they output single deterministic estimates, they cannot express uncertainty or generate alternative scenarios, which matters for disaster management and evacuation planning. The authors argue that generative frameworks address these gaps through synthetic data augmentation, stronger transfer to new regions with few or no examples, probabilistic outputs that show predictive confidence, and pretrained foundation models that carry over to many downstream tasks.

The survey also formally separates acquisition-level data types from modeling-level data instances. It names four sensing types: discrete event logs with coordinates and timestamps, continuous trajectories from moving agents, point readings from mobile monitors, and fixed raster grids of measurements. These can be converted into formats such as individual points, trajectory sequences, time series, spatial maps, or multidimensional tensors, depending on the model. To settle which architectures count as generative, the authors propose three criteria: explicit density modeling, implicit generation from latent noise, and conditional sequence synthesis through autoregressive factorization.

Under these criteria, large language models and diffusion models qualify alongside variational autoencoders and generative adversarial networks. The authors compare the model families directly, noting that autoregressive models give exact likelihoods but decode slowly and accumulate errors over long horizons. Variational autoencoders allow efficient parallel sampling but can blur fine spatial detail and risk posterior collapse. Generative adversarial networks produce sharp outputs quickly but are hard to optimize and offer limited uncertainty calibration.

Diffusion models balance fidelity and diversity well but are computationally slow at inference, a cost the review says can be reduced through consistency distillation. Masked autoencoders learn by reconstructing hidden portions of the input and are data efficient, though they need additional output heads to quantify variance. The survey catalogs applications across representation learning and forecasting, including trajectory models, urban image-text alignment systems, traffic and air quality forecasters, and language-model-based time series systems. The article excerpt ends before describing the review's recommendations for future work, so further details on next steps are not available here.

Articles.Title: How Generative Artificial Intelligence Is Transforming Spatial-Temporal Data Mining

stories.Headline: CacheMonai.AI Inc. Appoints Technology Executive, Inventor and Entrepreneur Michael David Harris to Board of Directors
stories.Summary:
CacheMonai.AI Inc., a developer of an AI-powered business analysis platform called Insights, announced that it has appointed Michael David Harris to its Board of Directors. The announcement, issued through a press release distributed by EIN Presswire on November 8, 2026, gives the dateline of November 5, 2026, in Los Gatos, California. Harris will serve as one of five voting directors as the company establishes its board, and he will also continue serving on its Board of Advisors. The company said the appointment comes as it advances its technology and explores enterprise partnerships and future investment opportunities.

The release describes Harris's background at length, noting that he founded Harris-Atlantis Ltd., which made high-end speaker systems for Apple II and Macintosh computers, and later led Harris Laboratories as chief executive. It also says he co-founded iREZ Research, joined VideoLabs as employee number 13, and spent 24 years as a founding member and Fellow of GlobalMed developing telemedicine technology for healthcare institutions and federal programs. According to the release, his work there included initiatives serving the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs and Department of Defense. The release credits him with contributing to more than $100 million in turnaround revenue growth over five years, authoring 14 patents, and receiving multiple technology leadership and innovation awards.

He currently serves as Chairman of PROJECTeM, LLC P.A. and as Fractional Chief Innovation and Product Officer with Consulting Technology Architects. Gregory Gallinat, CEO and Founder of CacheMonai, said in the release that Harris combines engineering innovation, entrepreneurial experience and commercial leadership, and that his presence on both boards strengthens the company's strategic leadership. Harris, quoted in the release, said CacheMonai has a pathway to help organizations gain deeper insights into their markets and make better strategic decisions. He said he has worked with Gallinat for more than 20 years and plans to help guide the company's innovation, commercialization strategy and expansion into enterprise markets.

The release notes that the two men have maintained a professional relationship spanning more than 25 years, and it describes the Insights platform as being developed to coordinate AI-assisted analysis of organizations, products, customer segments and market opportunities. The announcement is a corporate press release rather than independent reporting, and the release itself contains no information about compensation, equity, or the terms of Harris's appointment. It also does not say when the company expects to launch its enterprise offerings or complete its board formation. The release lists a media contact, Clayton Harris of PROJECTeM, LLC P.A., and EIN Presswire disclaims responsibility for the accuracy of the content.

Articles.Title: CacheMonai.AI Inc. Appoints Technology Executive, Inventor and Entrepreneur Michael David Harris to Board of Directors

stories.Headline: OPB’s First Look: Blue ocean strategy for AI
stories.Summary:
Portland startup Panthalassa unveiled a new factory on November 6, 2026, at the historic Kaiser Shipyard site along the Columbia River in Vancouver, Washington. The facility will manufacture wave-powered devices meant to support floating data centers on the open ocean. The company, which has raised more than $300 million this year, aims to build nodes at the plant that will generate energy from waves. Panthalassa takes its name from a super ocean that covered most of Earth's surface roughly 190 million years ago. OPB's Courtney Sherwood attended the ribbon-cutting ceremony.

The company hopes to seed deep oceans around the globe with self-driving buoys and then use the energy they capture to power floating artificial intelligence computation hubs. Its backers argue these hubs would avoid the carbon emissions, freshwater contamination and neighborhood disruption that have fueled a backlash against land-based data centers. The new factory marks the company's first move from custom manufacturing to an assembly line. It is also a test of the firm's theory that it can eventually make and deploy its nodes at additional factories around the world.

Panthalassa is based in Portland, and the article describes the Vancouver plant as a significant investment in the region. The reporting frames the venture as an attempt to answer heated debate over greenhouse gas emissions tied to energy-hungry AI data centers. Beyond the factory opening, the article does not name additional officials or give further statements from company leaders. It also does not specify a production timeline or how many nodes the plant will produce.

Articles.Title: OPB’s First Look: Blue ocean strategy for AI - Oregon Public Broadcasting - OPB

stories.Headline: Ontario startup's AI Checker has them pegged a 'scrappy underdog' in tech world
stories.Summary:
Originality.ai, a startup founded in Collingwood, Ontario, has been named on Deloitte's list of fast-growing tech companies to watch, according to a November 8, 2026 report. The company launched on November 27, 2022, with help from the Georgian Bay Accelerator program and was founded by Collingwood resident Jon Gillham. Its AI checker scans text to estimate how much was written by AI and how much by a human. The product also includes a plagiarism detector, a grammar checker, and a fact and AI hallucination detector. It has grown to 25 full-time employees, seven of whom work in Collingwood.

Gillham said the ranking validates the team's work at a self-funded company in a fast-moving field. Deloitte ranked Originality.ai ninth among companies in Ottawa, Toronto, Vancouver and Montreal, and the list shows 494 per cent growth. The idea came from Gillham's experience hiring writers for his earlier content marketing business, Content Refined, which he sold before starting Originality.ai. A free, limited version of the tool is available, and the Chrome extension is free, though commercial use requires a subscription. The company says tens of thousands of people use it, including teachers, students, law firms, newsrooms and marketing firms.

Gillham described the company as a "scrappy underdog" on the ethical-use side of the generative AI industry, where trillions of dollars are being invested. He said Originality.ai is one of a few leading companies monitoring where AI is used and where it should not be. He also said he did not expect the company to become a societally important business, but that the rise of ChatGPT and other generative AI made it something the company needs to get right. He said he would not have expected AI text creation to be as dominant as it is now. The Chrome extension lets someone show a teacher their writing process in a Google document if they face an accusation of using AI.

Articles.Title: Ontario startup's AI Checker has them pegged a 'scrappy underdog' in tech world

stories.Headline: Best AI Humanizer Tools Tested and Compared: 7 Options for Web Content
stories.Summary:
The article is a SitePoint roundup, published November 8, 2026, titled "Best AI Humanizer Tools Tested and Compared: 7 Options for Web Content." Its author is listed as DJ Div John. The piece says the best humanizer is the one that changes how a draft reads without changing what it says. To test the tools on equal terms, the author ran the same 103-word AI-written release note through each one in November 2026. That note contains a product name, two image formats, a settings path and the word "must," so the test checks whether each tool keeps the details a reader acts on.

The article sets out six criteria for choosing a humanizer: keeping meaning and facts intact, tone and style control, preserving technical terms, word limits, free use and sign-up requirements, and privacy of pasted text. It notes that everything pasted is sent to the vendor's servers, so unreleased features, client names and credentials should be kept out. The features, limits and prices for each tool were checked against the vendors' own pages on the same day. Word limits in the list range from 125 to 2,000 words per run, and Ahrefs counts characters instead. The roundup profiles seven tools: Humanize Max, QuillBot's AI Humanizer, GPTinf, Grammarly's AI Humanizer, Humanize AI, Undetectable AI and Ahrefs' AI Humanizer.

Each gets a short verdict, such as Humanize Max for setting tone and length together, or Humanize AI for fine control and API access. The author also describes a comparison table with styles, length control, word limits, free plans and sign-up requirements for each tool. The article is a commercial-style roundup, and the page notes that community articles are written by SitePoint Premium contributors and screened before publication. The article does not say whether any of these tools produce text that AI detectors fail to flag, and it notes that GPTinf's AI-likelihood score is an estimate rather than proof of authorship. Beyond the publication date and the test date, it gives no further timeline.

Articles.Title: Best AI Humanizer Tools Tested and Compared: 7 Options for Web Content

stories.Headline: A single AI forecast inflates US power auctions by $5.7B
stories.Summary:
A single AI-driven demand forecast has been shown to add $5.7 billion to the modeled cost of a US power capacity auction, according to an analysis that reran PJM's market. The independent market monitor, Monitoring Analytics, calculated in a recent report dated October 30, 2026 that PJM's July auction for the 2028-29 delivery year produced about $16.41 billion in capacity revenue. When the monitor removed forecast growth in demand from new and expanding data centers while keeping other assumptions fixed, the total fell to about $10.7 billion. The gap reflects expectations of future demand rather than any building already operating. The auction pays power suppliers to commit capacity years before the electricity is used, so forecasts directly shape the sums involved.

The consequences extend beyond wholesale markets into consumer prices, though the articles stress that the effects are hard to isolate. Australia's Bureau of Statistics reported a 6.1% quarterly rise in audio, visual, and computing equipment prices, and the Reserve Bank of Australia linked some of that increase to higher memory-chip costs tied to AI infrastructure demand. In the US, September consumer-price data showed computers, peripherals, and smart-home assistants up 9.7% over a year, while smartphones fell 9.9%. The San Francisco Fed estimated that information-processing equipment added only 0.2 percentage points to August's 3.4% personal consumption expenditures inflation rate. Virginia regulators have also created a separate rate class for Dominion Energy Virginia's large users, with minimum payments and a requirement to take and pay for electricity for at least 14 years for new large-load customers contracting on or after January 1, 2027.

Responsibility for these costs remains contested, and the articles frame it mainly through the institutions involved. The market monitor's analysis puts the modeled figure in the capacity market, and the articles note that it is only an estimate of generative AI demand, not a household surcharge. The Reserve Bank of Australia said AI's effect on overall consumer prices remained modest, citing fuel costs and domestic capacity constraints as other factors, and raised its cash rate to 4.85% on November 3. The Bank of England, which raised Bank Rate to 4%, judged the effect of AI and other non-energy risks on UK inflation to be much smaller than the energy shock. The articles also note that how these costs reach individual customers depends on contracts and local regulation, and that some large customers making long-term payments can spread existing costs across more consumption.

The articles indicate that the debate will continue as central banks, grid operators, and state regulators track AI-related demand and its pricing effects. Federal Reserve researchers have warned that some inflation data may not fully account for quality improvements in software and devices, which could change how the price increases are read. Planning for too little capacity risks shortages, while planning for projects that use less power than forecast could leave infrastructure with fewer customers than its financing assumed. These trade-offs will shape the next auctions and the rules governing how large users pay.

Articles.Title: A single AI forecast inflates US power auctions by $5.7B

stories.Headline: What Is Lumen Technologies (LUMN) Doing To Simplify AI Connectivity For Enterprises?
stories.Summary:
Lumen Technologies has expanded its collaboration with Microsoft to support enterprise adoption of AI on Azure, according to a November 8, 2026 article. The enlarged partnership links Lumen's cloud networking and application connectivity tools directly to Microsoft Azure cloud and AI services. The two companies also plan joint work on future network modernization projects meant to simplify how enterprises connect data and applications for AI use. The article describes Lumen as a global networking operation that supplies connectivity and communications services to business and mass-market customers. In this role, Lumen provides the data pipes and routing intelligence that feed enterprise AI workloads spread across different locations.

The article links the Azure push to Lumen's broader AI networking strategy and cites several figures from its business. It mentions Network as a Service, platform connectivity fiber commitments of around US$13 billion, and Alkira-based multi-cloud tools as routes into large enterprise AI projects. It also notes recent quarterly losses of US$265 million on US$2.72 billion of revenue, along with legacy product declines. The article says investors should watch whether joint deals show up in concrete metrics, such as Network as a Service customer counts, active ports, or disclosed AI-related connectivity wins. It points to upcoming earnings calls and 2027 updates to the company's US$3 billion annual capital expenditure and cost-saving plans as places where that proof may appear.

The article attributes the announcement to Lumen Technologies and Microsoft, and it does not quote either company's executives directly. It notes that the expanded collaboration fits a wider pattern identified by recent research on the business. The article is produced with AI automation from data and analysis by Simply Wall St and states that it is not financial advice. Related coverage in the same listing includes a Business Wire report from six days earlier on a co-selling expansion for AI-ready networks. Analyst forecasts for Lumen's longer-term direction are also referenced but not detailed in the text provided.

Articles.Title: What Is Lumen Technologies (LUMN) Doing To Simplify AI Connectivity For Enterprises?

stories.Headline: U.S. military accelerates AI push across Pacific as China tensions grow - Honolulu Star-Advertiser
stories.Summary:
The U.S. Pacific Command has been rapidly equipping its forces with artificial intelligence tools across Hawaii and the wider Pacific as tensions with China grow. Adm. Samuel Paparo has directed that AI be adopted across the entire command, according to Scott Brunstetter, the command's chief AI officer. Brunstetter spoke at the TechNet Hawaii Conference on Oct. 28, a military trade show focused on information technology and communications. His position, now officially titled "Chief Super Intelligence Officer" after President Donald Trump signed an executive order requiring officials to use the term "superintelligence," was created about 15 months ago at the command's headquarters at Camp Smith.

Brunstetter said the command concluded that the operational risk of not adopting AI outweighs the risk of adopting it. The military is applying AI to tasks ranging from logistics to intelligence analysis. Tagup, an AI company, has worked with Marine Corps Forces Pacific on logistics, including tracking medical supplies nearing or past their expiration dates. Tagup's president, Paul Plemmons, said the tools let planners iterate faster than a staff officer normally could. The command covers the largest geographic area of any U.S. combatant command, so the AI tools are meant to help gather and analyze data across the Pacific.

The growth of AI has also created physical challenges, since the systems depend on server farms and data centers that use large amounts of electricity and water. Brunstetter said power limits on Hawaii and the distance to cloud services have driven significant innovation in the field. Ricky Buchanan, chief of PACOM's Intelligence Information Systems Division, said commanders cannot let warfighters depend on tools that rely on mainland data centers. The military is building a 56,000-square-foot laboratory and data center in Kihei, due for completion early next year, which has drawn opposition from the community, environmentalists and Native Hawaiian groups. Buchanan also said commanders are cautiously exploring smaller mobile data centers, warning against creating a fixed target that adversaries could strike first.

Officials acknowledged that AI tools can make mistakes. In September, CNN reported that U.S. troops had nearly launched a boarding raid on a Chinese cargo ship based on an AI-assisted intelligence report that a Special Operations Command analyst later found to be false, a report one source said almost started a war. Brunstetter said the military does not blindly trust its data tools and that analysts must understand how they work. Plemmons said a trained human should always remain in the loop. Contractors such as Sigma Defense are also working to modernize Navy ships with software, since hardware upgrades can take six to 10 years.

Articles.Title: U.S. military accelerates AI push across Pacific as China tensions grow - Honolulu Star-Advertiser

stories.Headline: Rep. Yvette Clarke Stands on the Frontlines of AI Legislation
stories.Summary:
Rep. Yvette Clarke, a Democrat from New York, has pushed Congress to pass federal rules for artificial intelligence, a call the article ties to recent White House reports about possible voluntary industry regulation. She has introduced or co-sponsored several AI bills aimed at algorithmic bias, deepfakes, and intellectual property. Her most recent move was reintroducing the REAL Political Ads Act, which would require disclosure when generative AI is used to create images or videos in political ads. The bill was first introduced in May 2023. Clarke said Congress has fallen behind a rapidly advancing technology, leaving voters open to AI-generated misinformation.

Clarke's other proposals include the AI Civil Rights Act, introduced in December 2025 with Senator Edward J. Markey, which would bar biased AI algorithms from high-stakes decisions about housing, employment, education, credit, healthcare, and parole. She introduced the Algorithmic Accountability Act with Senator Ron Wyden in September 2025 to bring transparency to AI use in those same high-impact areas. In June 2026 she introduced the CREATOR Act with Representatives Beth Van Duyne and Valerie Foushee to protect artists against AI-enabled style impersonation. Adobe publicly supported that bill, according to the article. Clarke and Representative Glenn Ivey also introduced the DEEPFAKES Accountability Act of 2023, which would require digital watermarks on deepfakes and make it a crime to fail to identify malicious ones.

Clarke led 43 colleagues in a December 2025 letter urging that any moratorium or preemption of state AI laws be kept out of the FY26 NDAA, arguing that state laws are the only recourse consumers have until Congress acts comprehensively. The article notes that all 50 states introduced AI legislation in 2025 and 38 adopted or enacted 100 measures. Clarke's No Biometric Barriers to Housing Act, introduced in April 2025, would ban facial recognition, fingerprint scanners, and other biometric technologies in most federally funded housing. It also directs HUD to study how biometric and algorithmic tenant screening discriminates against renters.

All of her AI bills remain in committee, mainly House Energy and Commerce and House Oversight and Government Reform. The article also points to conflicts in the legislative process, reporting that roughly one in five members of Congress holds investments in AI developers, chipmakers, data centers, or cloud companies, and that about 44 lawmakers with AI holdings sit on committees with jurisdiction over AI policy. It adds that major AI firms spent roughly $7.5 million on federal lobbying in a single recent quarter, with cumulative spending past $37 million since 2024, according to a Project on Government Oversight investigation. The piece does not describe any scheduled vote or next step for Clarke's bills.

Articles.Title: Rep. Yvette Clarke Stands on the Frontlines of AI Legislation - Our Time Press

stories.Headline: Microsoft Is Reportedly Getting Pickier About AI Data Center Deals. Is the Stock a Buy Now?
stories.Summary:
Microsoft may be becoming more selective about the outside data center capacity it rents for artificial intelligence work. On Nov. 5, Bloomberg reported that the software giant has tightened oversight of some projects from neoclouds, which are firms that rent out AI computing capacity, including Nebius Group, IREN and the privately held Nscale. The Financial Times reported the same day that Microsoft will not exercise an option to more than double its Nscale deal at a Texas data center. Microsoft has not confirmed either report, so the details remain unverified.

The reports come as Microsoft's spending has climbed much faster than the cash its business generates. Free cash flow over the last four reported quarters was about $60 billion, down roughly 23% from about $78 billion in the four quarters ended September 2025. Much of the outside capacity arrives through finance leases, and Microsoft counts the full principal value of a lease in capital expenditures when it begins, while the cash is paid over many years. IREN said a customer-requested network design change and vendor timing pushed its goal of over $4 billion in annualized revenue into early 2027. Microsoft also had $364.6 billion in leases that had not yet started as of Sept. 30, mostly for data centers, up from $106.2 billion a year earlier.

Microsoft has not publicly explained the changes beyond what its executives have said in earnings calls. On the fiscal first-quarter call on Oct. 28, CFO Amy Hood said the company would access additional sources of funding when it believed doing so was attractive. A day later, Microsoft agreed to sell $25 billion in notes. Demand does not appear to be the problem, since Azure revenue rose 48% year over year in the fiscal first quarter and management expects 49% to 50% constant-currency growth in the fiscal second quarter.

The article's author, Daniel Sparks, argues that renting less would not quickly ease the free cash flow pressure, and that building more of its own data centers could add to near-term spending. He also says the stock looks expensive, trading near $535 at about 30 times adjusted earnings and roughly 66 times trailing free cash flow, and he has said he would prefer to buy closer to $465. Management expects capital expenditures to exceed $50 billion in the fiscal second quarter and to accelerate after that. The article does not describe any further decisions by Microsoft on these projects.

Articles.Title: Microsoft Is Reportedly Getting Pickier About AI Data Center Deals. Is the Stock a Buy Now?

stories.Headline: ToyBlocks: A controlled world for robot learning and evaluation
stories.Summary:
This is not a breaking news item, and the article carries enough detail to support the full structure, so I'm writing the full piece rather than the short form. Ai2, the Allen Institute for AI, published a blog post on Hugging Face on November 6, 2026, introducing ToyBlocks, a controlled simulation framework for studying robot learning. The framework is the first of what the researchers call FoundationWorlds, environments built around a robot arm and blocks on a tabletop. The authors say the setting is deliberately simple so that researchers can vary training data and model design, repeat tests, and trace why a robot fails at a task.

The article says ToyBlocks automatically generates skills and demonstrations without the time-consuming teleoperation needed on physical robots, in which a person remotely controls the arm. Skills such as pushing a block or flipping it onto another face are trained with reinforcement learning in Isaac Lab, Nvidia's open-source simulation framework, while a task-and-motion planner sequences those skills into full demonstrations. The authors report that the system runs hundreds of plans in parallel on a single graphics processing unit and reaches up to 24 times real-time performance. The framework also supports domain randomization, which varies block size, table height and other physical properties, so researchers can test how well models generalize.

The post credits the Ai2 team behind the work and points to its earlier projects in open robot learning, including MolmoAct 2, MolmoBot and MolmoSpaces. It describes ToyBlocks as built to meet four requirements: realistic physics and appearance, automatic generation of tasks at scale, challenges combining reasoning with dexterity, and broad coverage of possible tasks within the domain. The authors say that a narrow scope makes these requirements achievable, whereas open-ended domains would make them infeasible. They also describe a web interface that lets users connect a frontier model such as Claude and give the robot instructions in natural language.

The evaluations in the post examine how training data affects performance, spatial generalization of vision-language-action models, generalization to new letters and colors, multi-step planning, and transfer to physical robots. The authors note that studies of these action models have reached conflicting conclusions, with some finding them brittle to changes in layout and lighting and others finding them robust. They say the spatial generalization tests show that popular models generalize poorly at first, and that the team improved results and analyzed each technique's contribution, while concluding the problem remains far from solved. The authors describe ToyBlocks as a testbed for continuing that work, and they invite other researchers to design their own tasks and measures within it.

Articles.Title: ToyBlocks: A controlled world for robot learning and evaluation

stories.Headline: Egyptian and Nigerian English join the Open ASR Leaderboard
stories.Summary:
The Hugging Face team announced on November 6, 2026, that Egyptian and Nigerian English accents are joining the Open ASR Leaderboard, a benchmark for speech recognition models. The update follows an earlier addition of private data covering five accents, and a later split for Indian-accented English added with Voice Arena. The new data comes through a collaboration with Liva AI. The article does not give the size of the new Egyptian and Nigerian splits.

The additions expand the leaderboard's private, held-out data, which the team says helps reduce the risk of models being tuned to public test sets. The leaderboard will now report results grouped by Kachru's Three Circles, a framework for classifying English use around the world. Inner Circle accents from the US, UK, Australia and Canada are compared against Outer and Expanding Circle accents from India, Nigeria and Egypt. The team said it will split the Outer and Expanding Circles further as more accents are added. The breakdown idea was credited to Hume AI, which uses a similar approach on its own leaderboard.

Liva AI collects multimodal interaction data through consumer products used by real people. The article says that because Liva owns both the collection environment and distribution, it can build products aimed at specific model weaknesses across domains, industries, languages, modalities and interaction types. The team describes this as giving access to natural, high-context behavior, as opposed to artificially elicited or task-based speech. The article is written by Hugging Face staff, including Eric Bezzam, Ashley Mo and Aoi Otani, and frames the work as part of a continuing effort to broaden accent and language coverage in speech recognition evaluations. The article does not describe a specific timeline beyond the planned split of the Outer and Expanding Circles as more accents join.

Articles.Title: Egyptian and Nigerian English join the Open ASR Leaderboard

stories.Headline: Buoyant Releases Kinference: An Open Source Inference Control Plane for Kubernetes and vLLM
stories.Summary:
Buoyant, the company behind the Linkerd service mesh, has released Kinference, an open source inference control plane for Kubernetes and vLLM. The project, written in Rust and licensed under Apache 2.0, currently sits at version v0.1.0-alpha.7 on GitHub. It sits in front of a fleet of vLLM workers and decides where each incoming request should go, combining routing policies, token rate limits, KV-cache-aware load balancing and per-tenant metrics in one layer. It is aimed at development teams serving many open-weight models to many internal clients.

Kinference runs on any GPU-enabled Kubernetes cluster that operates vLLM and is configured through five Kubernetes custom resource definitions: GatewayBackend, InferencePolicy, InferencePool, InferenceProvider and InferenceWorkerSet. It has two parts, a traffic gateway and an inference handler that exposes a gRPC interface, which returns the chosen endpoint and a possibly modified request body. The handler watches vLLM KV-cache events and engine metrics, using NVIDIA's dynamo-kv-router crate to process cache events. Policies are declarative rules that can match on tenant, requested model, GPU pool state and semantic tags, and they live in git where they can be checked offline with the kinfctl command-line tool. Buoyant's benchmark used three L40S GPUs per pool, with each vLLM pod on one GPU.

Buoyant's own benchmarks compare Kinference against plain Kubernetes Service load balancing, which picks a pod at random for each connection. On a shared-prefix workload, median time-to-first-token fell from 6.88 seconds to 0.31 seconds, a drop of about 95 percent, and peak goodput rose about 7.4 times, from 14.0 to 103.0 requests per minute meeting the latency target. On multiturn traffic, median time-to-first-token fell about 65 percent. On prompts without shared prefixes, the company reported no significant median gain, with 6.92 seconds for the Service baseline against 6.83 seconds for Kinference. These figures are self-reported by the company, and the articles describe them as such.

Articles.Title: Buoyant Releases Kinference: An Open Source Inference Control Plane for Kubernetes and vLLM

stories.Headline: Zyphra ZYFA: FP8 FlashAttention for AMD MI355X, Up to 1.76x Faster
stories.Summary:
Zyphra has released ZYFA, a set of FP8 and BF16 prefill attention kernels for AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs, and published the code under the Apache 2.0 license. The kernels are aimed at long-context prefill, and the article reports that on real model activations the FP8 kernels run between 1.16 and 1.76 times faster than AITER, AMD's default kernel library. ZYFA is described as a drop-in replacement with a flash_attn_func interface, and it runs only on the MI355X, using ROCm 7.2.3 and PyTorch 2.12. The BF16 kernels are written in HIP, while the FP8 kernels are hand-scheduled assembly produced by a Python generator.

The speedup comes from how the work is split across the chip. FP8 matrix instructions run at twice the BF16 peak, but they only accelerate the two matrix products in attention, while the softmax between them runs on the vector unit at the same speed in both precisions. Zyphra reduces the vector cost by writing each FP8 probability with one multiply-add and one integer conversion, cutting softmax vector cycles per block from 896 to 384. Two waves share each SIMD so that one can issue matrix instructions while the other computes probabilities, and the article says the matrix pipe is then busy 86 percent of steady-state cycles, up from 60 percent. Accuracy is addressed by scaling each 64-key block of probabilities by a power of 2 before rounding and dividing by the sum of the rounded values, and against fp64 reference attention the article reports ZYFA's FP8 error at 0.22 times AITER's on Mistral-7B and 0.38 times on Qwen3-8B.

The article attributes the difference between benchmark and real-model gains to clock behavior. The MI355X clock depends on how many operand bits flip, and AITER lets more small probabilities become zeros or subnormals, which switches fewer bits and keeps its clock higher. On a Mistral-7B layer ZYFA runs at 1,628 MHz against AITER's 2,108 MHz, yet still needs fewer cycles overall, and Zyphra recommends benchmarking on real activations at sustained clocks. ZYFA powers the attention engine of the Zyphra Optimization Engine, which runs Zyphra Cloud. The article does not describe any further release plans beyond the technical paper and the open-source code.

Articles.Title: Zyphra ZYFA: FP8 FlashAttention for AMD MI355X, Up to 1.76x Faster

stories.Headline: Pod-Ed: Why Airline AI Needs Better Data Before Smarter Technology
stories.Summary:
Airways Magazine published an episode of its podcast, The Airways Podcast, on November 8, 2026, in which hosts Rohan Anand and Vinay Bhaskara spoke with Tim McMullen, vice president of aviation and travel technology at DataArt. The conversation focused on how airlines are modernizing their technology, and McMullen argued that the promise of artificial intelligence in aviation depends on the quality and accessibility of the underlying data. He said new applications must work alongside older systems that airlines use to handle bookings, schedule crews, and run daily operations. The episode is Season 10, Episode 8 of the series.

According to the discussion, airlines often operate technology stacks that span several decades, from passenger service systems first developed in the 1960s to newer crew scheduling platforms, loyalty databases, and mobile applications. McMullen said airlines cannot simply switch off existing systems and start again, so he favors selective modernization, in which new applications extract and interpret information already held in established platforms. He pointed to passenger service systems from Sabre and Amadeus as reliable infrastructure and noted the risk of older applications unexpectedly going out of service. He also cited AI assistance at United Airlines, Delta Air Lines, and American Airlines as examples of newer tools running alongside older systems, though he was describing the orchestration required rather than assessing any single airline's application.

McMullen was the main voice on these points, and the hosts contributed comparisons. Bhaskara distinguished low-cost carriers seeking efficient, predictable operations from premium carriers pursuing more individualized experiences, and he described the work of connecting different database structures. Anand drew on his time at Southwest Airlines to argue that technology decisions made decades earlier can constrain an airline's commercial strategy as its business changes. McMullen also described DataArt's work on a payment orchestration platform for ZIPAIR, a subsidiary of Japan Airlines, and his view that payment flexibility is part of the passenger experience. He added that data sharing across codeshares and partnerships raises questions about ownership, security and retention, and that such cooperation needs governance and clear rules.

The episode also covered the practical side of AI work and its human effects. McMullen described a workshop with an airline that sorted ideas into immediate improvements, follow-on projects, and larger strategic investments, some of which did not require AI at all. He said DataArt automated a manual process for an unnamed client in about nine weeks and that the work saved 83% of the time spent on it, though that figure is his own account and was not independently verified. On employment, he acknowledged that some businesses may need fewer staff but argued that experienced employees hold institutional knowledge that remains valuable. The articles do not describe any further publication or follow-up beyond the episode itself.

Articles.Title: Pod-Ed: Why Airline AI Needs Better Data Before Smarter Technology

stories.Headline: China AI bust threatens Xi’s ’Wall Street East’ ambitions
stories.Summary:
China's technology stock selloff is threatening President Xi Jinping's plan to turn household savings into a major source of funding for the country's tech sector. The SSE Star 50 index has dropped 40% in less than four months, wiping out at least $480 billion in market value. Losses have spread across companies tied to artificial intelligence, electric vehicles and semiconductor manufacturing. Beijing has responded by mobilising state-backed funds, insurers and regulators to support the market.

Goldman Sachs estimates that AI-related companies make up 42% of China's total stock market capitalisation, with more than 3,000 listed firms generating AI-related revenue. Their combined market value was put at around $10 trillion as of March. Several prominent names have taken heavy losses, with battery maker CATL down 35% this year and robot maker Unitree down by half since its August initial public offering. Shares of Suzhou TFC Communication and Victory Giant Technology have fallen as much as 26% over the past week. The selloff reflects high valuations, domestic competition, higher energy costs, tariffs and the possibility that the United States and Europe could restrict access to Chinese technology.

Weakening domestic demand and the long property crisis are adding to investor concerns. The CSI 300 index has fallen around 21% from its June peak, even after earlier stimulus measures aimed at supporting the economy. China's $21.5 trillion economy remains heavily reliant on exports, and the property downturn continues to weigh on household confidence. The weakness contrasts with gains elsewhere in Asia, where Taiwan's benchmark has risen 56%, South Korea's 36% and Japan's Nikkei 225 more than 25%. The Shanghai Composite remains near 4,000, well below its October 2007 peak of about 6,100.

For Xi, the stakes extend beyond market values. Beijing wants households to invest in equities, especially technology companies, to finance AI infrastructure and reduce reliance on property, which accounts for roughly 70% of household wealth. Repeated market collapses and regulatory interventions have damaged retail investor confidence, and past technology-sector crackdowns have made households cautious. Even after the decline, the STAR 50 trades at about 38 times forward earnings, compared with roughly 20 times for the Nasdaq 100. An extended correction would threaten investor wealth, China's technology ambitions and Xi's wider plan to build a stock-market alternative to the struggling property sector.

Articles.Title: China AI bust threatens Xi’s ’Wall Street East’ ambitions

stories.Headline: Morgan Stanley Sees a Big Opportunity for Itron (ITRI) in the AI Power Boom
stories.Summary:
Morgan Stanley's September 2026 report, titled "AI Beneficiaries: Investing in Second-Order Effects – Update: 100x AI Cultures," argues that companies using AI to raise employee productivity may outperform the firms that build the infrastructure. The bank developed an "AI Productivity Spread," which subtracts growth in average technical employee compensation from growth in revenue per technical employee, and analyzed about 750 public technology companies and roughly 40 million employee records. It concluded that firms with the highest spreads later delivered better stock returns than their peers. The report uses past examples, such as automakers, Walton family retail, Wi-Fi router makers and Netflix, to support the idea that second-order beneficiaries can outlast the first movers.

The report also looks beyond technology to broader corporate profits.
